benchmarks.name: 08_fft_split_fft
benchmarks.input_form: One complex vector. `void fft(std::vector<std::complex<double>> const& x, std::vector<double>& r, std::vector<double>& i)` — forward, unnormalized, negative-exponent DFT of x (length N), written split into r = Re(X) and i = Im(X). The ONLY dimension is N = x.size(); r and i have the same length N and are PRE-SIZED by the caller (the oracle writes r[j]/i[j] without resizing, baseline.hpp:56-57; the driver pre-sizes at cpu.cc:41-42 and cpu.cc:59-61). Values: real and imaginary parts drawn independently uniform in [-1, 1] (cpu.cc:70-71 via fillRand, utilities.hpp:144-159).
benchmarks.min_size: N = 2^k. There is NO positive floor on the scale axis: N = 0 (empty transform) and N = 1 (identity) are mathematically defined and are handled exactly by the validate() oracle (`if (N <= 1) return;`, baseline.hpp:63) — measured deviation 0.000e+00 vs an independent direct DFT at both. They belong to degenerate_cases, not to a size floor. The binding condition is power-of-two-ness, not magnitude. Scale points chosen at N >= 2^6.
benchmarks.max_size: 2^21 = 2097152 — forced by the OPERATION plus the grading invariant, not by the harness. The comparison is absolute (`std::abs(x-y) > 1e-4`, cpu.cc:92 -> utilities.hpp:409-416) while FFT output magnitude scales as sqrt(N). Measured max |correctFft - fftCooleyTookey| (two shipped, mathematically identical oracles, i.e. a pure rounding-order difference): 3.94e-14 @2^6, 3.86e-10 @2^13, 1.40e-09 @2^16, 7.92e-08 @2^18, 2.75e-07 @2^19, 4.13e-07 @2^20, 2.94e-06 @2^21, 6.39e-06 @2^22, 1.06e-05 @2^23. Beyond 2^21 the margin under 1e-4 falls below ~35x, so a correct implementation with a different butterfly order could false-fail. Recommended hard ceiling 2^21; chosen LARGE 2^20 keeps a 242x margin. No harness-imposed maximum exists (ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE is unbounded, enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79).
benchmarks.special_conditions: (1) N MUST be an exact power of two (adopted decision; independently re-confirmed by execution). Both shipped implementations are radix-2: correctFft halves k in a Rosetta DIF loop and bit-reverses with `>> (32 - m)`, m = (unsigned)log2(N) (baseline.hpp:20, 36, 45); fftCooleyTookey recurses on N/2 and writes only x[k] and x[k+N/2] for k < N/2 (baseline.hpp:63, 82), silently dropping the tail element at odd N. Measured against an independent O(N^2) DFT (sign=-1, unnormalized) with the driver's own fillRand(-1,1) inputs: N=3 dev 1.626 (BOTH functions, identically wrong), N=5 dev 2.136 (both), N=6 dev 1.530 / 3.321, N=7 dev 1.861 / 2.771 — all 4-5 orders of magnitude above the 1e-4 pass threshold. Powers of two: N=2 1.11e-16, N=4 3.1e-16, N=8 5.0e-15, N=16 2.5e-14, N=64 2.8e-13 — all correct. (2) correctFft additionally performs HEAP OUT-OF-BOUNDS WRITES at N = 5, 7, 31 (ASan-proven in thesis/docs/fft-family-consistency.md:12, :557; abort-vs-silent-corruption is allocation-layout dependent — in my own -O3 probes it did not abort). fftCooleyTookey is memory-safe at every N but silently wrong off powers of two. (3) r and i must already have size N. (4) Grading tolerance is an ABSOLUTE 1e-4 (cpu.cc:92) while |X_k| grows like sqrt(N) — this caps how large N may be before the tolerance stops discriminating correct implementations (see max_size).
benchmarks.size_semantics: TEST_SIZE / ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE is the ELEMENT COUNT N of the complex input vector (and of both output vectors). It is not a side length, not a log2 exponent, and nothing is derived from it (no nnz, no point count). Driver default TEST_SIZE = 1024 (cpu.cc:57); perf-run DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE = (1<<17) (drivers/problem-sizes.json, 08_fft_split_fft/serial).
benchmarks.complexity: O(N log N) time for both oracles (log2 N butterfly stages of N/2 butterflies each, plus an O(N) bit-reversal permutation in correctFft). fftCooleyTookey is the recursive variant: it additionally allocates two vectors of N/2^(d+1) complex<double> at every node of the recursion tree, i.e. Theta(N log N) allocation traffic and Theta(N) peak auxiliary memory (~2N complex doubles live at the deepest point). Measured scaling matches N log N: correctFft 0.0075 s @2^16 -> 0.284 s @2^20 -> 3.03 s @2^23 (quiet host).
benchmarks.domain_rationale: A radix-2 FFT has exactly one structural parameter, s = log2(N) = the number of butterfly stages, and one implementation-relevant secondary axis, where the working set (32N bytes: 16N for the complex input plus 16N for the two double output arrays) sits in the memory hierarchy. The three scale points are chosen roughly geometric in s and in three distinct memory regimes. SMALL 2^6 = 64: s = 6 stages, 2 KB working set, entirely L1/register resident. Six stages is the smallest count at which the bit-reversal permutation is a substantially non-identity map (only palindromic 6-bit indices are fixed) and at which a wrong stage order or a wrong twiddle recurrence is visible; it sits clearly above the degenerate points 0/1/2, which are a separate axis. At this size the direct O(N^2) DFT is a mathematically identical formulation of the same operation, so this point tests the transform's definition rather than any scaling strategy. MEDIUM 2^13 = 8192: s = 13, 256 KB working set — past L1 (48 KB) and inside a typical private L2. This is the first regime in which the strided butterfly access pattern costs anything and in which twiddle handling (recompute per butterfly vs. table) becomes a real distinction. It is also 8x the driver's own default validate TEST_SIZE of 1024 (cpu.cc:57), i.e. genuinely beyond what the shipped test already covers. LARGE 2^20 = 1048576: s = 20, 32 MB working set — past the 24 MB LLC of the measurement host, therefore firmly DRAM-bound, and 8x the perf driver's configured DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE of 2^17 (drivers/problem-sizes.json). Its upper bound is set by two measured constraints, the tighter of which wins: (a) the 10 s serial-oracle budget, satisfied with large margin (1.55 s median), and (b) the absolute 1e-4 tolerance against sqrt(N)-growing output magnitudes, which leaves 242x margin at 2^20 but only 34x at 2^21 and 9.4x at 2^23. All three points are powers of two by the adopted family decision, re-confirmed by execution. NOTHING here is derived from any candidate or model output: the stage count, the memory-regime boundaries, the O(N log N) cost model and the absolute-epsilon/sqrt(N) interaction are all properties of the operation, its specified domain and the shipped grading invariant.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases: Mathematically DEFINED for this operation and correctly handled by the validate() oracle (measured deviation vs an independent direct DFT, fillRand[-1,1] inputs): N = 0 — empty transform, output r and i empty; deviation 0.000e+00; fftCooleyTookey returns immediately (baseline.hpp:63). (correctFft at N=0 computes (unsigned)std::log2(0) = (unsigned)(-inf), formally UB, but performs no memory access because every loop bound is 0; it is not the grading oracle.) N = 1 — identity, X[0] = x[0]; deviation 0.000e+00; fftCooleyTookey early-returns. (correctFft at N=1 evaluates `>> (32 - 0)`, formal shift-by-32 UB, benign on x86 and numerically exact; again not the grading oracle.) N = 2 — smallest non-trivial radix-2 case, a single butterfly, X = [x0+x1, x0-x1]; deviation 1.110e-16. Value-domain degeneracies, defined at ANY power-of-two N: all-zeros input -> spectrum identically zero; constant input c -> X[0] = N*c and X[k] = 0 elsewhere (an exact-cancellation stress case for the absolute 1e-4 test); purely real input -> conjugate-symmetric spectrum, i[0] = i[N/2] = 0 (the worked example in the prompt is exactly this case). NOT a degenerate case of the operation: the extreme_values fill (+/-DBL_MAX, enhanced-fill.hpp:129-141) overflows to Inf/NaN inside the butterflies; that is a value-range artifact of the fill pattern, decided by the comparator's non-finite-reference rule (utilities.hpp:330-334, 362-372), and must not be read as a statement about the FFT's domain. NON-power-of-two sizes (3, 5, 6, 7, 31, ...) are NOT degenerate cases — they are simply OUTSIDE the implemented domain and produce silently wrong results (and, in correctFft, heap OOB writes).

benchmarks.name: 09_fft_fft_out_of_place
benchmarks.input_form: One-dimensional complex signal. `void fft(std::vector<std::complex<double>> const& x, std::vector<std::complex<double>> &output)` — unnormalized forward DFT with negative exponent, X[k] = sum_n x[n]·e^(-2*pi*i*k*n/N), natural (not bit-reversed) index order on both sides, computed OUT OF PLACE into `output`. Exactly ONE relevant dimension: N = x.size() (number of complex samples). The driver pre-sizes `output` to the same N and fills the input from two independent double vectors `real`, `imag` ~ U[-1,1] combined into complex (cpu.cc:59-60, 68-75). No matrix shape, no nnz, no point count.
benchmarks.min_size: N = 1 (= 2^0). Smallest in-domain size: the radix-2 domain is {2^k, k >= 0}, and at N=1 the transform is the identity X[0] = x[0], which both baselines produce correctly (measured: |cooley - directDFT| = 0.000e+00, |correctFft - directDFT| = 0.000e+00). N = 0 is ALSO mathematically defined (DFT of the empty sequence is the empty sequence; measured exit 0, sanitizer-clean, empty output) but 0 is not a power of two, so it is recorded as a degenerate case, NOT as the size floor. There is no operational reason for a floor above 1.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — forced by the HARNESS, not by the operation: `max_spec_size: 4096` in thesis/config/config.yaml:572 (module default thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:138), enforced as a hard reject in specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). A second, softer harness bound is `run_timeout_seconds: 60` (config.yaml:613) per differential run; a run executes the oracle MAX_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS = 2 times (cpu.cc:65 + utilities.hpp:25-27), so the 2^22 scale point consumes ~4.2 s of the 60 s on oracle time alone in the clean case. The operation itself imposes no upper limit beyond the power-of-two lattice and 32-bit addressability of the bit-reversal (baseline.hpp:45-49 works up to N = 2^32).
benchmarks.special_conditions:
1) N MUST be a power of two (N = 2^k, k >= 0). Both baselines are radix-2 and are the only definition of "correct" the pipeline has. MEASURED receipts at the pipeline flags (-O3, no sanitizer): N=3 -> both baselines deviate from a direct O(N^2) DFT by 1.387 (max|X| = 2.09), exit 0, silent; N=6 -> 2.471 / 1.428, silent; N=12 -> 5.561 / 4.075, silent; N=1000 (EVEN, non-power-of-two) -> `double free or corruption (!prev)`, exit 134 at plain -O3. So the restriction is NOT "odd N only" — every non-power-of-two N is invalid (the DIF loop `k >>= 1` reaches an odd k, after which `b = a + k` (baseline.hpp:32-35) writes past the end). Mechanism in the validation oracle is different but equally fatal: the even/odd split of size floor(N/2) drops x[N-1] at odd N (baseline.hpp:63-69).
2) x.size() == output.size(); the driver pre-sizes `output` (cpu.cc:59-60 / :40) and the prompt does not say whether the callee may resize. Any chosen size must be applied to BOTH vectors.
3) Value range must keep sum_n x[n] finite. The `extreme_values` fill pattern (+/-DBL_MAX, enhanced-fill.hpp:128-141, :199-200) is OUT of the value domain: MEASURED at N=1024 the oracle output is 511 NaN + 1 inf + 512 finite cells, and the driver's comparison `std::abs(correct-test) > 1e-4` (cpu.cc:88) is FALSE for a NaN operand, so half the output is simply not judged. The driver's own range U[-1,1] (cpu.cc:68-69) is safe at every size tested.
benchmarks.size_semantics: The size number is a plain ELEMENT COUNT: N = number of complex<double> samples = x.size() = output.size(). Not a side length, not an nnz seed, nothing derived. Evidence: cpu.cc:59 `std::vector<std::complex<double>> x(TEST_SIZE), correct(TEST_SIZE), test(TEST_SIZE);` and cpu.cc:60 `std::vector<double> real(TEST_SIZE), imag(TEST_SIZE);` — the fill vectors have the same length, one double each for the real and the imaginary part, so one spec "size" = one complex sample. ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE overrides exactly this number (cpu.cc:57 `ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024)`, enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). The separate perf path uses DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (cpu.cc:39-42), which the enhanced stage pins to (1<<4) and the correctness stage to (1<<8) (thesis/evaluation/tools.py:44) — it does not affect validate().
benchmarks.large: 4194304 (= 2^22). Operation- and budget-derived; MEASURED fftCooleyTookey (the grading oracle) 2.10 s median of 3, correctFft 1.03 s median of 3, both inside the 10 s budget. NOTE: the currently configured harness cap max_spec_size = 4096 (see max_size) forbids this value; under the cap the largest admissible power of two is 4096 (fftCooleyTookey 1.31 ms median of 5), which is still only 128 KiB per array and therefore CANNOT reach the out-of-cache regime that makes a large scale point meaningful for an FFT.
benchmarks.complexity: Theta(N log N) for both baselines. correctFft (baseline.hpp:16-56, perf reference in best()): iterative radix-2 decimation-in-frequency, (N/2)·log2(N) butterflies plus one N-element bit-reversal permutation pass. fftCooleyTookey (baseline.hpp:58-81, the actual GRADING oracle in validate()): recursive radix-2 decimation-in-time, same butterfly count but two heap allocations per recursion node, i.e. Theta(N) allocations and Theta(N log N) extra memory traffic — measured ~2x slower than correctFft at 2^20 and ~4.5x at 2^23. Measured scaling is consistent with N log N plus a cache-miss term: N=2^10 -> 0.22 ms, 2^14 -> 4.19 ms, 2^17 -> 55.2 ms, 2^20 -> 0.41 s, 2^21 -> 0.66 s, 2^22 -> 2.10 s, 2^23 -> 10.99 s, 2^24 -> 207 s (fftCooleyTookey medians).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
DOMAIN. The operation is the forward DFT, defined for every N >= 0. The two baselines that define "correct" here are both radix-2, so the *specified* domain (adopted decision) is N = 2^k. min_size is therefore 1 = 2^0, and no floor above that is justified: N=1 is the identity transform and both baselines give it exactly.

SMALL = 8 = 2^3. Smallest power of two at which the radix-2 transform has its complete structure and therefore discriminative power: (a) 3 butterfly stages, (b) an irrational twiddle set — W_8^1 = (sqrt2/2)(1-i); at N=4 the twiddles are exactly {1, -i}, so an implementation that hard-codes +/-1/+/-i passes N<=4 while being no FFT at all, (c) a bit-reversal permutation with more than one transposition (N=8: 1<->4 and 3<->6; N=4: only 1<->2). It is additionally the size of the operation's own worked example (baseline.hpp:13-14 / prompt). Measured agreement with a direct O(N^2) DFT at N=8: 6.66e-16 (oracle) / 1.11e-15 (perf reference).

MEDIUM = 1024 = 2^10. Ten stages, recursion depth 10 for the DIT oracle. This is the operation's own stock validation size (cpu.cc:57), i.e. the size at which the fixed ABSOLUTE epsilon 1e-4 (cpu.cc:88) was calibrated. Both complex arrays are 16 KiB, so the transform is L1-resident and purely arithmetic — no memory-hierarchy effects. Measured round-off headroom here is nine orders: |oracle - directDFT| = 1.35e-13 against eps = 1e-4, with max|X[k]| = 76.

LARGE = 4194304 = 2^22. Qualitatively different regime: 22 stages, 64 MiB per complex array — far beyond any L3 — so the bit-reversed / stride-2^k access pattern is fully memory-bound, and the DIT oracle's Theta(N) allocations dominate. Two constraints pinned the exact value, both measured: (i) the 10 s budget — 2^23 needs 10.99 s in the grading oracle, 2^24 needs 207 s; (ii) epsilon headroom — the two baselines' mutual deviation grows as roughly sqrt(N·log N): 1.39e-9 (2^16), 7.92e-8 (2^18), 3.70e-7 (2^20), 2.83e-6 (2^21), 5.87e-6 (2^22) against the fixed absolute eps = 1e-4. At 2^22 the margin is still ~17x, i.e. the scale point is gradeable; extrapolating, the fixed absolute epsilon would be exhausted near 2^30, so 2^22 is safely inside. Note that because max|X[k]| grows like sqrt(N) (measured 4.17 at N=8, 76 at 2^10, 6563 at 2^22), the absolute epsilon is an ever tighter RELATIVE tolerance — ~5e-8 relative at LARGE. This is a genuine property of the operation and one more reason not to push LARGE further.

The three points are 2^3 / 2^10 / 2^22 — structure-complete, calibration/in-cache, out-of-cache — each following from the radix-2 FFT itself, not from any observed candidate code.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
DEFINED and usable (all executed this session at the pipeline flags):
- N = 0 (empty input): DFT of the empty sequence is the empty sequence. Both baselines return without writing; exit 0, ASan+UBSan clean. Not a power of two, so it sits outside the special condition while remaining mathematically defined. Note for omp/mpi runs (config.yaml:597 covers all three): mpirun -np 4 on an empty input is a rank-count-vs-size edge, not a size-domain violation.
- N = 1 (= 2^0, in-domain): identity, X[0] = x[0]. Grading oracle exact (deviation 0.000e+00). The perf reference correctFft is value-correct but triggers formal UB (shift exponent 32, baseline.hpp:49) — receipt above; the differential gate forwards correctFft through validate(), so this UB is on the live path.
- N = 2 (= 2^1): the single-butterfly case, X = [x0+x1, x0-x1]; exact (1.11e-16).
- all_zeros: X == 0 for every N. Defined, but ZERO discriminative power — any implementation that writes zeros passes.
- all_same / constant c: X[0] = N·c, X[k] = 0 otherwise. Defined and strong — it pins the normalization (no 1/N, no 1/sqrt(N)) with a single cell.
- impulse (x = delta_0): X[k] = x[0] for all k. Defined; pins normalization exactly and exposes a missing bit-reversal permutation.
- ascending / descending / alternating / duplicate_at / sorted_except_one: all inside U[-1,1]-scale magnitudes, all defined.
NOT usable (must be excluded, measured):
- extreme_values (+/-DBL_MAX): the N-term sum overflows. At N=1024 the oracle output is 511 NaN + 1 inf + 512 finite, and cpu.cc:88's `std::abs(a-b) > 1e-4` is FALSE on NaN, so the verdict is decided by whichever finite cells remain. Mathematically undefined AND silently mis-graded.
- spike_at(k) (DBL_MAX/2 on the real part): same overflow family; every output bin receives the spike, magnitudes ~N·DBL_MAX/2 -> inf. Same NaN-tolerance problem. Treat as out of the value domain unless the range is overridden.
NOT degenerate cases, but out-of-domain (do not file them here): every non-power-of-two N (3, 5, 6, 7, 12, 1000, ...) — silent O(1) wrongness or heap corruption, see special_conditions.
benchmarks.pending_fix:
YES — this row is PROVISIONAL on four decisions that are documented but not implemented:
1) The power-of-two restriction itself. The adopted decision ("powers of two only") is not written into the prompt (all three variants still say nothing about N), not enforced in the spec generator, and contradicted by the harness default `static_base_sizes: [0, 1, 2, 7]` (specs.py:134) — 7 is out of domain for this benchmark. Until a power-of-two filter exists at spec generation, small/medium/large can be honoured but the static base specs cannot.
2) The differential gate's blind spot. The gate compares correctFft (through validate()) against fftCooleyTookey; MEASURED here, the two are bit-identical-wrong at N=3 (deviation between them 0.000e+00 while both are 1.387 away from the true DFT), so the gate cannot see silent out-of-domain wrongness at N=3. Whether the domain is restricted or the oracles generalised is still open (thesis/docs/fft-family-consistency.md, deviation #6).
3) NaN-tolerant comparison at cpu.cc:88. 4) max_spec_size = 4096 (config.yaml:572). LARGE = 2^22 requires raising it. Without that change the out-of-cache regime is unreachable and the "large" scale point degenerates into a second medium.
Also unfixed (cosmetic, does not affect sizing): the prompt's worked example prints -2.42421 at k=1 where the true value is -(1+sqrt2) = -2.414213562373095 (thesis/docs/fft-family-consistency.md, deviation #1).

benchmarks.name: 10_geometry_convex_hull
benchmarks.input_form: One unordered multiset of n 2-D points: `std::vector<Point> const& points` with `struct Point { double x, y; }` (the struct comes from the LLM-generated code — it is given verbatim in all three prompts). Exactly ONE size dimension: n = number of points. The driver never hands the operation a matrix, a side length or a derived nnz. Construction in the driver: two SEPARATE length-n `std::vector<double>` fill sites, `x` and `y`, both filled over the range (-1000.0, 1000.0), then zipped `points[i] = {x[i], y[i]}` (cpu.cc:29-39 for the timed path, cpu.cc:74-84 for validate). Coordinate domain under the driver's own generator: i.i.d. uniform in [-1000, 1000] per coordinate, drawn from unseeded `rand()` (utilities.hpp:144-159). Output: `std::vector<Point> &hull` = the hull VERTICES. Vertex ORDER is irrelevant (validate lexicographically sorts both lists before comparing, cpu.cc:98-103) but the vertex COUNT must match the oracle exactly (cpu.cc:95).
benchmarks.min_size: 0 — there is no size floor. The oracle is total on n >= 0: `if (points.size() < 3) { hull = points; return; }` (baseline.hpp:13-16) makes n = 0, 1, 2 well-defined, non-crashing AND mathematically correct (hull of the empty set = empty; of 1 point = that point; of 2 distinct points = the 2-point segment). Verified by execution: n=0 -> hull.size()==0; n=1 -> 1; n=2 -> 2 (both input points, returned in input order — harmless because validate sorts). For the SCALE axis the smallest size at which the hull is a genuine polygon and the monotone chain actually executes is n = 3 (verified: triangle -> 3 vertices). Sizes 0/1/2 therefore belong on the degenerate axis, not to a size floor — and they are unavoidable anyway: static_base_sizes = [0, 1, 2, 7] (thesis/config/config.yaml:562).
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — HARNESS-FORCED, not operation-forced. thesis/config/config.yaml:572 sets `max_spec_size: 4096` and thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 rejects any spec with `size > max_size` ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). The operation itself has no upper bound; the 10 s budget puts the true ceiling at n approx 16-24M (measured). CONSEQUENCE THAT MUST BE READ: under the CURRENT config, MEDIUM (120001) and LARGE (4800001) are unreachable and the ladder collapses to n <= 4096, i.e. roughly SMALL only. If the cap is not raised for this benchmark, the reachable in-cap ladder consistent with the same reasoning is 61 / 509 / 4093 (odd, ratio approx 8, all L1/L2-resident — it can still separate correctness conventions but can no longer separate asymptotic classes or memory regimes). The three-rung ladder above is the operation+budget answer the table asks for; the 4096 cap is a configuration decision layered on top of it.
benchmarks.special_conditions:
(1) NO structural precondition: no power of two, no divisibility, no minimum point count, no ordering, no distinctness. Any n >= 0 and any finite coordinate pair is in the domain. This is the opposite of the fft family — nothing here privileges 2^k, and every size the base driver uses (1<<14, 1024) is a power of two, so the power-of-two sublattice is the only part of the domain currently exercised.
(2) COORDINATE MAGNITUDE is a real but currently UNWRITTEN precondition. The orientation predicate `(c.x-a.x)*(b.y-a.y) - (c.y-a.y)*(b.x-a.x) > 0` (baseline.hpp:24-25) is evaluated in plain double. Once the coordinate dynamic range exceeds 2^53 the two products round to the same double, the difference cancels to exactly 0, the strict `> 0` test reports "not a turn", and a genuine hull vertex is popped — the oracle then returns a "hull" that does not contain all input points (thesis/docs/oracle-correctness-audit.md:189/454, BL-19, class D, "blocker before full run"). Under the driver's own generator ([-1000,1000]) this can never trigger; the enhanced `spike_at` pattern (x[k]=y[k]=DBL_MAX/2 at the SAME k in both fill sites) triggers it deliberately.
(3) CONVENTION silently enforced by the oracle and fully observable through the validator: the orientation test is STRICT, so points lying exactly on a hull edge but not at a corner are EXCLUDED (minimal vertex set). Verified: [(0,0),(2,0),(2,2),(0,2),(1,0)] -> 4 vertices, the edge midpoint dropped. The competing "keep all boundary points" convention is equally common and the prompt pins neither.
(4) GRADING INVARIANT: `test.size() != correct.size()` is an immediate fail (cpu.cc:95); otherwise both lists are lexicographically sorted (cpu.cc:98-103) and compared elementwise with absolute epsilon 1e-6 on x and y (cpu.cc:105). Since hull vertices are verbatim copies of input points (no arithmetic on the output), the epsilon is effectively an exact test — this benchmark is a SET/COUNT test, not a numeric-tolerance test. Note it does NOT use the shared `fequal`/`reportAndCompare*` helpers, so the concurrent non-finite-comparator rework of drivers/cpp/utilities.hpp does not touch this benchmark's grading.
benchmarks.size_semantics: size = n = the number of input points (element count), one Point per element. NOT a side length, NOT a derived nnz. Caveat for the spec machinery: thesis/enhanced_tests/benchmark_shapes.json records this benchmark as `fill_sites: 2`, `elements_per_site: ["n","n"]`, `total_elements: "n + n"`, because n points are produced by two length-n double fills — but the benchmark's own domain axis is still the single number n. In the timed path n = DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE = (1<<14) = 16384 (drivers/problem-sizes.json:92-95); in validate n = TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024), i.e. 1024 unless -DENHANCED_TEST_SIZE overrides it (cpu.cc:63, enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79).
benchmarks.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) extra space. Sort-dominated: `pointsSorted = points` (a full O(n) copy, baseline.hpp:18) followed by `std::sort` with a lexicographic (x, then y) comparator (baseline.hpp:20-22). The two monotone chains are amortised O(n): the single loop i = 2..n-1 pushes each point onto the upper chain once and onto the lower chain once, and each can be popped at most once (baseline.hpp:35-50). Output size is data-dependent: for uniform points in a rectangle E[h] = Theta(log n) (Renyi-Sulanke, approx (8/3)*ln n) — measured 19-23 at n=3001, 28-33 at n=120001, 41-45 at n=4,800,001, matching the prediction (21 / 31 / 41).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
Derived ONLY from the operation, its domain, its complexity and the 10 s budget — no candidate code was read or consulted.

min_size = 0 follows from the oracle being total (baseline.hpp:13-16) and from the hull being mathematically defined for the empty set, a single point and a pair. Sizes 0/1/2 are therefore degenerate-axis entries, not a floor.

No special condition constrains n, so the scale ladder is free. Three choices were made, each from a property of the operation:

(a) NON-POWER-OF-TWO, ODD sizes. Convex hull imposes no radix or divisibility structure (unlike fft), so the domain is all of N — yet every size the base driver ever uses is a power of two ((1<<14) timed, 1024 in validate). Choosing ODD n means every even chunking (OpenMP static schedule, MPI even split over ranks, divide-and-conquer halving in a Chan/QuickHull-style implementation) necessarily leaves a ragged tail. That path is part of the operation's domain and is currently never exercised. The choice is a property of the size axis alone; it cannot be candidate-adaptive because it is made before any candidate exists.

(b) GEOMETRIC LADDER, ratio 40 each step (3001 -> 120001 -> 4800001, spanning x1600 approx 3.2 decades). With an O(n log n) operation whose output only grows as log n, the interesting axis is exactly how far the discarded-point fraction and the memory behaviour move; a x40 step is large enough that each rung sits in a different regime and small enough that three rungs still cover three decades.

(c) EACH RUNG LANDS IN A DIFFERENT MEMORY REGIME, because the cost is a sort and the sort's cost is where the data lives:
  - SMALL n = 3001: 48 KB per Point array, 96 KB with the oracle's internal copy -> resident in L2. Pure-algorithm scale, no memory effects. E[h] approx 21 of 3001 points, i.e. ~99.3 % of points are discarded, so the amortised pop path runs thousands of times — the hull is a genuine polygon with a double-digit vertex count, which is what separates a correct chain from a broken one. Also small enough that even an O(n*h) gift-wrapping candidate (approx 63k orientation tests) finishes instantly, so SMALL isolates CORRECTNESS from performance.
  - MEDIUM n = 120001: 1.9 MB per array, 3.8 MB total -> out of L2, inside L3. An O(n*h) candidate does approx 3.7M orientation tests — still fast, so MEDIUM still isolates correctness, but the input is now large enough that any chunked/recursive/parallel decomposition really splits into many pieces (and, being odd, into unequal ones).
  - LARGE n = 4800001: 77 MB per array, 154 MB with the oracle's copy -> at least 4x any plausible L3 (16-32 MB), so the sort is decisively DRAM-bound and the full O(n log n) term is visible. This is the smallest of the candidate sizes for which that is unambiguously true, which is why it was preferred over 1.2M (only ~2x L3, marginal). An O(n^2) candidate needs approx 2.3e13 operations here, i.e. it hangs rather than merely slows — LARGE separates asymptotic classes decisively.

LARGE also had to satisfy the budget, and does: measured 1.94 s median for one oracle call, approx 5x inside the 10 s ceiling (see budget_adjustment for the bracketing that fixed the ceiling at n approx 16-24M).

Degenerate configurations (collinear, all-identical, duplicates, extreme magnitudes) are deliberately NOT folded into these three numbers — they are their own axis and are listed in degenerate_cases.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
All of the following are MATHEMATICALLY DEFINED for this operation and all were checked by executing the oracle (scratch probe, pipeline flags):
- n = 0 (empty point set): hull = empty. Oracle: size 0. Correct. Always exercised (static_base_sizes).
- n = 1: hull = that point. Oracle: size 1. Correct.
- n = 2 distinct points: hull = the degenerate segment, 2 vertices. Oracle: size 2 (returned in INPUT order, harmless because validate sorts). Correct. NOTE: this is the exact point where the family identity perimeter(hull(P)) breaks against 11_geometry_convex_hull_perimeter, which returns 0 for the same configuration (audit :186).
- n = 3 non-collinear: hull = the triangle, 3 vertices. Oracle: 3. Correct. Smallest size at which the chain actually runs.
- All points collinear, n >= 3: hull = the segment, 2 vertices (the two extremes). Oracle: 2, verified for y=x and for a vertical line. Correct under the minimal-vertex convention the oracle implements; a model keeping the intermediate collinear points fails. Reached by enhanced patterns ascending, descending, alternating, sorted_except_one, extreme_values (see custom_input_construction_needed).
- All points identical, n >= 2: hull = that single point, 1 vertex. ORACLE IS WRONG HERE: it returns the point TWICE (size 2) for n >= 3 (verified: 3 and 10 identical points -> hull.size()==2, both entries (3,4)) and also twice for n == 2 via the passthrough. A model returning the mathematically correct single vertex FAILS on the size check at cpu.cc:95. Reached by all_zeros and all_same.
- Duplicated points in a non-degenerate cloud (a repeated hull corner, or a repeated interior point): hull is unchanged (a set has no multiplicity). Oracle: correct in both cases (verified: square + duplicated corner -> 4; square + duplicated interior point -> 4). Reached by duplicate_at.
- Point exactly on a hull edge (not a corner): oracle EXCLUDES it (verified: square + edge midpoint -> 4). Defined but convention-dependent; the prompt pins nothing.
- Points in convex position (all n on a circle/convex polygon): hull = all n points, h = n. Fully defined, the worst case for the pop loop and for any parallel merge, and NOT reachable through any current fill pattern — this is the strongest argument for a custom construction.
- Extreme coordinate magnitudes (extreme_values, spike_at): defined mathematically, but OUT OF THE ORACLE'S RELIABLE DOMAIN — above a 2^53 dynamic range the double orientation predicate cancels and the oracle returns a hull that does not contain all the input points (audit BL-19). extreme_values happens to be harmless here only because it collapses the cloud to 2 distinct points; spike_at is not harmless.
Note on the SCALE axis: none of the above is a scale entry. small/medium/large are all non-degenerate uniform-random clouds.

benchmarks.name: 11_geometry_convex_hull_perimeter
benchmarks.input_form: One `std::vector<Point>` of n 2-D points, `struct Point { double x, y; }` (the struct comes from the prompt, not from utilities.hpp). The only dimension is n = the number of points. The driver builds it from two independent `double` vectors of length n filled over [-1000.0, 1000.0] and zipped into points[i] = {x[i], y[i]} — i.e. 2 fill sites, 2n scalars, uniform over the square [-1000,1000]^2. Output is a single `double` (the closed hull perimeter), compared with an ABSOLUTE epsilon of 1e-6.
benchmarks.min_size: 3 for the SCALE axis (smallest n at which "the smallest convex polygon that contains all the points" can be a polygon at all). The oracle accepts n = 0, 1, 2 and returns 0 — those are degenerate cases, not a size floor, and are NOT forbidden.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED BY THE HARNESS: thesis/config/config.yaml:572 `max_spec_size: 4096`, enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-295 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). The operation itself has no maximum, and the 10 s runtime budget would allow n ~ 3e7 (measured 4.98 s at n = 2e7). The harness cap binds four orders of magnitude below the time budget.
benchmarks.special_conditions: No structural precondition: no power of two, no sortedness, no matrix form; any n >= 0 with finite doubles is accepted. Two non-structural conditions bind the SCALE axis: (1) the points must be in general position (not all collinear) — the driver calls ENHANCED_FILL twice with the SAME pattern (cpu.cc:79-80), so every deterministic pattern sets x[i] == y[i] and puts every point on the line y = x; the hull collapses to a segment and the benchmark then measures the degenerate convention, not the hull algorithm (verified: n=16 'ascending' -> 5656.8542494924 = 2*sqrt(2)*2000 exactly). Only `random` (and the random-based duplicate_at/spike_at) yields a genuine 2-D hull. (2) coordinate dynamic range must stay below ~2^53 relative, otherwise the strict orientation predicate `(c.x-a.x)*(b.y-a.y) - (c.y-a.y)*(b.x-a.x) > 0` (baseline.hpp:24-26) cancels to exactly 0 in double and real hull vertices are popped (audit class D; the sibling geometry/10's extreme_values specs were gated numerically_unstable in the pilot).
benchmarks.size_semantics: n = element count = number of 2-D points. TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:67, `ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024)`) IS n; `ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE` overrides it directly (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). Nothing is derived from it — no side length, no nnz. thesis/enhanced_tests/benchmark_shapes.json confirms elements_per_site = ["n","n"], fill_sites = 2, total_elements = "n + n", explicit_values_supported = false.
benchmarks.complexity: O(n log n) time, dominated by `std::sort` over the n points (baseline.hpp:20-22); the monotone chain is one O(n) pass with amortised O(1) stack work per point (baseline.hpp:40-56) and the perimeter sum is O(h) with h = hull vertices. O(n) extra space (the `pointsSorted` copy plus the two hull stacks). Measured scaling is consistent: 256 -> 4096 (16x n) = 42 us -> 649 us (15.5x); 1e6 -> 1e7 (10x n) = 0.281 s -> 2.71 s (9.6x).
benchmarks.domain_rationale: The size number is a raw point count, the cost is O(n log n) and the OUTPUT is one scalar, so wall time is not the informative scale variable — the informative variable is how much of the input the algorithm has to prune. For points uniform in a square (exactly what the driver's two independent fillRand calls over [-1000,1000] produce), the expected hull vertex count grows only logarithmically, E[h] ~ (8/3)*ln n (Renyi-Sulanke). That gives three genuinely different regimes inside the permitted domain: SMALL n=16 -> E[h] ~ 7.4, roughly half the input is on the hull, the pruning stack barely grows and an O(n*h) gift-wrapping transcription of the prompt is indistinguishable in cost from a monotone chain; MEDIUM n=256 -> E[h] ~ 14.8, ~94% of points must be discarded, so the sort dominates the scan and the prune loop does real work while the input (4 KB) is still L1-resident, isolating the algorithmic regime change without a memory-hierarchy confound; LARGE n=4096 -> E[h] ~ 22.2, only 0.54% of points survive, pruning is essentially the whole algorithm, and the working set (points 64 KB + the oracle's internal copy 64 KB = 128 KB) exceeds a typical 32 KB L1 for the first time. The ladder is evenly log-spaced at 16x per step. SMALL is deliberately set above 7, the largest configured static base size (config.yaml:562 static_base_sizes [0,1,2,7]), so it contributes a new scale point instead of duplicating base coverage, and comfortably above the n>=3 polygon minimum. No power-of-two condition exists for this benchmark (unlike the fft family) — any n in [3, 4096] is a valid input; the 16x steps are only an even log spacing. None of the three points was derived from any candidate or model code: they come from the Renyi-Sulanke h/n regimes, the O(n log n) cost model, the L1 working-set boundary, and the harness's own size ceiling.

benchmarks.name: 12_geometry_smallest_triangle
benchmarks.input_form: One flat vector of n points in R^2: `std::vector<Point> points`, `struct Point { double x, y; }` (the struct is supplied by the PROMPT preamble, not by utilities.hpp). The driver builds it from two independent coordinate vectors: `x`, `y` each of length n, filled i.i.d. uniform on [-1000, 1000] by `fillRand` via `ENHANCED_FILL` (cpu.cc:79-80, utilities.hpp:144-159, unseeded `rand()`), then `points[i] = {x[i], y[i]}` (cpu.cc:86-89). No ordering, no distinctness, no structural requirement of any kind. The only relevant dimension is n = the point count. Output: a single scalar `double` (an area), compared with an ABSOLUTE tolerance of 1e-4 (cpu.cc:99 -> utilities.hpp:488-491).
benchmarks.min_size: 3 points (adopted decision, and independently what the oracle's own guard marks). Below 3 there is no triple at all, so "the minimum over all triangles" is a minimum over an empty family and is not defined by the operation. The oracle nevertheless returns 0.0 for n = 0, 1, 2 (baseline.hpp:13-15; verified by execution: n=0 -> 0, n=1 -> 0, n=2 -> 0). That 0 is an implementation convention, not a mathematical value, and the prompt never states it — so n<3 belongs in degenerate_cases, not in the scale axis.
benchmarks.max_size: none forced by the harness (ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE is an arbitrary compile-time integer and the container has ample memory — n points cost 32n bytes, so even n = 1e6 is 32 MB). The effective ceiling is the operation itself: C(n,3) at 1.83 ns/triple puts the 10 s budget at n ~ 3200, and the driver's absolute 1e-4 tolerance puts the discriminative ceiling at n ~ 1024 with the default +-1000 range (or n ~ 2048-3000 with value_range widened to +-1e5, beyond which the FP noise floor and the shrinking answer close in on the tolerance from both sides).
benchmarks.special_conditions: (1) n >= 3. Nothing else is structurally required: no power of two, no sortedness, no distinctness, no matrix form. (2) Coordinates must be finite and far enough below DBL_MAX that the intermediate differences in the shoelace formula do not overflow — at +-DBL_MAX the areas become inf/NaN and the oracle's `area < minArea` test (baseline.hpp:26) silently skips them, which is a defined-by-accident path rather than a defined operation. (3) THE BINDING CONDITION, measured: the driver compares with an ABSOLUTE epsilon of 1e-4 while the correct answer shrinks as ~n^-3. Measured fraction of independent draws whose reference answer is already BELOW the tolerance, default +-1000 range: 0/300 at n=4,5,8,16,32; 0/200 at n=64,128; 0/100 at n=256; 0/60 at n=512; 3/40 at n=1024; 5/12 at n=2048. So for any n >~ 1024 the tolerance swallows the whole answer and a candidate returning 0.0 passes. Remedy used here, candidate-independent and a standard spec knob: widen `value_range` to [-100000, 100000] (specs.py:409-412 -> ENHANCED_FILL_LO/HI). Areas are exactly scale-equivariant, verified bit-for-bit (every measured min-area value at +-1e5 has the identical mantissa to the +-1e3 value, scaled by exactly 1e4). (4) Upper bound on that widening, measured: the absolute disagreement between two mathematically identical area formulas (the oracle's shoelace vs. an edge-vector cross product) over all C(512,3) triples is 7.0e-10 at +-1e3, 5.7e-6 at +-1e5, and 7.3e-4 at +-1e6 — i.e. at +-1e6 the FP noise floor EXCEEDS the 1e-4 tolerance. +-1e5 is the correct choice: 18x below the tolerance in noise, >=390x above it in signal.
benchmarks.size_semantics: The size number is the NUMBER OF 2-D POINTS. `ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE` = n = `points.size()` = `x.size()` = `y.size()` (cpu.cc:67, 69-70; enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). It is not a side length and nothing is derived from it (no nnz, no sparsity). Oracle work = C(n,3), so work grows with the CUBE of the size number — a 2x size step is an 8x work step.
benchmarks.small: 8 points (value_range [-100000, 100000]; the default +-1000 is equally safe here)
benchmarks.medium: 256 points (value_range [-100000, 100000]; the default +-1000 is also safe here)
benchmarks.complexity: Theta(n^3): exactly C(n,3) = n(n-1)(n-2)/6 constant-time shoelace evaluations plus one comparison each, O(1) extra space (baseline.hpp:22-31 — a full triple loop i<n-2, j<n-1, k<n with no pruning and no non-degeneracy filter). Measured constant on an unloaded host: 1.83 ns per triple, confirmed independently at six sizes spanning 4.2e4 to 1.43e9 triples (1.752 / 2.147 / 1.862 / 1.651 / 1.778 / 1.834 ns per triple at n = 64 / 128 / 256 / 512 / 1024 / 2048) — a clean n^3 fit.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
Domain: the operation is min over all C(n,3) unordered triples of the triangle area. It is defined exactly when at least one triple exists, i.e. n >= 3 (adopted decision, matching baseline.hpp:13-15). Nothing about the operation privileges any particular n beyond that, so the three scale points are chosen from the algorithmic structure, the cubic cost and the driver's grading invariant — never from any observed candidate.

SMALL = 8. The smallest scale at which the answer is a genuine selection rather than a single forced value: C(8,3) = 56 triples. It sits clear of the n<3 early-return path (so it exercises the real code path), yet every triple is still hand-enumerable by a reviewer. It is also the scale that maximally exposes the characteristic error of this operation — an off-by-one in one of the three loop bounds (`i < size-2`, `j < size-1`, `k < size`, baseline.hpp:22-24): dropping the last point removes C(7,2) = 21 of the 56 triples, so the true minimum lies in the dropped set with probability 21/56 = 37.5% per draw, which is high enough to catch quickly and would be ~0.15% at n = 2048. Measured reference values at n=8 over 300 draws: median 4.80e3, minimum 9.15e1 — about 9x10^5 times the 1e-4 tolerance, so the verdict at SMALL is purely algorithmic with zero float-tolerance interaction.

MEDIUM = 256. The benchmark's own working scale: drivers/problem-sizes.json assigns this benchmark DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE = (1<<8) = 256 for serial and mpi (and (1<<7) = 128 for omp/kokkos), so 256 is the point count at which the benchmark's SPEEDUP is measured. Grading correctness at exactly that scale is the operationally meaningful middle rung. C(256,3) = 2,763,520 triples: enough work that a parallel implementation's decomposition, reduction and load balance all matter (the triple loop is triangular, so naive static scheduling is already visibly unbalanced here), while one oracle call costs ~5 ms. Measured over 100 draws with the default range: median 8.98e-2, minimum 1.31e-4, 0/100 below the tolerance — grading is unambiguous even without widening the range.

LARGE = 2048. Set by the 10 s budget against the cubic cost, nothing else. At the measured unloaded rate of 1.83 ns/triple, 10 s buys ~5.5e9 triples, i.e. n ~ 3200. 2048 gives C = 1.43e9 triples and a measured 2.62 s (median of 3), leaving ~3.8x headroom, deliberately kept because the host could not be returned to a quiet state to confirm anything larger (see budget_adjustment) and because validate() calls the oracle twice per trial (MAX_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS = 2, utilities.hpp:25-27) plus the candidate twice, so the per-run cost is ~4x the single-oracle figure. 2048 is also the largest rung at which the answer can still be made to clear the 1e-4 absolute tolerance by the standard `value_range` knob alone: with the widened +-1e5 range the measured reference values at n=2048 are min 3.9e-2, median 3.06, i.e. 390x-3e4x the tolerance, against an FP noise floor of 5.7e-6.

Ladder shape: 8 -> 256 -> 2048 in n is 56 -> 2.76e6 -> 1.43e9 in actual work (x4.9e4, then x517). The gap is intentional and follows from the cubic cost: the low rung has to be tiny to be a boundary test at all, and the high rung is pinned by the runtime budget; there is no room for an evenly geometric ladder inside a 10 s budget on an n^3 kernel.

No size in this ladder is shared with a sibling benchmark by convenience: 2048 follows from 1.83 ns/triple x C(n,3) <= 10 s, 256 follows from this benchmark's own problem-sizes.json entry, and 8 follows from C(8,3)=56 and the 21/56 loop-bound detection rate.

Both sentences must be added identically to the serial, omp and mpi entries of thesis/prompts/generation-prompts-thesis.json. The first sentence is needed regardless of the size floor, because coincident/collinear inputs are reachable at any n (the duplicate_at pattern produces one exactly coincident pair, and every deterministic fill pattern puts all points on the line y=x); the prompt today says only "the area of the smallest triangle that can be formed by any 3 points" and supplies a triangleArea() helper that happily returns 0 for a degenerate triple, so both readings ("degenerate triples count" and "three collinear points do not form a triangle") are defensible and the oracle silently enforces the first.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
Which degenerate inputs are mathematically DEFINED for this operation (all statements below verified by execution against the oracle):
NOT defined by the operation, only by the oracle — n = 0, 1, 2: the minimum runs over an empty family of triples. The oracle returns 0.0 (baseline.hpp:13-15, verified). The prompt is silent, and +inf / DBL_MAX (minimum over an empty set) and NaN are equally standard conventions. Excluded from the scale axis by the adopted "at least 3 points" decision; may be graded ONLY after the n<3 sentence is added to the prompt. Currently they are live via config.yaml:562 and must be gated off for this benchmark or the prompt fixed.
DEFINED, and a genuine boundary rather than a scale point — n = 3 exactly: one triple, answer = that triangle's area (verified: {0,0},{4,0},{0,3} -> 6). Worth testing on its own axis; it is not "small".
DEFINED — all points identical (n >= 3): every triple has area 0, answer exactly 0 (verified, n=64). Also produced by the all_zeros and all_same fill patterns.
DEFINED — all points distinct but collinear (n >= 3): answer exactly 0 (verified on y = 2x+1, n=64). Also produced by ascending, descending, alternating and sorted_except_one, all of which put the points on y = x.
DEFINED and structurally the most informative zero case — exactly ONE coincident pair in otherwise general position (duplicate_at(k), verified -> exactly 0): only the triples containing indices k and k+1 give 0, so the candidate must actually enumerate that pair; it catches implementations that de-duplicate points or that skip zero-area triples.
DEFINED ONLY BY THE NaN SKIP — extreme coordinates (extreme_values: x and y both alternate lowest/max, so the set collapses to just two distinct points): answer exactly 0 and finite (verified), but only because the inf-minus-inf triples produce NaN and `area < minArea` is false for NaN (baseline.hpp:26). This is an accident of the comparison, not a property of the operation.
DEFINED, and a legitimate NaN-robustness test — one extreme outlier (spike_at(k) = DBL_MAX/2): answer = the minimum over the remaining n-1 points (verified: n=64 -> 8.5359, bit-identical to the same draw without the spike). Passes only for candidates whose reduction is NaN-safe (`a < min`, std::min, fmin all are; a sum or a differently ordered reduction may not be).
NOTE: every zero-answer case above is exactly a case on which the unresolved "do degenerate triples count?" decision flips the expected value (thesis/docs/oracle-correctness-audit.md:481 measures the two readings differing by ~4e4 on live specs). benchmarks.name: 13_geometry_closest_pair_2d
benchmarks.input_form: One dimension: n = number of 2-D points. Signature `double closestPair(std::vector<Point> const& points)` with `struct Point { double x, y; }` (prompt, all three variants serial/omp/mpi — identical apart from the parallelism sentence). Driver domain: two independent coordinate arrays `std::vector<double> x(n), y(n)` filled uniformly in [-1000.0, 1000.0] and then zipped into points[i] = {x[i], y[i]} (cpu.cc:69-70, 79-80, 86-89). Output: a single double (minimum pairwise Euclidean distance), graded with an ABSOLUTE epsilon of 1e-4 via reportAndCompareScalar (cpu.cc:99; utilities.hpp:488-492). No structural precondition on the input: unsorted, duplicates allowed, unconstrained double coordinates.
benchmarks.min_size: 2 points. A "closest pair" presupposes that a pair exists; n = 2 gives exactly one pair and is the smallest well-defined instance. n = 0 and n = 1 are NOT forbidden by the harness (they compile, run, and are graded — the oracle returns 0, verified by probe), but they are degenerate, not scale points; see degenerate_cases. Formally: min_size for the SCALE axis = 2; no size floor is imposed globally.
benchmarks.max_size: None forced by the harness or by the operation — ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE is an unconstrained -D integer (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79) and the oracle has no upper precondition. The binding cap is the runtime budget: at the measured ≈7 ns per pair, a single oracle call reaches 10 s at n ≈ 53,000. A tighter practical cap is stages.enhanced_tests.run_timeout_seconds = 60 (config.yaml:613), which must cover 2 oracle calls (MAX_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS = 2) plus the candidate plus mpirun startup, i.e. roughly 2–3× the single-call time.
benchmarks.special_conditions: None structural. No power-of-two requirement, no sortedness, no distinctness, no coordinate-range constraint in the prompt or the driver contract — `std::vector<Point>` of arbitrary length with arbitrary double coordinates (baseline.hpp:11-31 handles any n; enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79 makes ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE an unconstrained -D integer). The only numeric precondition that matters in practice is a magnitude one the prompt does NOT state: coordinate differences must not overflow to +inf, otherwise the oracle degenerates to its DBL_MAX sentinel (baseline.hpp:21, 24-27; audit BL-06). All three scale points below stay inside the driver's own [-1000, 1000] fill range, where no overflow is possible.
benchmarks.size_semantics: The size number is the POINT COUNT, not an element count and not a side length. `TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024)` sizes `points`, `x` and `y` alike (cpu.cc:67, 69-70), and `init()` resizes all three to DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (cpu.cc:48-50). So a size of N means N points = 2N doubles in memory = N(N-1)/2 pairs of work.
benchmarks.complexity: Θ(n²) for the oracle: exactly n(n-1)/2 distance evaluations, each 2 subtractions, 2 × std::pow(·,2), 1 addition, 1 std::sqrt, plus one compare-and-update (baseline.hpp:22-29). Memory Θ(n); the inner loop rescans the whole point array once per outer iteration, so the working set is the entire array. Measured constant with the pipeline's flags on this host: ≈ 7 ns per pair (0.977 s at n=16384 = 134.2 M pairs; 3.73 s at n=32768 = 536.9 M pairs). Note the problem itself admits Θ(n log n) (divide-and-conquer / sweep), so the oracle is asymptotically one factor above the best known algorithm — the quadratic cost is a property of THIS reference, not of the operation.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
Derived only from the operation, its domain, the Θ(n²) oracle cost and the 10 s budget — no candidate code was inspected.

(1) Why not powers of two. The parameter is an arbitrary-length vector; nothing in the operation privileges 2^k. The driver's own sizes are all powers of two (validation default 1024, cpu.cc:67; serial DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (1<<14), problem-sizes.json:119-126), so inheriting them would leave the remainder path of every partitioning untested at every scale. All three scale points are therefore chosen PRIME. A prime n is coprime to every SIMD width (2/4/8 doubles), every tile size, and to the stage's fixed launch width of 4 (config.yaml:603-604 omp_threads: 4, mpi_ranks: 4), so any blocked, vectorised or rank-partitioned decomposition of an all-pairs minimum must handle a non-empty remainder. That is a property of the operation's parallelisation under the specified launch config, not of any observed implementation.

(2) Why these three magnitudes. The oracle rescans the full point array per outer iteration, so the memory regime is fixed by n·16 bytes, and the work by n²/2. The three points are one memory regime apart and roughly two orders of magnitude of work apart:
- SMALL = 101 → 1.6 KB, L1-resident; 5,050 pairs. The smallest scale at which the all-pairs structure is genuinely non-trivial while the answer still depends purely on the pairwise-minimum logic and not on memory behaviour. Far enough above the definition floor (2) that a wrong reduction cannot pass by luck, small enough that no algorithmic strategy has any room to matter.
- MEDIUM = 2003 → 32.0 KB, i.e. just past the 32 KB L1d capacity, so the inner rescan streams from L2; 2,005,003 pairs (×397 the work of SMALL). This is also where the asymptotic gap between the Θ(n²) reference and the Θ(n log n) algorithms for this problem first becomes large (2.0 M vs ~2.2·10^4 basic steps, ~90×), so the scale separates algorithmic choice from mere parallelisation. It sits one binary step above the driver's own validation default without inheriting it.
- LARGE = 30011 → 480 KB, past typical L2 into L3; 450,315,055 pairs (×225 the work of MEDIUM, ×89,172 that of SMALL). Chosen as the largest prime in the regime where the measured single oracle call stays comfortably inside the mandated 10 s (measured 3.13 s, worst rep observed 4.83 s), leaving ~3× headroom for the host noise documented below and for the fact that validate() calls the oracle MAX_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS = 2 times per run (cpu.cc:76; utilities.hpp:25-26) inside a 60 s per-run timeout (config.yaml:613).

(3) Accuracy note that follows from the scale, not from candidates. For n points uniform in a 2000×2000 square the minimum distance shrinks like Θ(1/n): measured oracle results are ≈18.05 at n=101, ≈0.868 at n=2003, ≈0.036 at n=30011. Against the fixed ABSOLUTE epsilon of 1e-4 (cpu.cc:99) the effective RELATIVE tolerance therefore loosens from ~6e-6 (SMALL) to ~1e-4 (MEDIUM) to ~2.8e-3 (LARGE). LARGE is still a meaningful check (0.28% relative), but the grading gets monotonically more permissive with scale; this is a property of the fixed absolute epsilon and should be stated wherever LARGE results are reported.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: yes: "If the vector contains fewer than two points, return 0." — This is the only restriction the prompt actually needs, and it is needed because the harness DOES grade n = 0 and n = 1 (config.yaml:562 static_base_sizes [0,1,2,7]; 8 of the 20 scheduled specs for this benchmark) against a convention (0.0) that is unobtainable from the prompt text, the signature, the supplied distance() helper, or the documented 6-point example. Note the consequence recorded in the audit: adding it edits all three prompt entries (serial/omp/mpi) in thesis/prompts/generation-prompts-thesis.json and invalidates any samples already generated for this benchmark, and the same sentence would have to be considered for 14_geometry_closest_pair_1d, which carries the identical guard. NO restriction is needed for the overflow case: the prompt already fixes the intended value through the distance() helper it supplies (+inf); there the ORACLE is what deviates, not the prompt.
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: yes — the generic ENHANCED_FILL mechanism cannot express a genuinely 2-D configuration. ENHANCED_FILL resolves to a single compile-time (or single runtime-config) pattern applied at every call site (enhanced-fill.hpp:449-461, 447), and cpu.cc:79-80 calls it twice, so x and y NECESSARILY receive the SAME pattern. Every structured pattern therefore collapses the point cloud onto a diagonal or a point: all_same/all_zeros → one point repeated n times; ascending/descending → collinear on y = x; alternating → two distinct points. Verified by probe. The inputs that actually discriminate a closest-pair implementation — one tight cluster far from a diffuse rest, points on a circle, a lattice with known step, or (the decisive one for divide-and-conquer) x sorted with y random so the closest pair is far apart in x-order — cannot be built at all. A benchmark-specific point-set constructor is required for the geometric cases; the current pattern set only reaches the "duplicate point" family.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
Own axis, all values below MEASURED with the pipeline's flags (scratchpad probe.cpp, output reproduced verbatim):

DEFINED BY THE ORACLE BUT NOT BY THE PROMPT (grading hazard):
- n = 0 (empty vector): oracle → 0. Mathematically undefined (min over an empty set); at least four C++ conventions exist (0, +inf, DBL_MAX, throw). baseline.hpp:13-15.
- n = 1 (single point): oracle → 0. Same problem — no pair exists. Confirmed: "n=1 -> 0 ; n=0 -> 0".
These are the 8 of 20 scheduled enhanced specs at sizes 0/1 flagged by audit finding BL-05 (config.yaml:562 static_base_sizes [0,1,2,7]).

MATHEMATICALLY DEFINED AND CORRECTLY HANDLED:
- n = 2, ordinary coordinates: exactly one pair; oracle → 5 for {(0,0),(3,4)}. The true definition floor.
- All points identical (fill patterns all_zeros(1) / all_same(2), applied to BOTH coordinate arrays): 1000 points → 0. Correct and a strong test (coincident points break naive divide-and-conquer strip logic).
- Exactly two distinct points, each repeated n/2 times (pattern alternating(5)): 1000 points → 0. Correct.
- One exact coincident pair among random points (pattern duplicate_at(7), k=500): 1000 points → 0. Correct; the sharpest cheap correctness test.
- Collinear, equally spaced points on y = x (pattern ascending(3) or descending(4) on both arrays): 1000 points → 2.83125838…, i.e. the consecutive spacing. Correct, but a NEGATIVE CONTROL: on a monotone collinear ramp a "consecutive pairs only" implementation coincides with the true minimum, so this input does not discriminate (matches the audit's own note at oracle-correctness-audit.md:54).
- One overflowing pair among finite points: {(0,0),(3,4),(DBL_MAX,DBL_MAX),(lowest,lowest)} → 5. Correct.

DEFINED MATHEMATICALLY BUT WRONG IN THE ORACLE:
- n = 2 with extreme_values (pattern 6): points (lowest,lowest) and (max,max); every pairwise distance overflows, so the `if (dist < minDist)` update never fires and the oracle returns its untouched initialiser 1.7976931348623157e+308 (= DBL_MAX). Measured. The mathematically correct answer is +inf (the prompt's own `distance()` helper and std::hypot both give +inf). No faithful implementation can pass this spec — audit finding BL-06.
- n = 3 with extreme_values: → 0, because the alternating fill makes point 0 and point 2 identical. Correct, so the defect is specific to n = 2.

NOT A DEGENERATE CASE HERE: NaN inputs are not produced by any fill pattern; the range-bounded patterns cannot generate them.

benchmarks.name: 14_geometry_closest_pair_1d
benchmarks.input_form: One 1-D input: `std::vector<double> x` of length n, values drawn uniformly from [-1000.0, 1000.0]. Output: a single `double` = min over all C(n,2) unordered pairs of |x_i - x_j|. The only dimension is n (element count); there is no second dimension, no derived count, no structural precondition on the values (unsorted, duplicates allowed, sign-free). Timed input: `ctx->x` of length DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (cpu.cc:36, filled cpu.cc:29). Validated input: a separate vector of length TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:53-55, filled cpu.cc:64). Comparison: `reportAndCompareScalar(correct, test, 1e-4)` — a single scalar with an ABSOLUTE tolerance of 1e-4 (cpu.cc:77).
benchmarks.min_size: 2 — the smallest n for which the operation is mathematically defined ("the closest two elements" requires two elements). At n < 2 the pair set is empty and the minimum is undefined; the oracle pins it to 0 (baseline.hpp:13-15, MEASURED: n=0 -> 0, n=1 -> 0), which is a convention, not a definition. n = 2 is defined but has exactly ONE pair, so every implementation that reads both elements returns the same value — it is a valid boundary case with zero discriminating power on the scale axis.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — forced by the harness: thesis/config/config.yaml:570-572 `max_spec_size: 4096` ("upper bound for spec sizes (validation rejects larger; keeps runtime bounded)"), enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 and applied to the deterministic mutants at specs.py:533. This cap binds ~18x before the 10 s runtime budget does (the budget's own size is n ~ 7.2e4, measured). Additionally an EFFECTIVE grading cap of ~1024 applies whenever the spec keeps the driver's default value range [-1000,1000]; above that the absolute 1e-4 tolerance stops discriminating (measured).
benchmarks.special_conditions:
1) n >= 2 for definedness (adopted decision: "enough points for the operation to be defined"). No power-of-two, no sortedness, no positivity, no distinctness requirement — any real vector of length >= 2 is a valid input.
2) HARD GRADING CONDITION, measured, specific to this benchmark: the graded answer SHRINKS as Theta(W/n^2) (W = width of the value range) while the tolerance is a FIXED ABSOLUTE 1e-4. Therefore any size point must satisfy W >= 1e-2 * n^2 (a 100x margin over the tolerance) or the check becomes vacuous. With the driver's own W = 2000 this caps usable n at ~450 for a 100x margin and ~1400 for a 10x margin. Measured mean answer / 1e-4 over 30 fillRand draws: n=4 -> 1.6e6x; n=256 -> 428x; n=1024 -> 21x (1/30 draws already <= tolerance); n=2048 -> 7.1x (3/30); n=4096 -> 1.26x (17/30 draws at or below the tolerance, i.e. a candidate returning 0.0 PASSES on most draws); n=8192 -> 0.49x; n=16384 -> 0.05x.
3) Consequence: sizes above ~1024 are only gradeable if the spec widens `pattern_params.value_range`. MEASURED at n=4096: range [-1e5,1e5] -> mean/eps = 109, 0/20 draws below tolerance; range [-1e6,1e6] -> 1103. Widening the range does not change the operation (the closest-pair distance is scale-equivariant), so this is a legitimate domain choice, not a task change.
4) Generator floor: fillRand quantises to a grid of step 2000/RAND_MAX = 9.3132e-7 (RAND_MAX = 2147483647, MEASURED). The smallest representable nonzero answer at the driver's range is therefore 9.3132e-7, and exact duplicates (answer exactly 0) start appearing around n ~ 1.6e4 and are systematic at n = 65536 (2 of 3 draws) — outside the 4096 spec cap, so not live for the spec set, but it bounds what the default generator can ever produce.
5) K-patterns (duplicate_at / sorted_except_one / spike_at) already require size >= 2 in the spec validator (specs.py:320-322).
benchmarks.size_semantics: The size number is the ELEMENT COUNT of the input vector, directly and with no derivation: `std::vector<double> x(TEST_SIZE)` at cpu.cc:55, with TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024) at cpu.cc:53 and ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE substituted verbatim at enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79. It is not a side length, there is no nnz or sparsity derivation, and no second dimension. The work is n(n-1)/2 pairs, i.e. quadratic in the size number. DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (problem-sizes.json:128-132) is a separate quantity that sizes only the TIMED input (cpu.cc:36) and does not affect validation; the enhanced stage builds with DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE=(1<<4).
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle: Theta(n^2) — exactly n(n-1)/2 pair evaluations, each one subtract + std::abs + compare, in the double loop baseline.hpp:22-29. No early exit, no pruning. Natural correct solution in 1-D: Theta(n log n) (sort, then min over adjacent gaps) — the divergence between the oracle's work and the natural solution's work is ~3 orders of magnitude at n = 4096 (8.39e6 pairs vs ~4.9e4 comparisons). Memory: Theta(n), one contiguous double array, so the oracle is compute-bound, not bandwidth-bound.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
The scale axis is set by three independent constraints, of which the runtime budget is the LOOSEST and never binds.

SMALL = 4. n < 2 is undefined (baseline.hpp:13-15); n = 2 has exactly one pair, so the answer is forced and nothing is discriminated; n = 2 and n = 7 are in any case already static base sizes (config.yaml:562 static_base_sizes [0,1,2,7]). n = 4 is the smallest size that hits the operation's sharpest STRUCTURAL edge: closest-pair is not partition-decomposable (unlike a sum or a max over elements — the closest pair can straddle any partition boundary), and the pipeline's enhanced stage launches with a FIXED width of 4 (config.yaml:603-604: omp_threads: 4, mpi_ranks: 4). At n = 4 each thread/rank owns exactly ONE element, so NO partition contains a pair at all and the answer is necessarily cross-partition. Any implementation that reduces partition-local minima returns its identity element instead of a distance. n = 4 also gives 6 pairs, so the closest pair is generically not index-adjacent. Discriminating power is total: MEASURED mean answer 156.2 = 1.56e6x the 1e-4 tolerance over 30 draws.

MEDIUM = 1024. The largest power of two at which the driver's OWN value range [-1000,1000] (cpu.cc:29/64) keeps the expected answer an order of magnitude above the absolute 1e-4 tolerance (cpu.cc:77) — MEASURED mean 2.098e-3 = 21x the tolerance, versus 7.1x at 2048 and 1.26x at 4096. This is derived from the operation (answer ~ W/n^2) and the grading invariant, not from convenience; the fact that it coincides with the driver's own calibrated TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:53) is a confirmation and has the side benefit that the enhanced verdict is directly comparable with the base-stage verdict. At the 4-way launch each thread/rank owns 256 elements, so the decomposition is real and the cross-chunk boundary is exercised on non-trivial chunks.

LARGE = 4096. The harness-forced maximum (config.yaml:572 max_spec_size: 4096, enforced at specs.py:293-294 "size %s exceeds max_spec_size"); 8.39e6 pairs; the asymptotic regime where the O(n^2) oracle and the O(n log n) natural solution are 3 orders of magnitude apart, which is what makes the size informative. The 10 s runtime budget does NOT bind: MEASURED oracle time at 4096 is 0.0877 s, 114x under the budget, and the budget's own size would be n ~ 7.2e4 (MEASURED 65536 -> 8.26 s median), i.e. ~18x above the harness cap. LARGE is only gradeable with a widened value_range (see special_conditions 2/3 and custom_input_construction_needed); with the driver's default range it is measurably vacuous.

The three points are 4 / 1024 / 4096. The 4x gap between medium and large is dictated by the harness cap, not chosen; the 256x gap between small and medium is the span between the decomposition floor and the tolerance ceiling, and there is nothing structurally distinct in between for this operation (no power-of-two requirement, no cache-blocking regime that changes the answer, no derived counts).
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: no — under the adopted domain restriction (n >= 2, "enough points for the operation to be defined") the restriction is realised as a spec-size floor, not as prompt text, and the prompt corpus stays untouched. CONDITIONAL: this only holds if sizes 0 and 1 are actually dropped from the spec set for this benchmark. They are NOT dropped today (config.yaml:562 static_base_sizes: [0, 1, 2, 7] guarantees them), and while they are retained the row's n<2 cases measure convention guessing rather than parallel programming (audit BL-07). If the project instead chooses to keep sizes 0/1 (audit option (c)), then it becomes "yes: If the vector contains fewer than two elements, return 0." — with the cost, recorded in the audit, that all samples for this benchmark must be regenerated.
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: yes — not a new container shape, but a size-coupled VALUE RANGE. Because the answer scales as Theta(W/n^2) against a fixed absolute 1e-4, every spec at n >~ 1024 must set `pattern_params.value_range` to satisfy W >= 1e-2 * n^2. Concretely: at LARGE = 4096 the spec must carry value_range = [-1e5, 1e5] or wider (MEASURED: mean/eps = 109, 0/20 draws below tolerance; with the default [-1000,1000] it is 1.26 and 17/30 draws are at or below tolerance, so returning 0.0 passes). No new code is required — the mechanism exists and is validated (specs.py:309-318 accepts any [lo, hi] with lo <= hi; specs.py:409-412 emits -DENHANCED_FILL_LO/HI; specs.py:434-437 the runtime-fill variant; enhanced-fill.hpp:18/42) — but the default random pattern does NOT set it, so it must be set deliberately per size. The fill site itself is standard: 1 site, total_elements = n, explicit_values supported (benchmark_shapes.json:137-145).

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
DEFINED for this operation (all values below MEASURED with the repo's own oracle):
- n = 2: defined, answer = |x0 - x1| (measured: [7,3] -> 4). Legitimate boundary, but only one pair exists so it discriminates nothing.
- all values equal (all_same, all_zeros): defined, answer exactly 0 (measured, n=16 -> 0 for both). Genuinely important — and it is exactly the value the oracle also returns for n<2, so 0 is ambiguous between "there is no pair" and "there is a coincident pair".
- duplicate_at(k): defined, answer exactly 0 (same mechanism).
- spike_at(k): defined, answer unchanged by the outlier (measured n=16 -> 9.0954), because the spike is far from every other element.
- ascending / descending ramp: defined, answer = the uniform gap (measured n=256 -> 7.8431372549018761 vs the exact gap 2000/255 = 7.8431372549019605; FP rounding makes the gaps differ by ~8e-14). This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL, not a test: all gaps are equal, so an "adjacent-index pairs only" implementation returns the right answer within the 1e-4 tolerance. Same phenomenon the audit records for the 2-D sibling's collinear ramp.

NOT DEFINED for this operation (convention, not mathematics):
- n = 0 and n = 1: no pair exists; the mathematical convention for min over an empty set is +infinity. The oracle pins 0 (measured). +inf, DBL_MAX and a throw all FAIL the absolute comparator, while NaN spuriously PASSES it. Both sizes are guaranteed by config.yaml:562. This is audit BL-07 and is the reason this row is provisional.
- extreme_values at n = 2 exactly: MEASURED the oracle returns 1.7976931348623157e+308 (= DBL_MAX), NOT the mathematically correct |max - lowest| = +inf. The reason: max - lowest overflows to +inf, and `inf < DBL_MAX` is false, so the sentinel initialiser at baseline.hpp:21 is never overwritten and leaks into the return value. No faithful implementation can pass this case; DBL_MAX is finite, so neither the current comparator nor the in-flight non-finite-reference contract rescues it. This is the exact analogue of audit BL-06, which is recorded only for 13_geometry_closest_pair_2d — for benchmark 14 it is confirmed here and not yet on record. At n >= 3 the alternating extreme pattern repeats values, so the answer is a well-defined 0 (measured n=4 -> 0).

benchmarks.name: 15_graph_edge_count
benchmarks.input_form: One dense row-major adjacency matrix of a DIRECTED graph plus its side length: `edgeCount(std::vector<int> const& A, size_t N)`. A holds exactly N*N entries, each in {0,1}; A[i*N+j]==1 means "directed edge i->j". The matrix is NOT symmetric and the diagonal is NOT reserved (self-loops occur). Output is a single `int` = the number of entries equal to 1. Relevant dimensions: N = side length = vertex count (this is what a spec's `size` sets); N*N = element count = the actual work; 4*N*N bytes = the working set that drives runtime.
benchmarks.min_size: 0 — no floor. N=0 (empty graph, 0 edges) is mathematically defined and the oracle handles it: both loops in baseline.hpp:17-23 have zero trip count, `count` stays 0, `A.data()` is never dereferenced. MEASURED: correctEdgeCount(A,0) = 0. Valid size form: any integer N >= 0 with A.size() == N*N. No power-of-two, parity, minimum-vertex or minimum-edge requirement exists.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED by the harness, not by the operation. stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096 (thesis/config/config.yaml:572), enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). The operation itself would stay well-defined up to N = 46340 (int-return overflow bound) and the machine would allow roughly N <= 16384 (1.07 GB).
benchmarks.special_conditions: (1) Shape: A.size() must equal N*N exactly — the driver allocates TEST_SIZE*TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:65) and the oracle indexes A[i*N+j] unchecked (baseline.hpp:19); a short A is an out-of-bounds read, not a defined input. (2) Binary entries: the oracle counts entries EXACTLY equal to 1, so "edge" is only well-defined if every entry is in {0,1}. The driver's generator guarantees this (cpu.cc:27-34 writes only 0 and 1) and there is NO ENHANCED_FILL site (benchmark_shapes.json:146-152, fill_sites=0), so the enhanced stage cannot violate it today. Any future custom construction MUST preserve it — a 2 or a -1 would be silently treated as a non-edge by the oracle while "A[k] != 0" candidates count it. (3) NO structural precondition: not symmetric, no zero diagonal, no connectivity, no minimum degree. Self-loops are allowed AND COUNTED (no `i != j` guard in baseline.hpp:19; MEASURED ~N/2 self-loops per instance, e.g. 66 of 128 at N=128). (4) Return-type bound: the `int` return holds N*N only while N <= 46340; irrelevant here because max_size is 4096 (worst case, an all-ones matrix, is 16,777,216 < INT_MAX). (5) No epsilon: validation is EXACT integer equality via reportAndCompareScalar (cpu.cc:84; utilities.hpp:483-485 -> `expected == got`).
benchmarks.size_semantics: `size` = N = the SIDE LENGTH of the N x N matrix (NOT the element count). The driver derives everything from it: ctx->A.resize(N*N) (cpu.cc:46) and, in validate(), std::vector<int> A(TEST_SIZE*TEST_SIZE) with TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(128) (cpu.cc:63,65). So a spec size of n means n*n input elements and 4*n*n bytes. Nothing is derived stochastically (no nnz, no density parameter): every entry is drawn independently, 1 with p ~= 0.5 (cpu.cc:30), diagonal included.
benchmarks.small: 64  — 4,096 elements, 16 KB working set (L1d-resident). MEASURED oracle median 0.000001 s.
benchmarks.medium: 513 — 263,169 elements, 1.05 MB working set (out of L1, L2/L3 regime). Deliberately NOT a power of two. MEASURED oracle median 0.000067 s.
benchmarks.large: 4096 — 16,777,216 elements, 64 MB working set (exceeds any LLC, DRAM-bandwidth-bound). MEASURED oracle median 0.017 s.
benchmarks.complexity: Theta(N^2) = Theta(element count), exactly and unconditionally: two nested loops over all N*N entries, one integer compare plus a conditional increment each, no early exit, no data-dependent branching in the control flow, no allocation (baseline.hpp:16-24). Runtime is therefore strictly linear in bytes touched — the operation is a pure memory-bound streaming reduction. Confirmed by measurement: 4,096 -> 263,169 -> 16,777,216 elements gives 1 us -> 67 us -> 17 ms, i.e. ~1.0 ns/element once out of cache and sub-linear only where the array fits in cache.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
min_size = 0 because the operation "count the 1-entries of an N x N matrix" is total over N >= 0: the empty graph has 0 edges, and the oracle's loops degenerate correctly (verified by execution). No condition of the operation forces a floor, so 0 and 1 belong on the degenerate axis, not in a size floor.

The special conditions follow from the oracle's exact form, not from convention: `== 1` (not `!= 0`) makes binary entries a genuine precondition, and the absence of an `i != j` guard makes self-loops countable edges.

SCALE LADDER. Because the work is exactly Theta(N^2) with a flat, data-independent inner body, the only thing scale can vary is (a) the position of the working set in the memory hierarchy and (b) how much work each worker gets. That gives an operation-intrinsic ladder, geometric in the WORK (uniform ~64x steps in element count, 4096x total span):
  - SMALL 64: 4N^2 = 16 KB fits in a 32-48 KB L1d, so the scan never leaves the innermost cache; a row is 64 ints = exactly 4 cache lines, and at the pilot's launch point (config.yaml enhanced_launch: omp_threads 4, mpi_ranks 4) each worker still gets 16 whole rows, so a row-block decomposition remains well-defined while parallelisation overhead dominates. This is the smallest N at which the regime "L1-resident, overhead-dominated" is cleanly realised.
  - MEDIUM 513: 1.05 MB leaves L1 by ~32x and sits in the L2/L3 range — the cache-resident streaming regime where parallel speedup first becomes visible. It is deliberately NOT a power of two: the only structural hazard a row-major flat scan has besides scale is the remainder of SIMD/blocked decomposition, and 513 = 3*9*19 leaves a tail of exactly 1 under every common vector width (513 mod 4 = mod 8 = mod 16 = 1) and under 4-way rank/thread splitting, for both the row-wise and the flat-N^2 reading (513^2 = 263169, mod 16 = 1). Making all three rungs powers of two would make every rung tail-free and systematically hide remainder handling. Non-power-of-two sizes are fully valid here (no FFT-style constraint), and pilot_001 already ran this benchmark at 1023.
  - LARGE 4096: 64 MB exceeds any LLC, so the oracle runs at DRAM bandwidth — the regime the benchmark is actually about. It is also doubly pinned from outside: it is the harness's hard cap max_spec_size = 4096 (config.yaml:572, enforced specs.py:293-294), and it is exactly the DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE the repository already configures for this benchmark's serial/omp/mpi timing runs (problem-sizes.json: (1<<12)). No larger size is admissible anywhere in the pipeline.

RUNTIME BUDGET. The 10 s serial-oracle budget is NON-BINDING for this operation and never becomes binding. LARGE=4096 measures 0.017 s = 0.17% of the budget. At the measured ~1.0 ns/element, 10 s would require ~1e10 elements, i.e. N ~ 100,000 and a ~40 GB matrix — 24x beyond max_spec_size and physically impossible on the machine. The binding constraint is therefore the harness cap, and I say so rather than inflating LARGE past it. (This is not a case for stopping the row: the budget is an upper bound, we are far inside it, and a different hard constraint fully determines LARGE.)

None of the three sizes was derived from any candidate or model output; the inputs to the choice were the operation, the Theta(N^2) complexity, the memory hierarchy, the harness cap and the measured oracle time.
