benchmarks.name: 16_graph_largest_component
benchmarks.input_form: One dense undirected graph. `int largestComponent(std::vector<int> const& A, size_t N)`: A is a flat row-major NxN adjacency matrix with exactly N*N entries; the only free dimension is N (= vertex count = matrix side length). Edge count is NOT an independent dimension: the oracle scans every row completely regardless of density (baseline.hpp:11-15), so cost depends on N alone. Return value is a single int compared for exact equality (cpu.cc:84 -> utilities.hpp:483-485, no epsilon).
benchmarks.min_size: N = 0. No mathematical floor exists and none is imposed by the driver: the oracle is total on every N >= 0 (measured: N=0 -> 0, N=1 -> 1). The operation only becomes *discriminating* (a strict maximum among >= 2 components) at N >= 3, but that is a discrimination property, not a validity floor, so N=0/1/2 belong in degenerate_cases and NOT in a size floor.
benchmarks.max_size: 12288 on this host/container, from two independently measured ceilings, not from the operation: (1) the 10 s oracle budget — 12288 = 1.85 s, 16384 = 16.15 s; (2) the pipeline's 60 s enhanced-tests run wall — validate() runs the O(N^2) generator twice, and at 16384 one generator pass alone measured 49.6-64.3 s. A third, theoretical ceiling from the Theta(N)-deep recursion (8 MiB stack / 80 bytes per frame = N ~= 104857) is unreachable, since that N would require a 44 TB adjacency matrix. LARGE was set to 8192, below the practical max, for reproducibility.
benchmarks.special_conditions: A must be a simple undirected graph in dense form: (1) |A| == N*N exactly; (2) every entry exactly 0 or 1 — the oracle's edge test is `A[node*N+i] == 1` (baseline.hpp:12), so an entry of 2 is silently a NON-edge (measured: N=8 with A[0][1]=A[1][0]=2 -> 1, i.e. no edge seen); (3) A symmetric — the oracle only ever reads row `node`, so an asymmetric matrix yields direction-dependent answers (measured: A[0][1]=1 alone -> 2; A[1][0]=1 alone -> 1); (4) zero diagonal (self-loops are ignored rather than rejected: N=8 diag=1 -> 1, so they are harmless but out of the stated domain). No power-of-two condition, no minimum vertex or edge count. The driver's own generator establishes (1)-(4) by construction (cpu.cc:26-35).
benchmarks.size_semantics: size = N = number of vertices = side length of the NxN row-major adjacency matrix. It is NOT an element count: the allocation is N*N ints (cpu.cc:65 `std::vector<int> A(TEST_SIZE*TEST_SIZE)`, cpu.cc:46-47 `ctx->A.resize(ctx->N * ctx->N)`), so an ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE of n means an n-vertex graph and a 4*n^2-byte matrix. Edge count is not configurable through the size knob.
benchmarks.complexity: Time Theta(N^2) — each of the N vertices is expanded exactly once and its expansion scans a full row of N entries (baseline.hpp:11-15, 28-34); density-independent in operation count. Memory Theta(N^2) ints for A (4*N^2 bytes) plus Theta(N) for `visited`. Recursion depth Theta(N) (measured maxdepth == N for both ER(1/2) and path graphs), at a measured 80 bytes/frame in the real oracle (objdump of dfs: 6 register pushes = 48 B + `sub $0x18,%rsp` = 24 B + 8 B return address).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
Cost is Theta(N^2) in BOTH time and memory, independent of edge density, so the ladder must step in N and each rung multiplies work by the square. The three rungs are chosen to cover three qualitatively different regimes of this specific operation, not as a geometric convenience ladder.

SMALL = 16. Chosen as the smallest rung that is still (a) structurally non-trivial — 16 vertices admit several components with a strict maximum (e.g. 9+4+3), unlike N<=2 which are pure degenerate cases; (b) BELOW the machine's worker count (container nproc = 20, measured), so the omp/mpi variants hit the "fewer vertices than threads/ranks" boundary where partitions are empty and a rank may own zero rows — a real correctness hazard the prompt's mpi variant invites ("every rank has a complete copy of A, result returned on rank 0"); and (c) below one machine word of vertices (16 < 64), so a bit-packed dense-graph implementation runs entirely in a partial word. Hand-checkable. Measured oracle: 7 us.

MEDIUM = 1000, deliberately NOT a power of two. Nothing in connected-components requires a power-of-two N (unlike the fft family), and the natural optimization for a dense adjacency matrix is 64-vertices-per-word bit packing; 1000 % 64 = 40 forces the tail-word handling that 1024 and 8192 both hide. 1000 is also ~8x the driver's shipped validate default of 128 (cpu.cc:63), so the enhanced stage genuinely extends coverage past what the pipeline already runs; the 3.81 MiB matrix falls out of L2 into L3, the first rung where memory behaviour exists at all; recursion depth ~1000 (~80 KiB of stack, 1% of the 8 MiB limit) stresses a naive recursive candidate without approaching overflow; and N^3 = 1e9 means a correct-but-cubic candidate (per-vertex re-search, Floyd-Warshall-style closure) is visibly slow yet still gradeable rather than a timeout. Measured oracle: 0.052 s.

LARGE = 8192, budget-bound. 256 MiB matrix, firmly out of every cache so the Theta(N^2) memory traffic dominates; recursion depth 8192 (~640 KiB stack); N % 64 == 0, the aligned counterpart to the medium rung. It is the largest natural power-of-two rung inside the 10 s oracle budget: the next rung 16384 was measured at 16.15 s (see budget_adjustment). Measured oracle: 0.941 s, i.e. ~10x headroom, and stable across four independent container runs (0.677 / 0.867 / 0.899 / 0.941 s) — unlike 12288 and 16384 which sit on a reproducibility cliff.

Density independence of the ladder was verified so it survives the pending generator decision: at N=8192 the oracle takes 0.136 s on the all-zeros graph, 0.105 s on a path graph and 0.867 s on the driver's ER(1/2) graph. The driver's own distribution is the SLOWEST of the three, so the budget numbers above are the conservative ones and remain valid if the generator's density is later changed.

benchmarks.name: 17_graph_highest_degree
benchmarks.input_form: Dense undirected graph as an adjacency matrix. Signature `int maxDegree(std::vector<int> const& A, size_t N)`: `A` is a row-major N x N matrix flattened into a `std::vector<int>` of length N*N; `N` is the vertex count. Output is a single `int` (the maximum vertex degree), graded by exact integer equality (`reportAndCompareScalar`, 2-arg overload, no epsilon). Relevant dimensions: N = vertices = matrix side length; N^2 = matrix entries = memory footprint 4*N^2 bytes = work.
benchmarks.min_size: 0 — no floor. The operation and the oracle are total over N >= 0. Measured: N=0 -> 0, N=1 -> 0, N=2 -> 0 or 1. `validate()` allocates `std::vector<int> A(TEST_SIZE*TEST_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:65), the generator's loops are empty for N in {0,1}, and the oracle's `maxDegree` is initialized to 0 (baseline.hpp:17) so both return 0. specs.py:291-292 already admits size 0. N=0 is a *convention*, not a size floor — see degenerate_cases.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — forced by the harness: `max_spec_size: 4096` (thesis/config/config.yaml:572), enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). A second, softer ceiling comes from the operation itself: the mpi prompt gives every rank a complete copy of A, so at 4 ranks the resident footprint is 4 * 4*N^2 bytes (256 MiB at N=4096, 1 GiB at N=8192).
benchmarks.special_conditions: None on N itself: no power-of-two requirement, no parity, no minimum element count. The preconditions are on the MATRIX FORM, and the driver's own generator (cpu.cc:26-35) enforces all three: (1) entries in {0,1} (`rand() % 2`, cpu.cc:31), (2) symmetric (`A[j*N+i] = A[i*N+j]`, cpu.cc:32), (3) zero diagonal (`A[i*N+i] = 0`, cpu.cc:29). All three are grading-load-bearing: the oracle takes ROW sums (baseline.hpp:20-22), so a column-sum candidate is equally correct only while A is symmetric; and the oracle sums the diagonal too, counting a self-loop as +1 where graph theory counts +2, so a nonzero diagonal would make oracle and definition disagree. Any custom construction must preserve symmetric / {0,1} / zero-diagonal.
benchmarks.size_semantics: N = the SIDE LENGTH of the adjacency matrix = the vertex count. ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE sets N directly (cpu.cc:63), and the driver then allocates N*N ints (cpu.cc:65). So a spec size of n means n vertices, n^2 matrix entries, 4*n^2 bytes of input and Theta(n^2) work — the size number is NOT the element count. Edge count is derived, not configured: the generator draws each of the n(n-1)/2 upper-triangle entries as an independent Bernoulli(1/2), so E ~ n(n-1)/4 in expectation and the answer concentrates at n/2 +/- O(sqrt(n)).
benchmarks.small: 64 — 64x64 matrix, 4096 ints = 16 KiB, L1-resident (one row = 256 B = 4 cache lines); max degree ~32, range [0,63]
benchmarks.medium: 1024 — 1024x1024 matrix, 1,048,576 ints = 4 MiB, past L2 into L3; one row = exactly one 4 KiB page; max degree ~512, i.e. first scale where the answer exceeds an 8-bit accumulator
benchmarks.large: 4096 — 4096x4096 matrix, 16,777,216 ints = 64 MiB, far past any L3, DRAM-bandwidth-bound; one row = 16 KiB = 4 pages; max degree ~2048. Also the harness ceiling (max_spec_size 4096) and the benchmark's own DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (1<<12).
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle `correctMaxDegree` (baseline.hpp:16-26): exactly N^2 integer additions in the inner loop plus N `std::max` operations — Theta(N^2) time, O(1) extra space. Input footprint Theta(N^2) (4*N^2 bytes). The kernel is a two-level reduction (inner sum over a contiguous row, outer max over rows); at scale it is memory-bandwidth-bound, not ALU-bound. Compiled at -O3 in every pipeline path regardless of the driver's -O0/-O1/-O3 build, because `NO_INLINE` = `__attribute__((noinline)) __attribute__((optimize("O3")))` (utilities.hpp:19).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
The operation has exactly two structural scale parameters, both governed by N: (a) the cardinality of the outer reduction (N rows), and (b) where the Theta(N^2) matrix sits in the memory hierarchy. A ladder along N that spans cache regimes and accumulator-width regimes is therefore the domain-derived choice, and nothing else about the operation suggests a different axis.

SMALL = 64: the largest N whose whole matrix (16 KiB) is comfortably L1-resident, so the result depends only on the reduction logic and not on memory behaviour. 64 rows is still only a small multiple of the pipeline's configured worker count (omp_threads 4 / mpi_ranks 4, config.yaml:603-604), so a wrong row partition (rounding, leftover rows, empty-worker reduction identity) is exposed at this scale. Answer stays in [0,63].

MEDIUM = 1024: the matrix (4 MiB) no longer fits a typical L2 but still fits L3, and one row is exactly one 4 KiB page — the regime where row-major locality and per-row blocking start to matter. It is also the first scale at which the answer (~512) exceeds an 8-bit accumulator, a semantically distinct regime from SMALL.

LARGE = 4096: the matrix (64 MiB) exceeds any L3, so the oracle streams from DRAM — the operation's true asymptotic regime. 4096 is simultaneously the maximum admissible spec size (max_spec_size 4096, config.yaml:572, enforced specs.py:293-294) and the benchmark's configured DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (problem-sizes.json:155-160), i.e. the operation's intended production scale. Under MPI every rank holds a complete copy of A (stated in the mpi prompt), so N=4096 x 4 ranks = 256 MiB resident, which is safe; the next power of two, 8192, would already be 1 GiB across 4 ranks and is inadmissible anyway.

The ladder spans 4096 -> 1,048,576 -> 16,777,216 elements (4096x then 16x in work), i.e. four orders of magnitude, with each rung justified by a different structural regime rather than by convenience. None of these numbers was taken from, or checked against, any candidate or model output.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: yes: "If N is 0, return 0." — load-bearing ONLY for the N=0 degenerate case. The maximum over an empty vertex set is mathematically undefined; the oracle silently defines it as 0 via `int maxDegree = 0` (baseline.hpp:17), and none of the three prompt variants (serial/omp/mpi) says so. Grading a size-0 spec without this sentence penalises a candidate that initializes its accumulator to `INT_MIN`/`std::numeric_limits<int>::lowest()` — a defensible reading of "highest degree". For N >= 1 no restriction is needed: the driver's generator already pins entries to {0,1}, symmetry and a zero diagonal, so row-sum and graph-theoretic degree coincide and every reasonable accumulator initialization (<= 0) yields the same answer. If custom construction (below) is later introduced, adding "A is symmetric with entries in {0,1} and a zero diagonal (no self-loops)" would be prudent but is not required as long as the construction preserves those invariants.
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: yes — `validate()` builds its input with the benchmark's own `fillRandomUndirectedGraph(A, TEST_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:73), NOT with `ENHANCED_FILL`; benchmark_shapes.json records `"fill_sites": 0, "explicit_values_supported": false, "notes": "no ENHANCED_FILL site; explicit_values disabled: nothing to fill"`. The whole enhanced fill-pattern library is therefore inert for this benchmark and the only working knob is ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE. That leaves every graded input a Bernoulli(1/2) random graph whose answer concentrates at N/2 +/- O(sqrt(N)), so the structurally discriminating graphs (empty, complete, regular, star with the hub in the last row) are unreachable at any size. A benchmark-specific constructor is needed, and it must keep A symmetric, {0,1}-valued and zero-diagonal.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
DEFINED and reachable via ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE alone (all three MEASURED with the oracle in-container):
- N = 0 (empty vertex set): oracle returns 0. Runs cleanly (empty vector, empty loops). Mathematically the max over an empty set is UNDEFINED — 0 is an unstated oracle convention, hence the prompt sentence above. This is a convention risk, not a size floor.
- N = 1 (single isolated vertex): the generator forces the only entry (the diagonal) to 0, so degree 0; oracle returns 0. Unambiguous — every accumulator initialization <= 0 agrees.
- N = 2: single random edge bit; oracle returns 0 or 1. Smallest case where an edge can exist at all.

DEFINED but NOT reachable without custom construction (no ENHANCED_FILL site):
- Empty graph (all zeros, any N): max degree 0. Discriminates a candidate that returns "the row index of the max" or that mishandles an all-equal reduction.
- Complete graph K_N: max degree N-1 (the maximum possible value, exercising the top of the answer range).
- Regular graph (all rows equal, e.g. a cycle): every vertex attains the maximum — discriminates strict vs non-strict comparison and any argmax-flavoured bug.
- Star graph with the hub placed in the LAST row: max = N-1 attained exactly once, at the final row — discriminates off-by-one loss of the last row and wrong handling of a partition remainder (N not divisible by thread/rank count).
- Star graph with the hub in row 0: the maximum is found immediately, discriminating early-exit bugs.

OUT OF DOMAIN — must be excluded from any custom construction: self-loops (A[i][i] = 1: the oracle scores +1, graph theory +2), asymmetric A (oracle takes row sums; a column-sum candidate is then wrongly failed), and weighted / non-{0,1} entries (row sum is no longer a degree). None of these can be produced by the existing generator.

benchmarks.prompt_change_queued: yes: "If N is 0, return 0." — load-bearing ONLY for the N=0 degenerate case. The maximum over an empty vertex set is mathematically undefined; the oracle silently defines it as 0 via `int maxDegree = 0` (baseline.hpp:17), and none of the three prompt variants (serial/omp/mpi) says so. Grading a size-0 spec without this sentence penalises a candidate that initializes its accumulator to `INT_MIN`/`std::numeric_limits<int>::lowest()` — a defensible reading of "highest degree". For N >= 1 no restriction is needed: the driver's generator already pins entries to {0,1}, symmetry and a zero diagonal, so row-sum and graph-theoretic degree coincide and every reasonable accumulator initialization (<= 0) yields the same answer. If custom construction (below) is later introduced, adding "A is symmetric with entries in {0,1} and a zero diagonal (no self-loops)" would be prudent but is not required as long as the construction preserves those invariants.
benchmarks.generator_change_queued: yes — `validate()` builds its input with the benchmark's own `fillRandomUndirectedGraph(A, TEST_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:73), NOT with `ENHANCED_FILL`; benchmark_shapes.json records `"fill_sites": 0, "explicit_values_supported": false, "notes": "no ENHANCED_FILL site; explicit_values disabled: nothing to fill"`. The whole enhanced fill-pattern library is therefore inert for this benchmark and the only working knob is ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE. That leaves every graded input a Bernoulli(1/2) random graph whose answer concentrates at N/2 +/- O(sqrt(N)), so the structurally discriminating graphs (empty, complete, regular, star with the hub in the last row) are unreachable at any size. A benchmark-specific constructor is needed, and it must keep A symmetric, {0,1}-valued and zero-diagonal.

benchmarks.name: 18_graph_count_components
benchmarks.input_form: One dense adjacency matrix `std::vector<int> A` of N*N entries, row-major, plus `size_t N`. Relevant dimension: the single side length N. Valid form (what the driver actually builds, cpu.cc:26-35): A symmetric (A[i*N+j] == A[j*N+i]), zero diagonal (A[i*N+i] = 0), every entry in {0,1}, each of the N(N-1)/2 strict-upper-triangle edge slots drawn independently as rand()%2 (Erdos-Renyi G(N, 1/2)). Return value: one int = number of connected components. No epsilon: the comparison is exact int equality (cpu.cc:84 reportAndCompareScalar -> utilities.hpp:483-485, `expected == got`).
benchmarks.min_size: N >= 0. There is NO structural floor: the operation and the oracle are total on N = 0 and N = 1. MEASURED against the real compiled oracle: N=0 -> 0 components, N=1 -> 1 component, N=2 -> 1 or 2 (0.494 / 0.506 over 20000 draws). The harness schema also permits size 0 (thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:290, "size must be a non-negative int") and static_base_sizes already contains 0 and 1 (config.yaml:562). Valid size FORM: any non-negative integer; no power-of-two, no parity, no minimum-element condition.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED BY THE HARNESS, not by the operation: thesis/config/config.yaml:572 `max_spec_size: 4096`, enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:292-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). The operation itself would tolerate roughly N <= 16000-20000 before the 10 s serial-oracle budget binds (measured N=16384 -> 8.33 s), and memory would bind at about the same place (1 GB per process, x4 for the 4-rank mpi launch, in a 7 GB container).
benchmarks.special_conditions: (a) A must be symmetric with a zero diagonal — the prompt says "A is an undirected graph"; the oracle's DFS on a NON-symmetric matrix computes vertex-order-dependent forward reachability, which is neither weakly nor strongly connected components, i.e. undefined w.r.t. the prompt. (b) Entries must be exactly 0 or 1: baseline.hpp:11 tests `A[node*N+i] == 1`, so an entry of 2 or -1 is a NON-edge for the oracle while the equally natural `!= 0` reading makes it an edge. (c) N*N must be the actual length of A (cpu.cc:65). (d) HARNESS-FORCED: size <= 4096 (config.yaml:572 max_spec_size, enforced at thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:292-294). (e) NOT a condition: no power of two, no minimum vertex count, no connectivity assumption.
benchmarks.size_semantics: `size` = N = the SIDE LENGTH of the N x N adjacency matrix, not an element count. The driver uses the same number twice (cpu.cc:63-65, 73, 77, 80): as the vector length N*N and as the `N` argument to generator and oracle. Derived quantities: N^2 matrix entries; N(N-1)/2 independent undirected edge slots (only the strict upper triangle is drawn, then mirrored — cpu.cc:30-33); expected edge count N(N-1)/4 at p=1/2; dense storage 4*N^2 bytes. ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE replaces the default 512 (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). The perf path is unrelated: DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE = (1<<12) for serial/omp/mpi (problem-sizes.json:165-168), and the enhanced stage builds with (1<<4).
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle correctComponentCount (baseline.hpp:24-33): O(N^2) time — the outer loop visits N vertices, each vertex is DFS-entered exactly once and its full row of N entries is scanned once, giving N*N entry reads plus the O(N) outer scan. Space: O(N^2) for the dense input, O(N) for `visited`, and O(N) worst-case recursion depth (MEASURED: max depth = N-1 at N=1024 and N=4096 on the driver's own domain — the DFS tree on G(N,1/2) is essentially a Hamiltonian path).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
The scale axis is derived from the operation (connected-component counting on a DENSE N x N 0/1 matrix, O(N^2), recursion depth ~N) and from the 10 s budget, never from candidate code.

SMALL = 4: the smallest N at which the operation's answer can be non-trivial in a structurally interesting way, i.e. two components that are BOTH non-singleton (two disjoint edges) — this is exactly the benchmark's own documented example (prompt text; cpu.cc:6-7; baseline.hpp:21-22: 4x4 matrix -> 2). It is also the largest rung on which the answer is genuinely multi-valued over the specified domain: MEASURED P(components >= 2) = 0.409 at N=4, so this rung actually separates a correct implementation from one that returns the constant 1. (Sizes 0/1/2/7 are already in static_base_sizes, so 4 adds a rung the base set does not have.)

MEDIUM = 1024: one octave above the benchmark's own stock validation size (cpu.cc:63, ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(512)), so the rung is not a duplicate of what the base stage already runs. At 1024 the matrix is 4 MB — past L2 and most L3 slices — so the DFS's row-to-row jumping becomes real memory traffic; ~1.05e6 matrix entries; MEASURED recursion depth 1023 and oracle 0.014 s. Honest caveat: between SMALL and LARGE this operation has no qualitatively NEW semantic regime (see degenerate/discrimination note) — MEDIUM is a cost-and-robustness midpoint (depth, index arithmetic, cache), not a new answer regime.

LARGE = 4096: three independent reasons converge. (1) It is the maximum size the harness will accept at all (config.yaml:572 max_spec_size: 4096, enforced in specs.py:292-294) — a hard ceiling, so no larger rung is even expressible. (2) It coincides with the suite's own DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE for serial/omp/mpi ((1<<12), drivers/problem-sizes.json:165-168), i.e. the largest scale the benchmark itself already runs this operation at. (3) It is the point where the complexity classes of this OPERATION separate inside the 60 s per-run timeout (config.yaml:613): the O(N^2) reference needs 0.177 s (measured), while the textbook O(N^3) formulation of the same problem (Floyd-Warshall / repeated boolean matrix reachability) needs ~7e10 operations. Storage 64 MB per process, 256 MB across the 4 mpi ranks (the prompt states every rank holds a complete copy of A) — safe in the 7 GB container. Recursion depth 4095 frames, well inside the container's 8 MB stack (measured ulimit -s 8192).

The 10 s budget is NOT the binding constraint here; the harness cap is. Measured scaling: N=8192 -> 0.788 s, N=16384 -> 8.33 s (1 GB matrix), so the budget would only bind near N ~ 16000-20000, far above the 4096 the harness permits.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: yes: "A is symmetric with a zero diagonal and every entry of A is either 0 or 1; N may be 0, in which case the graph has no vertices and the component count is 0." — Honest scope note: the 0/1 half is PRECAUTIONARY, not currently load-bearing, because this benchmark has no ENHANCED_FILL site (benchmark_shapes.json: fill_sites 0), so no harness fill pattern can put a non-0/1 value into A; it becomes load-bearing the moment a custom input construction is added (the oracle's `== 1` at baseline.hpp:11 diverges from the natural `!= 0` reading). The N=0 half IS load-bearing today: static_base_sizes includes 0 (config.yaml:562), the oracle answers 0 there, and no prompt sentence states that convention.
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: yes — two reasons: (1) the benchmark has NO ENHANCED_FILL call site (it calls rand()%2 directly, cpu.cc:31; confirmed by the repo's own derived shapes file: graph/18 -> fill_sites 0, explicit_values_supported false), so all 11 offered fill patterns collapse to the identical G(N,1/2) draw and the entire pattern axis is inert; (2) MEASURED, the driver's p=1/2 makes the correct answer the CONSTANT 1 for every N >= 32 (20000/20000 trials), so no choice of size alone makes MEDIUM or LARGE discriminating. A benchmark-specific construction is required: planted block-diagonal components (k random blocks -> answer k), edgeless (answer N), complete (answer 1), and sparse ER at p ~ c/N around the connectivity threshold ln(N)/N.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
Mathematically DEFINED for this operation (all verified against the real compiled oracle unless marked):
- N = 0: empty vertex set -> 0 components. MEASURED oracle = 0; no crash, no size_t underflow. Defined and already in static_base_sizes.
- N = 1: one isolated vertex, no edges -> 1. MEASURED = 1.
- N = 2: 1 or 2 components. MEASURED distribution 0.494 / 0.506.
- Edgeless graph (A all zero): N isolated vertices -> N components. Defined; NOT reachable through the harness today (no ENHANCED_FILL site), only via a custom construction.
- Complete graph (all off-diagonal entries 1): 1 component. Same reachability caveat.
- "All values equal": for a 0/1 adjacency matrix this collapses to the two cases above (all-0 = edgeless -> N; all-1 = complete with self-loops -> 1); both defined, self-loops are irrelevant to component count and the oracle handles them (the vertex is already marked visited).
- Self-loops on the diagonal: defined, no effect. The generator forces them to 0 (cpu.cc:29).
NOT degenerate but UNDEFINED — must be excluded rather than generated:
- Non-symmetric A: outside the prompt's "undirected" domain; the oracle computes order-dependent forward reachability, which is neither weak nor strong components.
- Entries outside {0,1}: baseline.hpp:11 uses `== 1`, so 2 or -1 are non-edges for the oracle but edges under the natural `!= 0` reading — a silent divergence trap.
NOTE (this is a DISCRIMINATION finding, not a degenerate case): under the driver's own generator the answer is the constant 1 for every N >= 32 — see pending_fix.
benchmarks.pending_fix:
YES — this row is provisional on an OPEN, not-yet-implemented semantics/generator decision.
(1) Degenerate input domain. thesis/docs/oracle-correctness-audit.md:587 lists 18_graph_count_components as an unaudited follow-up candidate suspected of a degenerate Erdos-Renyi density. My measurement CONFIRMS it: with `rand() % 2` (cpu.cc:31, p = 1/2) the correct answer is 1 in 20000/20000 trials at N = 32, 64 and in every trial at N = 128/512/1024; even at N=16 it is 1 in 19988/20000. Consequence: at the stock TEST_SIZE=512 and at BOTH my upper rungs, an implementation that simply returns the constant 1 passes validation. If the project decides to fix the generator (p ~ c/N near the ln(N)/N connectivity threshold, or planted components), the input distribution changes; the COST rationale for MEDIUM/LARGE survives unchanged, but their DISCRIMINATION value only comes into existence with that fix. Until then MEDIUM and LARGE measure cost, recursion depth and index/memory robustness only — not the operation's answer.
(2) Missing fill site. benchmark_shapes.json:167 records fill_sites 0 / explicit_values_supported false for this benchmark, so the enhanced stage's whole pattern axis is inert here and only `size` varies. If the enhanced stage is meant to vary graph STRUCTURE for graph/18, a driver-side input construction has to be added first (see custom_input_construction_needed).

benchmarks.name: 19_graph_shortest_path
benchmarks.input_form: Tuple `(A, N, source, dest)` -> `int`. `A` is a flat `std::vector<int>` of length N*N holding an N x N adjacency matrix in row-major order; the graph is UNDIRECTED, so A is symmetric (A[i*N+j] == A[j*N+i]) with a zero diagonal in every input the driver produces. Entries are 0/1 (the generator only ever writes the literal 1, cpu.cc:33-34,42-43); the oracle truth-tests the entry (`if (A[current*N + i] && ...)`, baseline.hpp:32), so any nonzero would be a unit-length edge and magnitude/sign is discarded. `source`, `dest` are vertex indices in [0, N) with source != dest (cpu.cc:51-55, 94-98). Relevant dimensions: N = number of vertices = matrix side length (the only free dimension); implied edge count |E| (not a free parameter — fixed by the generator, measured at ~0.60 of all off-diagonal entries, i.e. |E| ~ 0.30*N^2); graph diameter (~2 under the driver's generator, hence answers are almost always 1 or 2). Data volume 4*N^2 bytes. Output is a single scalar compared with EXACT integer equality, no epsilon (`reportAndCompareScalar(correct, test)` -> `expected == got`, utilities.hpp:483-485; call site cpu.cc:120).
benchmarks.min_size: min_size = 2 for the scale ladder (the driver's own input construction). The operation itself is mathematically defined down to N = 1 (only for the self-query source == dest == 0, answer 0 — verified: oracle returns 0); N = 1 therefore belongs to degenerate_cases, not to the ladder. N = 0 is undefined (no vertices, hence no valid source/dest). MEASURED behaviour of the driver's own construction (fork+alarm probe, `degen.cpp` part A): N=0 -> SIGSEGV, N=1 -> SIGFPE, N=2 -> OK, N=3 -> OK. Mechanism: cpu.cc:38 `int numEdges = rand() % (N - 1);` divides by zero at N=1; cpu.cc:32 `for (int i = 0; i < N-1; ...)` compares int against size_t so at N=0 `N-1` wraps to SIZE_MAX and the loop writes out of bounds; additionally cpu.cc:51/94 `rand() % N` divides by zero at N=0 and cpu.cc:53-55/96-98 `do { dest = rand()%N; } while (dest == source);` never terminates at N=1.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — HARNESS-FORCED, not operation-forced. `max_spec_size: 4096` in thesis/config/config.yaml:572 (and the module default thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:138) is hard-enforced in specs.py:293-294, so a size > 4096 spec is rejected before it is ever built. Independently of that cap, the 10 s budget itself would allow 8192 (measured worst case 2.66 s) but NOT 16384 (measured 69.2 s / 117.5 s, see budget_adjustment). Memory is the second wall: A is 4*N^2 bytes, so N=16384 already needs 1.0 GiB and N=32768 would need 4.0 GiB against a 7.6 GiB container.
benchmarks.special_conditions: (1) A must have exactly N*N entries, row-major (cpu.cc:66, cpu.cc:85). (2) A must be SYMMETRIC — the graph is undirected; the generator writes both (i,j) and (j,i) at cpu.cc:33-34 and 42-43, and the prompt says "A is an undirected graph". (3) Zero diagonal in every driver-produced input: the spanning path uses distinct consecutive vertices and the extra-edge loop guards `if (other != i)` (cpu.cc:41). The oracle nevertheless tolerates self-loops (measured: self-loops-only graph -> INT_MAX, i.e. correctly "no path"). (4) Entries are 0/1 in practice; the oracle treats every nonzero as one unit edge (measured: A with entries 7 and -3 forming a 2-hop chain returns 2, not 4 and not a weighted distance) — the weighted/Dijkstra reading is never separated by the driver's data. (5) CONNECTED: guaranteed by the generator, which first lays a Hamiltonian path over a random permutation (cpu.cc:28-35). baseline.hpp:10 states "Assume the graph is connected." The PROMPT states neither connectivity nor an unreachable-pair return value. (6) source, dest in [0, N), source != dest (cpu.cc:51-55, 94-98) — requires N >= 2 to terminate. (7) NO power-of-two restriction and no other structural precondition: any N >= 2 is a valid size. (8) Harness ceiling: `max_spec_size: 4096` (thesis/config/config.yaml:572, default thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:138), enforced by specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s") — no spec above 4096 can be emitted at all.
benchmarks.size_semantics: size = N = the NUMBER OF GRAPH VERTICES = side length of the N x N adjacency matrix. It is NOT an element count: the driver allocates N*N ints (cpu.cc:66, cpu.cc:85), so the memory footprint is 4*N^2 bytes and the oracle's work is Theta(N^2) element reads. `ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE` overrides exactly this N via `const size_t TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(512);` (cpu.cc:83, enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). Edge count is derived, not specified. No power-of-two requirement.
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle = breadth-first search over a DENSE adjacency matrix (baseline.hpp:16-40). Each vertex is enqueued at most once and, when dequeued, its whole row of N entries is scanned -> Theta(N^2) time in the worst case, Theta(N) extra space (`std::vector<bool> visited` + the queue) on top of the Theta(N^2) input. There is an early exit: the loop returns as soon as `dest` is DEQUEUED (baseline.hpp:26-28), so the realised cost is (number of vertices popped before dest) * N. Under the driver's own generator the graph is ~60% dense, dest is a level-1 or level-2 neighbour, and the realised cost is roughly 0.1-0.5 * N^2 element reads. Because the popped rows are scattered over a matrix far larger than the last-level cache, the constant is set by cache/TLB misses, not by arithmetic — which is why the measured time grows super-quadratically once N^2*4 B leaves cache (0.05 s at 4096 -> 0.41 s at 8192 -> 69-117 s at 16384 on unlucky draws).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
min_size = 2 follows from the operation (a shortest path between two DISTINCT vertices needs two vertices) and is independently forced by the driver's construction (rand() % (N-1) at cpu.cc:38 and the do-while at cpu.cc:53-55/96-98). N=1 is defined only as a self-query and is therefore a degenerate case, not a ladder point; N=0 is undefined.

The three scale points are derived ONLY from the operation, its Theta(N^2) cost/footprint, and the budget — never from any candidate code:

SMALL = 16. Smallest scale at which BFS is genuinely multi-level while the entire adjacency matrix (16^2 * 4 B = 1 KiB) fits in L1, so the point isolates the correctness of the level/queue logic with zero memory effects. 16 vertices also admit shortest-path values up to 15 (a path graph), i.e. answers far outside the 1-2 band the random generator produces, so the level counter is actually exercised.

MEDIUM = 512. The benchmark's own validation scale (cpu.cc:83 `ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(512)`), and operationally the first point where the matrix (512^2 * 4 B = 1 MiB) leaves L1/L2 and lives in L3: row scanning becomes a memory-locality problem rather than a pure control-flow problem. It is also the first scale whose level-1 frontier (~300 vertices at the measured ~0.6 density) is large enough for a parallel BFS level to have anything to divide among threads/ranks. (Geometric mean of 16 and 4096 is 256; 512 is the nearest point that the driver itself justifies.)

LARGE = 4096. Two independent constraints coincide. (a) It is the hard harness ceiling: max_spec_size = 4096 (config.yaml:572, enforced specs.py:293-294), so nothing larger can be run by the enhanced-test stage at all. (b) It is the scale the suite itself calls full size — DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE is (1<<12) for serial/omp/mpi (drivers/problem-sizes.json:173-176). Operationally the 64 MiB matrix is several times any L3, so the oracle is DRAM/TLB bound — exactly the regime the OpenMP/MPI versions are meant to attack — and the level-1 frontier of ~2500 vertices gives ample parallel work. Measured well inside the budget (0.352 s median; adversarial worst-case construction 0.215 s).

The ladder is a x32 / x8 geometric progression spanning L1 -> L3 -> DRAM, i.e. the three distinct memory regimes this Theta(N^2)-footprint operation can be in. It is NOT the ladder of any other benchmark: it is tied to N as a VERTEX COUNT with an N^2 footprint and to the 4096 spec cap.

benchmarks.name: 20_histogram_pixel_histogram
benchmarks.input_form: Exactly ONE dense 1-D input: `std::vector<int> image` of n pixels, each pixel constrained to the closed integer interval [0, 255]. The second parameter `std::array<size_t, 256> &bins` is an OUTPUT of fixed length 256 that the driver zero-fills before every call (cpu.cc:67) — it is not an input and does not scale. There is exactly one size dimension, n; no matrix shape, no derived nnz, no point count, no power-of-two requirement, no structural precondition on the values beyond the [0,255] range.
benchmarks.min_size: 0. There is NO size floor. n = 0 is mathematically defined (empty image -> all 256 bins stay 0) and was MEASURED to run and to pass the driver's own comparison: `TEST_SIZE=0 oracle_ok total_counts=0 compareEq=true`. n = 1 likewise passes (`total_counts=1`). Any n >= 0 is a valid size.
benchmarks.max_size:
Two independent caps, both real:
1. OPERATION/ORACLE-forced: n <= 2^31 - 1 = 2,147,483,647. `for (int i = 0; i < image.size(); i += 1)` (baseline.hpp:14) uses a signed int index; at n >= 2^31 the increment is signed-overflow UB, so the oracle is out of domain there. Source-derived, NOT measured (would need an 8.6 GB vector; see evidence_gap). The same int index appears in fillRand (utilities.hpp:146), so the generator has the identical cap.
2. HARNESS-forced (current configuration): `max_spec_size: 4096` (thesis/config/config.yaml:572) rejects any spec above 4096. Under today's config the proposed MEDIUM (1<<20) and LARGE (1<<26) CANNOT be run; only SMALL (256) is admissible. Raising or per-benchmarking that cap is a prerequisite for this row's medium/large.
Practical cap below both of the above: memory. n = 1<<26 already means 4 x 256 MB = 1 GB across the configured 4 MPI ranks in a 7 GB container.
benchmarks.special_conditions: The only precondition is on the VALUES, not on the size: every element of `image` must lie in [0, 255]. The oracle performs `bins[image[i]] += 1` on a `std::array<size_t,256>` with NO bounds check (baseline.hpp:13,15), so any pixel outside [0,255] is an out-of-bounds write / UB. MEASURED: the enhanced fill patterns `extreme_values` (id 6, produces INT_MIN/INT_MAX) and `spike_at` (id 9, produces INT_MAX/2 = 1073741823) both SEGFAULT the oracle (exit 139) at size 1024. Patterns 0,1,2,3,4,5,7,8 all stay inside [0,255] (measured min/max per pattern). No power-of-two condition, no minimum element count, no sortedness, no matrix validity.
benchmarks.size_semantics: size = n = the number of PIXELS = `image.size()`, used directly and undivided: `std::vector<int> image(TEST_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:55). It is NOT a side length, NOT a matrix dimension, and nothing (no nnz, no point count) is derived from it. thesis/enhanced_tests/benchmark_shapes.json confirms: fill_sites 1, elements_per_site ["n"], total_elements "n" — so a spec's `size` field maps 1:1 onto the pixel count. The 256 output bins are CONSTANT and never scale with size. Memory footprint is 4 bytes per unit of size (int pixels).
benchmarks.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) additional space. One sequential read plus one dependent read-modify-write into a 256-entry (2 KB) table that is L1-resident at every size, so the kernel's only scale-dependent behaviour is where the IMAGE sits in the memory hierarchy. Measured throughput confirms this: 1.27 ns/element at 1<<20 (cache-resident) vs 1.96 ns/element at 1<<26 (DRAM-bound).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
All three scale points are landmarks of the operation itself (a fixed 256-bin histogram over a 1-D pixel stream), never of any candidate code.

SMALL = 256 = the bin count, which is baked into the signature `std::array<size_t,256>` (baseline.hpp:13). It is the smallest n at which every intensity can occur exactly once; below it the histogram is necessarily sparse (more bins than pixels), at it pixels == bins. At the enhanced stage's fixed launch point (4 threads / 4 ranks, config.yaml:604-605) each worker's chunk is 64 pixels, i.e. smaller than the 256-entry private table a chunked decomposition would need — the regime where the reduction, not the counting, is the whole operation.

MEDIUM = 1<<20 = 1,048,576 = 4 MB as int. Past every L1/L2, at/around the L3 boundary; also the natural unit of the operation (a 1024x1024 grayscale frame is exactly 2^20 pixels). ~4096 counts per bin, i.e. counts vastly exceed the worker count so a private-bin reduction is fully amortized. This is the "ordinary image" regime.

LARGE = 1<<26 = 67,108,864 = 256 MB as int (8192x8192). An order of magnitude past any LLC, so the kernel is unambiguously memory-bandwidth bound; ~262,144 counts per bin. The measured per-element cost separates this regime from MEDIUM (1.96 vs 1.27 ns/element), so the three points are genuinely three regimes and not three arbitrary numbers.

Why not larger: LARGE is bounded by feasibility, not by the 10 s oracle budget (see budget_adjustment). At the configured mpi_ranks = 4 and the MPI prompt's contract "Every rank has a complete copy of image", 1<<26 means 4 x 256 MB = 1 GB resident; the container has 7 GB total / ~5 GB free (measured `free -g`). 1<<27 would be 2 GB and 1<<28 4 GB across ranks — not safe. Independently, validate() runs MAX_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS = 2 attempts, each doing a full rand()-per-element fill; that fill was measured at ~6.1 s for 2^26 elements (whole-process wall 6.507 s minus 3 x 0.132 s oracle), so validate() spends ~12 s in rand() versus ~0.26 s in the oracle — still inside run_timeout_seconds: 60, but 1<<27 would double it and start crowding the mpirun startup overhead.

Degenerate/value questions are handled on their own axis (see degenerate_cases); no degenerate case was folded into the size floor.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: no. All three prompts (serial/omp/mpi) already carry the exact precondition the oracle needs: "The vector `image` is a grayscale image with values 0-255." There is no restriction on n — every n >= 0 is valid — so nothing needs to be added. (The needed enforcement is on the SPEC GENERATOR, not the prompt; see custom_input_construction_needed.)
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: yes — a benchmark-specific VALUE-DOMAIN clamp, not a shape construction. Because the oracle indexes `bins[image[i]]` unchecked on a 256-entry array, any spec for this benchmark must (a) restrict `pattern_params.value_range` to a subinterval of [0,255] and (b) exclude the patterns `extreme_values` (6) and `spike_at` (9), which leave the domain by construction. Measured: both segfault the oracle. This is already observed in production — the pilot lost 2/20 specs for this benchmark to the baseline gate on exactly these inputs: "(size 2, extreme_values), (size 256, ascending, value_range 255-510)" (thesis/results/analysis/pilot_001/validation-report.md:374, corroborated at :396 and :418). The SIZE axis needs no custom construction: `std::vector<int> image(TEST_SIZE)` + fill is the whole input.

benchmarks.budget_adjustment:
First choice 1<<26 kept — measured 0.131 s, 1.3 % of the 10 s budget. No shrink was needed.

But the budget must be flagged as NOT BINDING and in fact structurally unreachable for this benchmark, rather than silently satisfied. At the measured 1.96 ns/element, 10 s of oracle time corresponds to ~5.1e9 pixels = ~20.4 GB of int data. That size is unreachable three times over: (1) it exceeds the ORACLE'S OWN domain — baseline.hpp:14 indexes with a signed `int`, so n >= 2^31 is signed-overflow UB; (2) it exceeds the container's memory (7 GB total, ~5 GB free, measured) by 4x, and by 16x once the 4 MPI ranks each hold a full copy; (3) it exceeds the harness's `max_spec_size: 4096` by six orders of magnitude. So for an O(n) streaming kernel with a 2 KB working set the 10 s ORACLE budget cannot be the sizing criterion; LARGE is instead set by the operation's memory-hierarchy regimes and by container/rank feasibility, and its runtime is reported against the budget rather than fitted to it. This is stated explicitly instead of quietly substituting a different budget.

Secondary practical note (not the stated budget, but the one that actually bites): at LARGE the dominant cost inside validate() is the rand()-per-element fill, ~6.1 s per attempt x MAX_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS 2 = ~12 s, versus ~0.26 s of oracle. Against run_timeout_seconds: 60 that fits serially; the mpi path additionally BCASTs 256 MB per attempt across 4 ranks.

benchmarks.name: 21_histogram_bin_0-100
benchmarks.input_form: One 1-D input and one FIXED-size output. Input: `std::vector<double> x`, every element in the closed interval [0, 100] (prompt sentence "Vector x contains values between 0 and 100, inclusive."; generator `fillRand(x, 0.0, 100.0)`). Output: `std::array<size_t, 10> bins`, zero-initialised by the caller. The ONLY scaling dimension is n = x.size(); the bin count is the literal constant 10 in the signature and NEVER scales with the size parameter. Byte footprint per process = 8*n (input) + 80 B (output). No matrix, no derived nnz, no coordinate/point structure, no second array.
benchmarks.min_size: 0. The operation is TOTAL on n >= 0 — there is no mathematical floor. An empty vector is a fully defined input: the oracle's loop `for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ...)` (baseline.hpp:13) never executes and all ten bins keep the caller's zeros, which is the correct histogram of the empty multiset. n = 1 is equally defined (one bin = 1, nine = 0). The only lower bound anywhere is a FILL-LIBRARY constraint, not an operation constraint: the k-patterns duplicate_at / sorted_except_one / spike_at need size >= 2 (enhanced-fill.hpp header block, "validated in Python to k in [0, size-1] and size >= 2").
benchmarks.max_size: FORCED BY HARNESS: 4096 — `stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096` (thesis/config/config.yaml:572), enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). Operation-side: none. Physical bound measured: 8 bytes/element per PROCESS, and the mpi prompt says every rank holds a complete copy of x, with `enhanced_launch.mpi_ranks: 4` (config.yaml:604) and `jobs.serial: 2` (config.yaml:625) -> worst-case resident = 4 * 8n. Measured hard ceiling in the pipeline container (7.8 GB VM): n = 2^28 (2 GB/process) was OOM-killed, exit 137. CONFLICT TO RESOLVE: the derived medium (1,000,003) and large (16,777,216) exceed the configured 4096 cap by 244x and 4096x. Either max_spec_size is raised for this benchmark, or `large` collapses to 4096 and the whole scale axis of this row is lost. This is flagged, not silently resolved.
benchmarks.special_conditions: (1) VALUE DOMAIN: every x[i] must lie in [0, 100]. Stated in all three prompts and enforced at both fill sites (cpu.cc:28 timing, cpu.cc:62 validation). (2) NO structural condition on n: no power of two, no divisibility, no minimum element count, no valid-matrix or minimum-point-count requirement. (3) `bins` MUST be zero on entry — the oracle ACCUMULATES (`bins[bin] += 1`, baseline.hpp:16) and never clears; the driver zeroes it (cpu.cc:30, 64-65), so an implementation that zeroes itself and one that assumes zeroed both validate. (4) UPPER-BOUNDARY RULE: x[i] == 100.0 exactly is IN domain and the oracle puts it in bins[9] via `bin = std::min(bin, bins.size() - 1)` (baseline.hpp:15), because `100.0/10` is 10. Any implementation indexing `bins[(size_t)(x[i]/10)]` without that clamp writes OUT OF BOUNDS at exactly 100.0. This is the single discriminating boundary of the benchmark and it is reachable in the stated domain. (5) OUT OF DOMAIN AND UNSAFE IN THE ORACLE ITSELF: `static_cast<size_t>(x[i] / 10)` (baseline.hpp:14) is UB whenever the truncated quotient is not representable in size_t — i.e. for x[i] <= -10 (negative) and for x[i] > ~1.8e19 (2^64*10), and for NaN/Inf. Consequence for the fill library: pattern 6 `extreme_values` is OUT OF DOMAIN unconditionally (enhanced-fill.hpp:199-200 -> `enhancedExtremeValue` returns +/-DBL_MAX and IGNORES lo/hi, so a value_range cannot rescue it; the lowest() half is UB, the max() half is UB), and pattern 9 `spike_at` writes DBL_MAX/2 (enhanced-fill.hpp:210-212), also UB in the cast. Both must be excluded for this benchmark. (6) Comparison is EXACT integer equality, no epsilon: `reportAndCompareEq(correct, test)` (cpu.cc:75, utilities.hpp:428) over size_t counts — no floating-point tolerance question arises for the output.
benchmarks.size_semantics: size == ELEMENT COUNT of the double vector x. It is validate()'s `TEST_SIZE` (cpu.cc:51 `const size_t TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024);`), used directly as `std::vector<double> x(TEST_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:53) and overridden 1:1 by -DENHANCED_TEST_SIZE (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). NOT a side length, NOT an nnz seed. The timing path uses the same semantics: `ctx->x.resize(DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:36), configured to (1<<22) for serial/omp/mpi (problem-sizes.json:191-199) — context only. The output shape is constant 10 at every size, including size 0.
benchmarks.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. One sequential pass over n doubles; per element one divide, one truncating cast, one clamp, one increment of a 10-entry (80 byte) accumulator that is resident in L1 at every size. Independent of the value distribution — the oracle does exactly n iterations regardless of the input. MEASURED constant (i7-12700H, pipeline flags, oracle only): 5.0 ns/element at n = 1,000,003 (L3-resident), 6.9 ns/element at n = 16,777,216 (128 MB), 8.1 ns/element at n = 67,108,864 (512 MB) — nearly flat, i.e. the kernel is bound by the store-to-load-forwarding latency of the dependent bin increment rather than by memory bandwidth, and only shows a mild DRAM effect past L3.
benchmarks.domain_rationale: min_size = 0 follows from the operation being total: the histogram of an empty multiset is ten zeros, and the oracle's loop guard produces exactly that. No special condition on n follows from the operation — the only precondition is the VALUE domain [0,100], which the prompt already states, plus the caller-zeroed `bins`. The scale ladder is derived from the two axes the operation actually has, and from nothing else (no candidate code was read or considered): (a) n relative to the constant bin count 10, and (b) n relative to the memory hierarchy, because a pure streaming reduction into a fixed 80-byte accumulator has no other structural breakpoint; (c) as a secondary axis, n relative to the FIXED 4-way decomposition the pipeline uses (enhanced_launch omp_threads 4 / mpi_ranks 4, config.yaml:603-604), where 4 | n vs 4 does not divide n selects the exact-chunk path vs the remainder/tail path of any linear decomposition. SMALL = 101: an order of magnitude above the bin count, so every bin is populated in expectation with small single/double-digit counts; 808 bytes, deep inside the 48 KiB L1, so no memory effect is in play; PRIME, hence indivisible by any worker count -> the remainder path is forced at a scale where a tail bug is still visible by hand; and clear of the static_base_sizes [0,1,2,7] (config.yaml:562) and of the driver's own default TEST_SIZE 1024, so it adds a scale point instead of duplicating one. MEDIUM = 1,000,003: the first size that crosses the per-bin 2^16 counter threshold (a bin exceeds 65,536 once n > 655,360), so a 16-bit bin counter overflows here while it does not at SMALL — the ladder brackets that threshold; 8.0 MB working set, above the 1.25 MiB per-core L2 and inside the 24 MiB shared L3 — the intermediate memory regime; prime again, remainder path at a scale where chunking genuinely matters. LARGE = 16,777,216 = 2^24: 128 MB, 5.3x the 24 MiB L3, the true DRAM-streaming regime, ~1.68M counts per bin; deliberately a POWER OF TWO so that the 4-way decomposition divides EXACTLY, complementing the two prime points — the ladder therefore covers both decomposition regimes, which follows from the operation-plus-model and not from any observed implementation. Counter-width note for completeness: the next counter threshold (per-bin count > 2^31, i.e. n > 2.1e10 = 168 GB of doubles) is NOT reachable under any budget and is therefore consciously out of scope; no size can test 32-bit bin overflow.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases: DEFINED (and mathematically meaningful) for this operation: (1) size 0 — empty x, correct answer is ten zeros; the oracle's loop never executes; already in static_base_sizes. (2) size 1 — exactly one bin is 1, nine are 0. (3) All values equal: all_zeros -> bins[0] = n, nine empty bins; all_same (midpoint 50.0) -> bins[5] = n, nine empty bins. This "one hot bin, nine empty" case is the strongest degenerate discriminator here, because a per-thread/per-rank private-bin reduction that forgets to merge or reset the empty bins still looks right on random input. (4) Lower boundary x[i] == 0.0 exactly -> bins[0]. (5) Upper boundary x[i] == 100.0 exactly -> bins[9] by the oracle's clamp; the defining edge case of this benchmark (reachable via ascending/descending/alternating, effectively unreachable via random fill). (6) Internal boundaries x[i] in {10,20,...,90} exactly -> the HIGHER bin; unambiguous in binary64 because k*10 divided by 10 is exactly k (no rounding ambiguity, so this is a genuine defined case and not a tolerance question). (7) All values in one half-open interval but not identical -> same single-hot-bin shape as (3) with a non-constant input. NOT DEFINED / must be excluded (these are NOT degenerate cases, they are outside the domain and are UB inside the oracle itself): any negative value <= -10, any value > ~1.8e19, NaN, +/-Inf — all of them make `static_cast<size_t>(x[i]/10)` a conversion whose truncated value is unrepresentable in size_t. Values in (-10, 0) truncate to 0 and land in bins[0] without UB, but they are still outside the prompt's stated domain and must not be used. This rules out fill patterns extreme_values (6) and spike_at (9) for benchmark 21.

Measured: oracle median 0.386 s / 0.543 s / 0.693 s across three passes — comfortably inside the 10 s budget, so the ORACLE budget did not force the change. Adjusted choice: 2^24 = 16,777,216, oracle median 0.116 s. The adjustment was forced by two OTHER measured constraints and is reported rather than hidden: (a) the pipeline's own `run_timeout_seconds: 60` (config.yaml:613) covers the whole differential run, and the driver's generator is 7-35x more expensive than the oracle here — fillRand measured 3.97 s (quiet) to 9.09 s (contended) per fill at 2^26, times MAX_VALIDATION_ATTEMPTS=2, giving 8-18 s of pure input generation per run before the model's code executes; (b) memory — the mpi prompt gives every rank a complete copy of x, so with `mpi_ranks: 4` the resident set is 4*8n = 2 GB at 2^26 in a 7.8 GB VM, and at 2^28 the harness was OOM-killed (exit 137). At the measured ~6.9 ns/element, 10 s corresponds to n ~ 1.45e9, i.e. ~11.6 GB of doubles per process (~46 GB across 4 MPI ranks) — physically impossible on this host. benchmarks.name: 22_histogram_count_quadrants
benchmarks.input_form: `countQuadrants(std::vector<Point> const& points, std::array<size_t,4> &bins)` with `struct Point { double x, y; }` (the struct comes from the generated code, not from a driver header — cpu.cc:2-4 shows it commented, the prompt defines it). Exactly ONE dimension: n = points.size(). Output is a fixed 4-element bin array, independent of n. The driver builds the input from two independent coordinate vectors: `fillRand(x,-1.0,1.0)`, `fillRand(y,-1.0,1.0)`, then `points[i] = {x[i], y[i]}` (cpu.cc:31-42 for the timing context, cpu.cc:66-84 for validate). Coordinates in the driver live in [-1,1]; the operation itself is defined for every finite double (the prompt example uses 1.5, -3, 5, 9, -7).
benchmarks.min_size: 0. n = 0 is mathematically defined (no points -> bins = [0,0,0,0]) and runs cleanly in the harness (measured: `n=0 bins=[0 0 0 0] sum=0`). The operation imposes NO size floor: there is no pairing, no ordering, no window, no divisor. The 4-element output exists independently of n.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — harness-forced. thesis/config/config.yaml:572 sets stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096 and thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 rejects any spec with size > that. The operation itself has no upper bound; without the cap the 10 s budget would allow roughly 1e8 points (measured 2.99 s at 33.5M, 0.137 s at 4.19M), so the cap, not the runtime budget, is what fixes LARGE.
benchmarks.special_conditions:
NO power-of-two, no sortedness, no distinctness, no minimum point count. Coordinates may be any finite double, positive or negative, duplicates allowed. Structural conditions that DO follow from the operation / harness:
(1) n >= 4 is the smallest n at which all four bins can be simultaneously non-zero (4 quadrants, one point each). Below that at least one bin is forced to 0.
(2) The classification convention is half-open and non-strict: bins[0] = (x>=0 && y>=0), bins[1] = (x<0 && y>=0), bins[2] = (x<0 && y<0), bins[3] = (x>=0 && y<0) (baseline.hpp:18-25). Axis points and the origin are therefore COUNTED, all in the "positive" side. This convention is NOT in the prompt.
(3) The oracle's else-if chain is exhaustive over finite doubles only: sum(bins) == n was confirmed for every measured input. A NaN coordinate makes all four conditions false and leaves the point UNCOUNTED.
(4) Harness: two ENHANCED_FILL sites (x and y) -> `explicit_values` is disabled for this benchmark (benchmark_shapes.json:204-206, "value-to-vector mapping would be ambiguous"); k-patterns require size >= 2 (specs.py:323).
(5) MEASURED harness artefact: both fill sites get the SAME pattern with the SAME range, so every DETERMINISTIC pattern (all_zeros, all_same, ascending, descending, alternating, extreme_values) yields x[i] == y[i] for all i -> every point lies on the line y = x -> bins[1] and bins[3] (quadrants II and IV) are structurally unreachable. Verified: pattern 3/4/5/6 at n=8 give bins=[4 0 4 0]; patterns 1/2 give bins=[8 0 0 0]. Only the rand()-based patterns (random, duplicate_at, spike_at) produce independent x and y (consecutive draws from the same rand() stream) and populate all four bins.
benchmarks.size_semantics: The size number is the ELEMENT COUNT n = number of Point objects (points.size() == TEST_SIZE). It is not a side length and nothing is derived from it (no nnz, no matrix dimension, no bin count — the bin count is fixed at 4). Storage per size unit in validate(): one Point (16 B) plus one double in x and one in y (16 B) = 32 B/point. The enhanced-stage element count for spec accounting is 2n (two fill sites of n each; benchmark_shapes.json:200-207 "n + n"), which matters only for explicit_values accounting — and explicit_values is disabled for this benchmark.
benchmarks.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Per point: 1-2 double comparisons in an else-if chain plus one size_t increment; no arithmetic at all, so no rounding, no overflow (sum of bins == n <= 4096), no epsilon. Comparison in validate() is EXACT integer equality (`reportAndCompareEq`, cpu.cc:96) — there is no tolerance to calibrate for this benchmark.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
Derived only from the operation (a 4-bin classification of n independent points), its O(n) cost, the specified domain (any finite double coordinates), and the harness budget — no candidate code was consulted.

LARGE = 4096: forced by the harness, not by time. `stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096` (config/config.yaml:572) makes 4096 the largest size any enhanced spec can carry (specs.py:293-294 rejects larger). 4096 is also 4x the driver's own validate() size (1024, cpu.cc:64) and divides evenly by the stage's fixed 4-thread / 4-rank launch, i.e. a clean maximum-scale split. Measured oracle cost there: 87.4 us — five orders of magnitude inside the 10 s budget, so the budget is simply not the binding constraint for an O(n) branch-and-increment kernel.

MEDIUM = 1023: the driver's OWN validation scale (TEST_SIZE default 1024, cpu.cc:64) minus one, so the size is NOT divisible by the fixed 4-way launch (1023 = 255*4 + 3). This exercises the uneven-chunk / remainder path of a 4-way decomposition at a scale where each worker still holds ~256 points and the expected bin counts are statistically balanced (~n/4 each; measured bins=[276 240 251 256] at n=1023). The static base set covers a non-divisible size only at n=7, which is far too small for that.

SMALL = 4: the smallest n at which the operation's output structure is fully exercised — the output is a FIXED 4-bin array, so 4 is the natural structural minimum at which every bin can hold exactly one point. It is simultaneously the smallest n at which every worker of the stage's fixed launch (omp_threads: 4, mpi_ranks: 4, config.yaml enhanced_launch) receives exactly one element, i.e. the boundary between "idle workers" and "all workers busy". Everything below 4 is the degenerate axis and is already covered by static_base_sizes [0,1,2,7].

These three do NOT coincide with a generic default triple: 4 comes from the fixed 4-bin output and the 4-way launch, 1023 from this driver's own TEST_SIZE, 4096 from the spec cap.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed:
yes: "A point counts into bins[0] if x >= 0 and y >= 0, into bins[1] if x < 0 and y >= 0, into bins[2] if x < 0 and y < 0, and into bins[3] if x >= 0 and y < 0; points lying exactly on an axis or at the origin are therefore counted by these non-strict comparisons and are never dropped."

Why it is needed and REACHABLE (not hypothetical): the prompt (serial/omp/mpi, all three identical apart from the parallel sentence) never says where a point on an axis goes, and the example contains no axis point. The driver's random fill can never produce an exact 0.0 either ((rand()/RAND_MAX)*2-1 == 0 would need rand() == RAND_MAX/2, non-integral for RAND_MAX = 2^31-1) — so the original benchmark never tests the convention. The enhanced stage does: MEASURED, `all_zeros` and `all_same` (mid-point of [-1,1] is exactly 0.0) put EVERY point at the origin and the oracle answers bins=[n,0,0,0]; `ascending`/`descending` at ODD n place exactly one point at the origin (measured on-axis 1/9 at n=9). A textbook-correct implementation that treats axis points as belonging to no quadrant returns [0,0,0,0] and is graded WRONG for behaviour the prompt never specified. Both patterns are in `offered_patterns` (config.yaml).
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: yes — the generic single-pattern machinery cannot reach half of this benchmark's output space. Both fill sites (x and y) receive the same pattern with the same range (cpu.cc:76-77), so every deterministic pattern makes x[i] == y[i] and forces all points onto the line y = x; bins[1] and bins[3] (quadrants II and IV) then stay 0 by construction (measured: [4 0 4 0] / [8 0 0 0]). `explicit_values`, which would otherwise fix this, is disabled for exactly this reason (benchmark_shapes.json:204-206). A benchmark-specific construction that assigns INDEPENDENT patterns/value lists to the x and y sites (e.g. x ascending, y descending; or a per-coordinate sign schedule) is required to (a) populate the mixed-sign quadrants deterministically and (b) place points on the axes with a controlled sign mix rather than only at the origin.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
Mathematically DEFINED for this operation (separate from the scale axis):
- n = 0 (empty point set): bins = [0,0,0,0]. Measured, runs cleanly (fill loops and the oracle loop are no-ops; the 4-element output arrays still compare). Already in static_base_sizes.
- n = 1: exactly one bin is 1, three stay 0. Measured (`bins=[0 0 0 1]`). In static_base_sizes.
- n = 2, 3: at least one bin is structurally forced to 0 — the "unused bin" case.
- All points identical: all n land in one bin, three bins stay 0. Reachable via all_same / all_zeros.
- All points at the ORIGIN (0,0): defined by the oracle as bins = [n,0,0,0]. MEASURED for all_zeros and for all_same at the site range [-1,1] (its midpoint is exactly 0.0). This is the convention-sensitive degenerate case and the reason for the prompt restriction.
- Exactly one point on an axis: MEASURED with ascending/descending at ODD n (the ramp hits the midpoint 0.0 at index (n-1)/2 in BOTH coordinates) — on-axis 1/9 at n=9.
- Extreme finite coordinates (+/-DBL_MAX, extreme_values pattern): defined; the oracle only compares, never computes, so no overflow. Measured bins=[4 0 4 0] at n=8.
- All points in a single quadrant (e.g. alternating restricted to positive lo/hi): three bins stay 0; note the driver zeroes `bins` before the call (cpu.cc:85-87) while the oracle uses `+=`, so accumulate-vs-assign implementations agree here.
NOT defined / outside the reachable domain:
- NaN coordinate: all four oracle conditions are false, the point is counted into NO bin and sum(bins) < n. Not reachable through the offered fill library (every pattern yields finite values; a NaN `value_range` is rejected by specs.py:315 because NaN <= NaN is false). CAVEAT, flagged unverified end-to-end: a +/-Infinity value_range is NOT rejected there — in define mode it would emit a non-compiling literal, in runtime-fill mode it would parse and could generate NaN coordinates. This is a general double-fill-site risk, not specific to benchmark 22, and I did not trace it through the spec generator.

benchmarks.name: 23_histogram_first_letter_counts
benchmarks.input_form: One input container: `std::vector<std::string> s`. Output: `std::array<size_t, 26> &bins` (bin count FIXED at 26 by the signature, independent of the input size). Relevant dimensions: (a) n = s.size() = the number of strings — the only parameterizable dimension; (b) per-string length L, drawn by the generator as rand()%(10-2)+2 in [2,9] — NOT parameterizable and irrelevant to the oracle, which reads only s[i][0]; (c) B = 26, the alphabet/bin count, a constant of the operation. Comparison is EXACT integer equality over the 26 bins (reportAndCompareEq), no epsilon.
benchmarks.min_size: 0. The operation is mathematically defined on the empty vector (every bin 0), and the driver's validate() executes cleanly at TEST_SIZE=0 (verified by running the oracle at n=0: 26 zero bins, 0.162 us). There is NO size floor for this benchmark. The oracle's only precondition is per-element, not per-size (see special_conditions).
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED BY THE HARNESS, not by the operation. thesis/config/config.yaml:572 sets stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096 and thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 rejects any spec with size > max_spec_size. The operation itself has no upper bound (the driver's own performance path runs it at DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE = 1<<22).
benchmarks.special_conditions: Per-ELEMENT precondition (the only real one): every string must be non-empty AND its first character must be a lowercase ASCII letter 'a'..'z'. The oracle does `bins[s[i][0] - 'a'] += 1` with no bounds check and no emptiness check (baseline.hpp:15-17). An empty string yields '\0' via std::string::operator[](0) -> index -97 -> out-of-bounds write (UB); an uppercase letter or digit likewise lands outside [0,26). The driver guarantees the precondition twice over: fillRandString(s, 2, 10) produces lengths in [2,9] (utilities.hpp:133) from 'a'+rand()%26 (utilities.hpp:136), and validate() then overwrites s[j][0] with rand()%26+'a' (cpu.cc:65, cpu.cc:71). NO power-of-two requirement, NO minimum element count, no matrix/geometry validity condition. Bin count is fixed at 26 by the signature. Additional harness condition: the fill-PATTERN axis is inert here — the benchmark has zero ENHANCED_FILL sites (thesis/enhanced_tests/benchmark_shapes.json: "fill_sites": 0, "no ENHANCED_FILL site: uses fillRandString (deliberately not wrapped)"), and generate_test_specs.py:142-146 tells the spec model verbatim that "the `pattern` field has NO effect here — only `size` matters". Only ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE varies.
benchmarks.size_semantics: TEST_SIZE = the ELEMENT COUNT of the string vector (how many strings are histogrammed), not a string length, not a side length, and nothing derived. String lengths stay at rand()%8+2 in [2,9] for every size. The output is always 26 bins regardless of TEST_SIZE, so the comparison surface is constant while the input scales.
benchmarks.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Exactly one character read (s[i][0]), one subtraction and one increment per element; the 26-bin output array is a fixed-size constant. Runtime is INDEPENDENT of string length — the oracle never touches s[i][1..]. (Input construction is O(n * Lbar) with Lbar ~ 5.5, but that lies outside the timed region.)
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
min_size = 0 because the histogram of an empty multiset is the all-zero histogram — a defined value, not an error; nothing in the oracle or the driver imposes a floor. max_size = 4096 is imposed by the harness (max_spec_size), not by the operation.

The scale ladder is anchored on B = 26, the only structural constant this operation has (alphabet size = bin count), plus the O(n) cost model. The regimes of a B-bin histogram over n items are separated by n/B:

- SMALL = 26 = B. The smallest n at which full bin coverage is even possible. With uniform random first letters the expected number of occupied bins is 26*(1-(25/26)^26) ~= 16.6, so ~9 bins are still zero: the sparse-occupancy regime, where a candidate that forgets to zero-initialise bins, or that writes only to touched bins, diverges. n = B is also below any plausible thread/chunk count multiple, so remainder/chunking errors and per-thread privatization (26*T private bins > n input elements) surface here.

- MEDIUM = 104 = 4B. Just above the coupon-collector expectation 26*H_26 ~= 100.25, i.e. the smallest 4x multiple of the alphabet at which ALL 26 bins are expected to be non-empty. This is the dense-but-shallow regime (~4 counts per bin) where a wrong reduction still yields small, plausible-looking counts rather than obviously absurd ones — precisely the regime that exact-equality comparison catches and eyeballing would not.

- LARGE = 4096. Two independent reasons converge: (i) it is 4x the driver's own default TEST_SIZE of 1024 (cpu.cc:52), so it is a genuinely held-out scale relative to what the base correctness stage exercised; (ii) it is exactly the harness ceiling. Operationally it is the fully dense regime, ~157 counts per bin, maximal write contention on the 26 shared counters for an OpenMP/MPI reduction, and large enough that a lost or double-counted chunk shows up as a bin-sum mismatch rather than being masked.

None of these numbers were derived from any candidate or model code; they come from B = 26, the coupon-collector threshold, the driver's own default TEST_SIZE, and the harness cap.

benchmarks.name: 24_histogram_count_quartile
benchmarks.input_form: One 1-D input: x = (v_0 ... v_{n-1}) in R^n, held as std::vector<double> of length n (cpu.cc:55). Output: std::array<size_t,4> bins, a FIXED 4-tuple independent of n, with the invariant sum(bins) = n. The operation maps each element to frac(v) = v - (int)v and classifies frac into one of four half-open sub-intervals of the unit interval: [0,0.25), [0.25,0.5), [0.5,0.75), [0.75,1) (baseline.hpp:15-29). The ONLY varying dimension is n; there is no second dimension, no matrix, no index vector. benchmark_shapes.json confirms fill_sites=1, elements_per_site=["n"], total_elements="n", explicit_values_supported=true.
benchmarks.min_size: 0. n = 0 is mathematically well-defined for this operation (a count over the empty multiset is 0 in every bin) and is executed by the oracle without UB: measured `empty (n=0) -> [0 0 0 0]`. There is NO mathematical size floor — no minimum point count, no pair requirement, no invertibility condition. n = 0 and n = 1 therefore belong on the degenerate axis, not to a size floor (they are also in the harness's static base set, config.yaml:562 static_base_sizes [0,1,2,7]).
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED BY THE HARNESS, not by the operation: thesis/config/config.yaml:572 `max_spec_size: 4096`, enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). A second, far higher cap follows from the operation's reference implementation: the oracle's loop index is `int` (baseline.hpp:16 `for (int i = 0; i < x.size(); i += 1)`), so n must stay <= INT_MAX = 2147483647. The harness cap binds by five orders of magnitude.
benchmarks.special_conditions:
NO size-shaped condition: no power-of-two requirement, no minimum element count, no valid-matrix form, no sortedness, no distinctness. Every n in [0, 4096] is admissible, and every offered fill pattern works at every one of the chosen sizes (the k-patterns duplicate_at / sorted_except_one / spike_at need only size >= 2, specs.py:322).

The binding conditions are on VALUES, not on size — every element v must satisfy 0 <= v < 2^31 (= 2147483648):
(a) v >= 0: the four intervals the prompt states partition [0,1) and contain no negative number, while the oracle's truncating frac(v) = v - (int)v yields frac in (-1,0] for v < 0 and its if-chain tests `frac < 0.25` first, sweeping ALL negatives into bins[0]. Measured: x = [-1.3,-0.3,-2.5,-3.75] -> [4 0 0 0]. For v >= 0 truncation and floor coincide, so every enumerated fractional-part convention agrees and the prompt's bin list becomes exhaustive.
(b) v < 2^31: `(int) val` (baseline.hpp:18) is UB above INT_MAX. Boundary measured exactly: 2147483647.0 -> bins[0] (correct), 2147483647.5 -> bins[2] (correct), 2147483648.0 -> bins[3] (mathematically frac = 0, i.e. bins[0]), 2^52 -> bins[3] (wrong), DBL_MAX -> bins[3], DBL_LOWEST -> bins[0], DBL_MAX/2 -> bins[3].
The driver's own generator satisfies both: fillRand(x, 0.0, 100.0) at cpu.cc:30 and cpu.cc:64, uniform in [0,100] (utilities.hpp:144-159).
benchmarks.size_semantics: size == n == the ELEMENT COUNT of the single double vector x. ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE overrides the driver's TEST_SIZE 1:1 (cpu.cc:53 `const size_t TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024);` + enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79), and TEST_SIZE is used directly as the vector length (cpu.cc:55). No derivation (no side length, no nnz, no sparsity). Memory footprint = 8*n bytes; in MPI mode every rank holds a full copy (prompt: "Every rank has a complete copy of x").
benchmarks.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Exactly one pass over x; per element one truncating double->int cast, one subtraction and 1-3 comparisons; the accumulator is a fixed 4-entry array whose size does not depend on n. The reference is memory-streaming and branch-bound: with the driver's uniform fill the 4-way if-chain is essentially unpredictable, which is why the measured cost is ~22 ns/element rather than ~1 ns/element. Measured linearity across five decades: n=16 -> 4.40e-07 s, n=1024 -> 2.33e-05 s, n=4095 -> 8.96e-05 s, n=4194304 -> 1.249e-01 s, n=67108864 -> 1.600e+00 s (i.e. 27.5 / 22.8 / 21.9 / 29.8 / 23.8 ns per element).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
Derived ONLY from the operation, its specified domain, its O(n) complexity and the harness/runtime bounds — no candidate code was read or considered.

The operation is a pure single-pass streaming reduction of n doubles into a 4-bin histogram. It has NO algorithmic regime change with n: no recursion depth, no blocking, no conditioning, no output growth (the output is always 4 counters). Consequently the scale axis is defined by the only three things that genuinely change with n for THIS operation: (i) whether the operation's output structure can be exercised at all, (ii) the benchmark's own established validation scale, (iii) the maximum data volume the stage permits and how the vector decomposes across parallel workers.

SMALL = 16 = 4 bins x 4 workers. This is the smallest n at which the operation's full output tuple is exercised — with the driver's uniform fill P(all four bins non-empty) = 1 - 4(3/4)^n + 6(1/2)^n - 4(1/4)^n = 0.96 at n=16 (0.63 at n=8, 0.29 at n=6) — AND at which each of the 4 workers of the stage's fixed parallel launch point (config.yaml:603-604 omp_threads: 4, mpi_ranks: 4) receives an element for every bin. Below this the answer is structurally degenerate (some bin necessarily or almost surely 0), which is the degenerate axis, not the scale axis. 16 elements are still hand-checkable.

MEDIUM = 1024. The benchmark's OWN stock validation scale (cpu.cc:53, the literal default the driver ships), i.e. the size at which this operation is established to be exercised, and the scale at which the four counts become statistically stable (expected 256 per bin, relative sd ~5%), so a systematic misclassification of one bin boundary is visible in the counts rather than lost in sampling noise. It is exactly divisible by the 4-worker launch point, so it is the clean-decomposition point of the ladder.

LARGE = 4095. The stage's hard ceiling is 4096 (config.yaml:572, specs.py:293-294). 4095 is the largest PERMITTED size that is odd, so it is not divisible by any worker count > 1: for a data-parallel reduction over a vector — which is exactly what this operation is under the omp and mpi prompts — the chunk-remainder path is an intrinsic property of the operation's parallel formulation, and no power-of-two size ever exercises it (4095 = 4*1023 + 3 at the pilot's 4 ranks). At maximum permitted volume it also maximises the exposure of an unsynchronised bin accumulation. The one element of volume given up versus 4096 is nil (measured 8.96e-05 s vs 8.79e-05 s), the coverage gained is not.

Spacing: 16 -> 1024 -> 4095 is x64 then x4; the ladder is justified point-by-point (output-structure floor / driver-established scale / harness ceiling with remainder), not by a geometric convention, because an O(n) branch-bound histogram has no scale-dependent regime that a geometric ladder would probe.

RUNTIME BUDGET: non-binding here, and reported rather than re-negotiated. LARGE costs 8.96e-05 s of the 10 s budget (0.0009%). The 10 s ceiling would correspond to n ~ 4.2e8 elements (extrapolated from the measured 1.600 s at n=6.71e7), i.e. ~3.4 GB of doubles per MPI rank and within a factor 5 of the oracle's `int`-loop limit of 2^31-1 — 100000x above what the harness accepts. The budget is therefore a satisfied ceiling, not the selection criterion; the harness cap max_spec_size=4096 is.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: yes: "Assume every element of x is non-negative and strictly smaller than 2147483648 (2^31)."
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: no — a plain 1-D vector of n doubles with a single fill site (benchmark_shapes.json: fill_sites 1, total_elements "n"); the stock ENHANCED_FILL/fillRand(0.0, 100.0) already lies inside the safe value domain and ENHANCED_FILL_LO/HI covers the rest.
