benchmarks.name: 32_scan_sum_of_prefix_sum_array
benchmarks.input_form: One 1-D `std::vector<double> x` of length N; the single relevant dimension is N. Signature `double sumOfPrefixSum(std::vector<double> const& x)`. Operation: y = sum_{k=1..N} P_k with P_k = sum_{i<=k} x_i (INCLUSIVE scan, then total reduction) — the prompt example [-7,2,1,9,4,8] -> 15 discriminates inclusive (15) from exclusive (-2), so the semantics is pinned by the prompt itself. Default value range at the fill site: [-100.0, 100.0] (cpu.cc:58). Single fill site, total_elements = "n" (thesis/enhanced_tests/benchmark_shapes.json). Result is a scalar double compared with an ABSOLUTE epsilon of 1e-5.
benchmarks.min_size: 0 — no size floor. The oracle is total on N >= 0: at N = 0 `prefixSum` is empty and `std::accumulate(..., 0.0)` returns 0.0, which is also the mathematically correct answer (sum over the empty prefix-sum array). MEASURED: correctSumOfPrefixSum({}) = 0, correctSumOfPrefixSum({-7}) = -7. Unlike scan/34 there is no sentinel artefact, so 0 and 1 are genuine degenerate cases, not a floor.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED BY THE HARNESS. thesis/config/config.yaml:572 `max_spec_size: 4096`, enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s"). This, not the runtime budget, is the binding upper constraint for this benchmark: the 10 s budget would only bind around N ~ 1.5e8 (see measurement_detail), roughly 4.5 orders of magnitude higher.
benchmarks.special_conditions: NONE that are structural: no power-of-two requirement, no minimum point count, no matrix validity, no sortedness, no uniqueness — every std::vector<double> of every length is in the domain and the oracle is total on it. The only real precondition is NUMERICAL and MEASURED: `validate()` compares the scalar with an ABSOLUTE tolerance 1e-5 (cpu.cc:69 -> utilities.hpp:488-491, `!(std::abs(expected-got) > epsilon)`), while |result| grows like sigma*N^1.5/sqrt(3). The effective RELATIVE tolerance therefore tightens as N^-1.5, and a mathematically identical but differently-ordered correct implementation (block scan + carry, i.e. exactly what the OpenMP/MPI prompts ask for) drifts past 1e-5 at N ~ 65536 with the default +/-100 range. Measured worst |oracle - blocked8| over 5 draws: N=16 4.5e-13, N=257 1.5e-10, N=1024 1.3e-09, N=4096 2.4e-08 (ok, ~400x margin), N=65536 1.2e-05 (EXCEEDS), N=1048576 5.3e-04, N=16777216 1.29. The same drift is driven by the value range: at N=4096 the deviation is 4.1e-10 at +/-1, 3.4e-08 at +/-1e2, 8.6e-06 at +/-1e4 (borderline), 1.5e-04 at +/-1e6 (EXCEEDS). Domain condition to respect: keep value_range within about +/-1e3 at size 4096 (the default +/-100 leaves ~300x margin). Secondary harness condition: explicit_values specs are capped at 64 values (config.yaml:576 explicit_values_max_size, expected_value_count = n), so of the three scale points only SMALL=16 can carry an explicit_values spec.
benchmarks.size_semantics: size == ELEMENT COUNT of the one input vector. `validate()` does `std::vector<double> input(TEST_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:50) with `TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024)` (cpu.cc:48), and `ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE` replaces that default verbatim (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). Nothing is derived from the size (no side length, no nnz, no matrix dimension); benchmark_shapes.json gives elements_per_site ["n"], total_elements "n", fill_sites 1. The timing path uses DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE the same way (cpu.cc:31, configured (1<<22) serial in drivers/problem-sizes.json) but never validates.
benchmarks.complexity: O(N) time, O(N) auxiliary space. baseline.hpp:13 allocates a second vector of N doubles, :14 one `std::inclusive_scan` pass, :15 one `std::accumulate` pass — 2 sequential O(N) passes with ~2 reads + 1 write per element, i.e. memory-bandwidth bound, no data-dependent branching, no preconditions. The dependence structure is a serial carry (P_k = P_{k-1} + x_k) plus an associative reduction.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
min_size = 0 follows from the oracle being total: an empty prefix-sum array has sum 0, and `std::accumulate(..., 0.0)` returns exactly that (baseline.hpp:13-15, MEASURED = 0). No structural condition exists because the operation places none on its input — any real sequence of any length has a prefix-sum array and a sum of it.

The scale points are derived from the only two size-dependent properties this operation actually has, plus the harness cap — never from any candidate code:

(i) DEPTH OF THE CARRY / BLOCK DECOMPOSITION. A scan is defined by an associative carry, so every decomposition of it is "W local block scans + W-1 carry combinations", where the block sum is local_partial_b + carry_b * len_b. The enhanced stage's decomposition width is fixed by the HARNESS at W = 4 (config.yaml:602-604, omp_threads: 4 / mpi_ranks: 4). Two mathematically distinct cases of that recurrence exist: W | N (every block equal length) and W does not divide N (a short remainder block, so carry_b multiplies a different len_b).
  - SMALL = 16 = 4*W: the smallest size at which all four fixed workers get a NON-EMPTY, MULTI-element chunk (4 each), so the full 4-block / 3-carry chain is exercised in the evenly-divisible case. It also sits above the static base set [0,1,2,7] (config.yaml:562), so it adds a scale point instead of duplicating one, and it is <= 64, i.e. the only one of the three that explicit_values specs can reach.
  - MEDIUM = 257 = 4*64 + 1: deliberately NOT divisible by W (prime, hence coprime to any other plausible width 2/8/16 as well). Remainder exactly 1 is the extreme form of the short-last-block case, which an evenly divisible size can never reach. 257/16 ~ 16 and 4096/257 ~ 16, so the three points form a clean ~16x geometric ladder that follows from the endpoints rather than from convenience.
  - LARGE = 4096: the harness maximum (max_spec_size, config.yaml:572). For an O(N) memory-bound kernel there is no algorithmic regime change above the block-carry structure, so the meaningful LARGE is simply "the largest the stage admits".

(ii) NUMERICAL DIFFICULTY. |result| grows ~ sigma * N^1.5 / sqrt(3), while the comparison tolerance is ABSOLUTE 1e-5 (cpu.cc:69). LARGE = 4096 is therefore also the point of maximal, still-safe numerical stress: measured |result| <= 1.55e7 and worst reassociation deviation 2.4e-08 against a 1e-5 tolerance (~400x margin), whereas 65536 already breaks it (1.2e-05). So the harness cap and the tolerance limit happen to agree: 4096 is the last power-of-two-scale size at which a CORRECT differently-ordered implementation is still guaranteed to pass, and it is what max_spec_size permits. Raising max_size for this benchmark would turn the test into a floating-point-reassociation test rather than a correctness test.

benchmarks.name: 33_scan_reverse_prefix_sum
benchmarks.input_form: One flat 1-D sequence of 32-bit signed integers, x ∈ Z^n, plus a pre-sized output vector of the same length n (`std::vector<int> const& x`, `std::vector<int>& output`). The only dimension is n. Operation: output[i] = Σ_{j=n-1-i}^{n-1} x[j], i.e. the INCLUSIVE scan of the REVERSED sequence, written back in forward index order (baseline.hpp:15-21; verified against both prompt examples: [1,7,4,6,6,2] → [2,8,14,18,25,26]). Values are drawn at a single fill site with range [-100, 100] (cpu.cc:62); fillRand's integral branch (utilities.hpp:151, `rand() % (max-min) + min`) actually yields [-100, 99].
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — HARNESS-FORCED, and it binds this row: `stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096` (thesis/config/config.yaml:572), enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 ("size %s exceeds max_spec_size"). MEDIUM and LARGE below therefore require raising that setting; if it stays at 4096 the ladder collapses to ≤ 4096 and the DRAM/streaming regime cannot be reached at all. Operation-side ceilings, all far above 4096: n ≤ 10,737,419 (int accumulator, spike_at present), n ≤ 21,474,836 (int accumulator, |v| ≤ 100 only), n ≤ 2,147,483,647 (oracle's `int` loop index). Practical ceiling from the 10 s budget on the measurement host: ~50M is already over budget in the tail, 100M is over budget outright (measured, see below).
benchmarks.special_conditions: No structural precondition: any n ≥ 0 and any int values are a valid input form — no power of two, no minimum point count, no matrix validity. The only real preconditions are arithmetic, on the ORACLE, not on the shape: (1) the oracle accumulates in `int` (std::inclusive_scan over `std::vector<int>`, default `std::plus<int>`), so every partial suffix sum must fit in int; with the fill site's declared magnitude bound |v| ≤ 100 this holds provably for n ≤ 21,474,836, and for n ≤ 10,737,419 when the spike_at pattern injects one INT_MAX/2 = 1,073,741,823 element (enhanced-fill.hpp:157, 210-212). (2) the oracle's reversal loop index is `int i = x.size() - 1` (baseline.hpp:17), so n must fit in int: n ≤ 2,147,483,647. (3) `output` must already have length ≥ n — the driver guarantees this (cpu.cc:54). VERIFIED VIOLATION, not merely theoretical: the `extreme_values` fill pattern (INT_MIN/INT_MAX alternating, enhanced-fill.hpp:199-201) makes the oracle signed-overflow (UB) at every ODD n, and is clean at every even n.
benchmarks.size_semantics: n = the ELEMENT COUNT of the single input vector x, and simultaneously the length of `output` — nothing is derived, squared, or interpreted as a side length. The enhanced stage's spec `size` maps 1:1 onto it: `-DENHANCED_TEST_SIZE=n` replaces the literal 1024 at cpu.cc:52 via ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79), and cpu.cc:54 sizes x, correct and test to it. thesis/enhanced_tests/benchmark_shapes.json:296-304 records elements_per_site ["n"] / total_elements "n" / fill_sites 1, so an explicit_values spec of size n needs exactly n values. (Separate and unrelated: the correctness stage's performance path uses DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE = (1<<22) = 4,194,304, drivers/problem-sizes.json:299-303 — context only, it never reaches validate().)
benchmarks.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) extra space. The oracle does two linear passes: an n-iteration `push_back` reversal into a fresh, unreserved `std::vector<int>` (geometric growth ⇒ ~2n extra element copies and a transient ~1.5x allocation peak) followed by an O(n) `std::inclusive_scan`. Measured ~27.6 ns/element at n = 10^7 (page-fault- and copy-dominated, single-threaded); ~4 ns/element while L1-resident at n = 1001.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
min_size = 0: the reverse inclusive scan of an empty sequence is the empty sequence — mathematically defined, and verified to execute cleanly (ASan+UBSan, out.size()=0). It is NOT a size floor; it belongs to degenerate_cases.

The scale axis is set by the two things that actually change a scan's behaviour as n grows: (a) where the working set sits in the memory hierarchy, and (b) how the decomposition splits — the block/tile count, the carry chain length across blocks, and whether the last block/rank is partial. The reversal adds a third, size-parity property: the index map i ↦ n-1-i has a fixed point exactly when n is odd. All three points are chosen from those properties alone; no candidate code was consulted.

SMALL = 1001. 4.0 KB per vector, 12 KB for validate's three vectors (x, correct, test — cpu.cc:54) ⇒ fully L1-resident; a single tile / a single thread's chunk in any realistic decomposition, so it tests the base case and the two end boundaries of the reversal. ODD ⇒ (i) a self-mapping midpoint at i = 500 under i ↦ n-1-i, and (ii) a non-empty remainder for EVERY tile width ≥ 2 and for the stage's 4-way launch (1001 = 4·250 + 1).

MEDIUM = 500000. 2.0 MB per vector, 6 MB across validate's three ⇒ past per-core L1/L2, resident in a shared L3; thousands of tiles, so the cross-block carry chain is genuinely long. EVEN ⇒ the reversal is a pure pairing with no fixed point — the complementary regime to SMALL. 500000 = 2^5·5^6: an EXACT 4-way split (125000 per thread/rank at the enhanced stage's fixed launch point, config.yaml:602-604) and exact for every tile width up to 32, but not a multiple of 64 ⇒ balanced decomposition with a misaligned cache-line/vector tail.

LARGE = 10000001. 40 MB per vector, ~143 MiB measured peak RSS for the oracle alone ⇒ far beyond any LLC, squarely in the DRAM-streaming regime, ~4 orders of magnitude above SMALL. ODD again ⇒ fixed point at i = 5,000,000 and an unbalanced 4-way split (4·2,500,000 + 1: the remainder-rank case, now at scale rather than at 1001). The exact value is pinned by the operation's arithmetic domain, not by the clock: 10,000,001 is the largest round size at which the ORACLE'S int accumulator is PROVABLY overflow-free for every offered magnitude-bounded fill pattern including spike_at — 100·10,000,000 + 1,073,741,823 = 2,073,741,823 ≤ INT_MAX, margin 73,741,824. Pushing to 20,000,001 (measured 0.69 s, comfortably in budget) would cross that bound and make correctness of the reference contingent on the random walk not drifting, which is not a property one should have to argue.

Consequence worth stating plainly: the 10 s runtime budget is NOT the binding constraint here. It would permit n ≈ 3.6·10^8 (0.276 s at 10^7, linear), which is (a) past the int-accumulator domain and (b) ~5.8 GB inside validate() — infeasible in the 7.6 GiB container. The binding constraints are, in order: the harness cap of 4096 (must be raised), the int accumulator, and memory. The budget is satisfied with ~36x headroom, so the row is not budget-limited and I did not stretch LARGE to fill it.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: no. Every restriction derived here is enforceable on the INPUT GENERATOR, not on the candidate's contract: the shape is unconstrained (any n ≥ 0, any int values), and thesis/docs/benchmark-example-consistency.md:93 already records that the prompt's two worked examples match the oracle exactly (independently re-verified above). The one genuine domain violation found — `extreme_values` × odd n ⇒ signed-overflow UB in the oracle — is an ORACLE/SPEC-DOMAIN problem, not something a model can be told to avoid, so the fix belongs in the spec filter (exclude pattern `extreme_values` for this benchmark, or restrict it to even n) or in the oracle's accumulator type. benchmarks.name: 34_scan_largest_contiguous_subarray_sum
benchmarks.input_form: One 1-D integer array. `int maximumSubarray(std::vector<int> const& x)` -> scalar `int`. The ONLY dimension is n = x.size(); there is no second dimension, no derived count (no nnz, no side length, no point count). Values are integers drawn uniformly from [-100, 99] by the driver's generator (`fillRand(x, -100, 100)` with the integral branch `rand() % (max-min) + min`, utilities.hpp:151). Output is a single int compared by EXACT integer equality (`reportAndCompareScalar(correct, test)` -> `expected == got`, utilities.hpp:483-485) — no epsilon, no tolerance. TEST_SIZE in validate() therefore means plain element count of x.
benchmarks.min_size: Operationally n >= 1 (the maximum over the family of NON-EMPTY contiguous subarrays x[i..j] needs at least one element). NO size floor is imposed anywhere in the code path: the driver allocates `std::vector<int> x(TEST_SIZE)` for any TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:53) and the spec validator only requires `size >= 0` (specs.py:290-291). n = 0 is therefore a live, harness-reachable input and is treated as a degenerate case (see degenerate_cases), NOT as a floor: the oracle returns its untouched accumulator INT_MIN there (measured: -2147483648).
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED BY THE HARNESS, not by the runtime budget. thesis/config/config.yaml:572 `max_spec_size: 4096`, enforced in thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294 (`size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s` -> spec rejected). The 10 s budget alone would permit roughly n ~= 92,000-93,000 (measured, see measurement_detail), i.e. the config cap is ~22x more restrictive than the budget for this benchmark. The operation itself imposes only the far-away int-overflow ceiling n < ~2.1e7 at |values| <= 100.
benchmarks.special_conditions: NO structural condition on n: no power of two, no divisibility, no minimum point/element count, no valid-matrix form. Any n is a mathematically valid input length for this operation. The one genuine precondition is a VALUE-domain condition, not a size condition: the oracle accumulates the running sum in `int` (baseline.hpp:16-18), so the input must satisfy max_{i<=j} |sum x[i..j]| < 2^31. With the call site's range |x[i]| <= 100 this holds for any n < 2^31/100 ~= 2.1e7, i.e. it never binds on this ladder (at LARGE = 4096 the worst-case |sum| is 409,600 vs INT_MAX = 2,147,483,647 — measured/printed by the probe). It DOES bind for the enhanced fill patterns: pattern 6 `extreme_values` (INT_MIN/INT_MAX alternating) makes the oracle execute signed-overflow UB for n >= 3 (partial sum INT_MIN+INT_MAX = -1, then -1+INT_MIN overflows); n = 2 is still well defined (measured -> 2147483647). Pattern 9 `spike_at` (INT_MAX/2) stays safe while 100*n < 2^30, i.e. for all n <= ~1.07e7. Second, non-size condition: the empty-subarray convention (K1 non-empty, which the oracle implements, vs K2 empty-allowed) is NOT pinned by the prompt — an unresolved semantics blocker, see pending_fix.
benchmarks.size_semantics: The size number is the plain ELEMENT COUNT n of the single input vector x (`std::vector<int> x(TEST_SIZE)`, cpu.cc:53). Nothing is derived from it: no side length, no nnz, no point count, no matrix shape. Oracle work is exactly n(n+1)/2 add-and-compare steps, so doubling the size number quadruples the reference cost. In the enhanced stage the number is injected as -DENHANCED_TEST_SIZE and replaces the benchmark's own validate() default of 1024; the separate -DDRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (1<<8 in the correctness/perf stages via thesis/evaluation/tools.py:44, 1<<4 in the enhanced stage) sizes only the timing Context and never the validation input.
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle `correctMaximumSubarray` is O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space: the double loop performs exactly n(n+1)/2 add-and-compare steps (baseline.hpp:15-21). Note the asymmetry that shapes this row: a natural correct candidate is O(n) (Kadane) or O(n log n) (divide-and-conquer), so the reference is quadratically more expensive than any sane submission — the oracle, not the candidate, is what the size budget must be measured against. The same quadratic function is also `best()` in the timing path (cpu.cc:45-48), which is a known documented distortion (thesis/docs/oracle-correctness-audit.md:511).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
SCALE AXIS (n = element count), derived only from the operation, its complexity, the harness cap and the measured budget — no candidate code was consulted.

1. There is no structural precondition to satisfy (no power of two, no matrix form, no point minimum), so the ladder is a pure element-count ladder and the only real question is where its floor and ceiling sit.

2. FLOOR (SMALL = 64). Definedness would allow n = 1, but the tiny sizes 0, 1, 2, 7 are already the config's `static_base_sizes` (config.yaml:562) and belong to the degenerate axis. The scale axis must start where the operation's structure is actually present. Two operation-intrinsic requirements set that point: (a) the enhanced stage launches at a FIXED parallel width of 4 (config.yaml:603-604, omp_threads 4 / mpi_ranks 4), and a maximum-subarray decomposition is only meaningful once each of the 4 blocks holds a non-trivial run — at n = 64 the blocks are 16 elements each, so the combine of (prefix, suffix, total, best) across boundaries is genuinely exercised instead of one block trivially containing the whole answer; (b) with the call site's symmetric fill (P(negative) ~= 1/2) an array of 64 has ~32 sign changes, so the optimal subarray is a proper interior run rather than the entire array (measured at n=64: answers 620, 466, 401, 397 — all far below the whole-array sum, confirming an interior optimum).

3. CEILING (LARGE = 4096). This is the largest size the harness admits at all (max_spec_size 4096, specs.py:293). The 10 s budget is not the binding constraint here — measured, 4096 costs the oracle ~12 ms, three orders of magnitude of headroom — so LARGE is set at the cap rather than at the budget. Raising the cap would be a config decision; if it were raised, the budget-derived LARGE would be ~92k (measured), which is where I would place it instead.

4. SPACING and the ragged-block point (MEDIUM = 511). For a quadratic oracle a x8 ladder in n is the natural spacing: each step multiplies reference work by 64, so the three points span 4096x of oracle cost while all stay inside the budget (64 -> 511 -> 4096, ratios 7.98 and 8.02). MEDIUM is deliberately 511 and not 512: a parallel maximum-subarray has two distinct structural failure modes, (i) missing a subarray that spans a block boundary and (ii) mishandling the remainder when n is not divisible by the launch width. A ladder whose every point is divisible by 4 never exercises (ii) at a scale where blocks are still large — only at the degenerate base sizes 2 and 7, where blocks are smaller than the rank count and the code path degenerates. 511 = 3x128 + 127 under the stage's 4-way launch puts the remainder path on the ladder at full block size, while 64 and 4096 keep clean splits. This is a property of the operation's decomposition, not of any observed implementation.

5. Rejected alternatives: reusing the driver's own validate() default of 1024 (convenience, not derivation, and it exercises neither the ragged split nor the cap); pushing LARGE to the budget-derived ~92k (rejected — the spec validator would reject the spec, so the number would be fictional); starting the ladder at 8 or 16 (rejected — at fewer than ~4 elements per rank the 4-way decomposition is degenerate and the point duplicates the static base sizes).

Note the two interact: the second sentence removes n = 0 from the domain and would make the config's static size-0 spec out-of-domain for this benchmark. Under BL-10 Options 1/3/4 and BL-11 Options 1/3 no prompt change is made and this row's sizes stand unchanged.
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: no — the driver's generator is a single flat `fillRand(x, -100, 100)` over a `std::vector<int>` of length TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:53, 61); every enhanced fill pattern applies to it directly, there is no derived count, no structural shape and no repair loop to replicate. benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
All probed by executing the real oracle (probe.cpp, same flags as the pipeline). DEFINED and reachable:
- n = 0 (empty vector): mathematically max over an empty family = -infinity; the oracle returns INT_MIN = -2147483648 (MEASURED) as its untouched initialiser — defensible as a K1 sentinel but nowhere specified. Reachable: static_base_sizes contains 0 and an accepted explicit_values size-0 spec exists (BL-11).
- n = 1: defined, answer = x[0] including negative values (MEASURED: {7} -> 7, {-7} -> -7).
- all zeros, any n: defined, 0.
- all values equal, positive: defined, n*v (MEASURED: eight 5s -> 40).
- all values equal, negative: defined under the oracle's K1 as v (MEASURED: eight -5s -> -5); under K2 the answer is 0. This is the live ambiguity, at ANY size.
- all-negative array in general: defined under K1 = max element (MEASURED: [-3,-1,-7,-2] -> -1). Important reachability finding: the all-negative regime is NOT limited to hand-written explicit_values specs — the `ascending`/`descending` ramp pattern with this call site's range [-100,100] produces element i = -100 + (i mod 201), so EVERY element is negative for any n <= 100 (MEASURED: ascending n=8 -> -93). SMALL = 64 therefore sits inside that regime for ramp patterns.
- prompt's own example (n = 9): oracle -> 6, matching the documented example (MEASURED).
NOT mathematically safe (out of the oracle's own value domain, so not a legitimate degenerate case for grading):
- `extreme_values` (INT_MIN/INT_MAX alternating) for n >= 3: signed-overflow UB inside the oracle's int accumulator. n = 2 is still well defined (MEASURED -> 2147483647).
Not degenerate at all, listed for completeness: n = 2 and n = 7 (config static base) are ordinary small inputs with no special handling.
benchmarks.pending_fix:
YES — this row is explicitly PROVISIONAL on two open class-B semantics decisions, both recorded as "decision deliberately left open" in thesis/docs/oracle-correctness-audit.md:
(1) BL-10 (:340-351): the empty-subarray convention. The oracle implements K1 (maximum over NON-EMPTY subarrays, seeded at INT_MIN); the prompt's wording and its positive-answer example admit K2 (empty subarray allowed, answer max(K1, 0)) equally. Options 1-4 open; Option 2 changes the prompt in all three parallelism models and forces full regeneration, Option 3 forces regeneration/filtering of this benchmark's all-negative specs.
(2) BL-11 (:352-364): the n = 0 return value (INT_MIN sentinel, an accumulator artifact). Options: exclude size 0 for this benchmark, state the contract in the prompt, or exclude size-0 verdicts at analysis time.
(3) Family-wide, documentation-only so far (:216): integral oracles executing UB on the out-of-domain values that `extreme_values`/`spike_at` inject. This benchmark is affected identically (int accumulator, UB for extreme_values at n >= 3).
Impact on THIS row: the three scale points 64 / 511 / 4096 are unaffected by all three decisions and stand as they are. What is provisional is the interpretation of results at the SMALL end — because the ramp patterns are all-negative for every n <= 100, SMALL = 64 lands inside exactly the input class BL-10 makes ambiguous, so K1-vs-K2 mismatches there must not be read as model errors until BL-10 is settled. If BL-11 Option 2 (or the "x contains at least one element" clause) is chosen, n = 0 leaves the domain and the config's static size-0 case for this benchmark must be dropped.

benchmarks.name: 35_search_search_for_last_struct_by_key
benchmarks.input_form: One-dimensional: `std::vector<Book> const& books` with `struct Book { std::string title; int pages; }`. The only dimension is n = books.size(). Only the `int pages` field participates in the operation; `title` is inert — validate() assigns the literal "title" (5 chars, SSO, no heap allocation) to every element (cpu.cc:75). Output is a single `size_t` index, compared for EXACT equality (reportAndCompareScalar without epsilon, cpu.cc:87 -> utilities.hpp:483-485). Value domain of `pages` under the stock harness: uniform integers in [1, 999] (fillRand's `rand() % (max-min) + min` called with lo=1, hi=1000, utilities.hpp:144-157), plus one forced value 72. sizeof(Book) = 40 bytes (MEASURED in the container, libstdc++ std::string = 32 B + int + padding).
benchmarks.max_size: Forced ceiling n <= INT_MAX = 2147483647, from the int loop counters in baseline.hpp:17 (`int i = books.size() - 1`), cpu.cc:74 (`for (int j = 0; j < input.size(); ...)`) and utilities.hpp:144-146 (fillRand's `for (int i ...)`); above that the narrowing is implementation-defined and the reverse scan would start at a wrong index. Unreachable in practice — at 40 B/element INT_MAX would need ~86 GB. The real ceiling is host memory: MEASURED, n = 2^24 = 16777216 (670 MB of Books) was OOM-killed (exit 137) on the 7775 MiB WSL2 VM under contention, while n = 2^23 = 8388608 (320 MB) ran fine.
benchmarks.special_conditions: No mathematical precondition at all: no power-of-two, no minimum element count beyond n>=1, no sortedness, no matrix/geometric validity. The single structural precondition is imposed by the DRIVER, not by the operation: cpu.cc:72 writes `pages[rand() % pages.size()] = 72` AFTER the fill, so every generated input contains at least one qualifying element and the oracle's "not found" branch (baseline.hpp:22, `return books.size()`) is structurally unreachable. This holds for EVERY ENHANCED_FILL pattern, because ENHANCED_FILL (cpu.cc:71) runs before the forced write. Second condition, also driver-imposed: n >= 1, because that same line divides by pages.size(). A separate, unrelated floor exists on the PERF path only: reset() computes `max = pages.size()/4` then `rand() % (max-min)` (cpu.cc:31-32), which requires DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE >= 4; the enhanced stage sizes validate(), not DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE, so this does not constrain the row.
benchmarks.size_semantics: Plain element count: n = number of Books in the vector = TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024) (cpu.cc:65). Not a side length, no derived nnz, no power-of-two meaning. Memory footprint = n * 40 bytes for the Book vector (sizeof(Book) = 40 measured) plus n * 4 bytes for the int staging vector that validate() fills first: 20 KiB / 2.5 MiB / 160 MiB of Books at small / medium / large.
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle: O(n) worst case, O(1) best case, O(1) EXPECTED under the driver's own fill. Reverse linear scan with early exit at the first element with pages < 100 (baseline.hpp:17-21). Under the stock construction pages ~ Uniform{1..999}, so P(pages < 100) = 99/999 = 0.0991 and the expected iteration count is 1/0.0991 ~= 10.1 — INDEPENDENT of n. Measured confirmation at n = 4194304: returned indices n-15, n-9, n-4, n-13 across runs, oracle time flat at ~1 microsecond from n=512 to n=8388608. The full O(n) scan is reachable only through fill patterns that leave nothing below 100 except the driver's forced 72, i.e. ENHANCED_FILL_PATTERN=2 (all_same -> enhancedMidValue(1,1000) = 500; enhanced-fill.hpp:144-150, 187-188). Space: 40 n bytes for the Book vector + 4 n bytes for the int staging vector.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
The operation is a last-match linear search: one 4-byte compare per element, zero arithmetic, stride-40 access into an array of Books. There is no numerical conditioning, no combinatorial blow-up, and no algorithmic threshold — the only property that genuinely changes with n is cache residency, and (for omp/mpi) whether the max-index reduction has enough work per worker. The scale ladder is therefore a memory-hierarchy ladder derived from the MEASURED sizeof(Book) = 40 B, and from nothing else.

SMALL = 512: 512*40 = 20 KiB, fits entirely in a 32 KiB L1. This is the fully cache-resident regime; with the 20 hardware threads measured in the container each OpenMP worker gets ~26 elements and each MPI rank a comparably tiny slice, which is exactly where remainder/boundary handling in an index reduction is exercised. Deliberately NOT the stock TEST_SIZE 1024, because 1024*40 = 40 KiB already spills a 32 KiB L1 and is thus not a clean cache-resident point.

MEDIUM = 65536: 65536*40 = 2.5 MiB, past any private L2 (1-2 MiB), resident in L3. MEASURED worst-case oracle 0.000223 s = 3.4 ns/element.

LARGE = 4194304: 4194304*40 = 160 MiB, 5-20x any realistic LLC, so the scan is unambiguously DRAM-bandwidth-bound. MEASURED worst-case oracle 0.027194 s = 6.5 ns/element — 1.9x the MEDIUM per-element cost. The regime separation between the three points is measured, not asserted.

The ladder is 2^9 / 2^16 / 2^22, one consistent octave progression across the three cache levels. It was derived solely from the operation (compare-only, memory-bound), sizeof(Book), and the cache hierarchy; no candidate or model code was inspected at any point.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: no. The scale domain requires nothing in the prompt: no power-of-two, no sortedness, no minimum count beyond n>=1, and n>=1 is enforced structurally by the driver (cpu.cc:72), never by the model. The one latent ambiguity — what to return when NO book has pages < 100 — is unreachable under the stock construction for every fill pattern, so it cannot produce a false verdict as long as cpu.cc:72 stands. IF a future custom construction ever drops that forced write, the prompt would at that point need exactly this sentence: "If no Book has fewer than 100 pages, return books.size()."
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: no. The stock validate() construction (ENHANCED_FILL(pages,1,1000) -> forced 72 -> title="title") is valid and yields a well-defined, unique answer at every n >= 1, at all three scale points, under every fill pattern (verified by running the oracle on patterns 1/2/3/5/6 and on a duplicate-heavy input). Custom construction would be needed only for the two items that sit off the scale axis: n = 0 (the stock harness SIGFPEs there) and the no-qualifying-element case (structurally suppressed by cpu.cc:72).

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
All of the following were executed against the real oracle and are reported as measured, not reasoned:

DEFINED and reachable through the stock harness:
- n = 1: forced 72 lands at index 0 -> answer 0.
- n = 2, 3: all-match -> n-1; no-match -> n (sentinel).
- all values equal (pattern 2 all_same = enhancedMidValue(1,1000) = 500): answer = the forced-72 index (n=16 -> 3).
- all values qualify (pattern 1 all_zeros): answer n-1 (n=16 -> 15). pages = 0 is outside the physical meaning of "pages" but perfectly defined for the predicate `< 100`.
- extreme_values (pattern 6, INT_MIN/INT_MAX alternating): INT_MIN < 100 qualifies -> answer n-2 for even n (n=16 -> 14). Negative page counts, again physically nonsensical but mathematically defined.
- alternating (pattern 5, 1/1000): answer n-2 (n=16 -> 14).
- ascending ramp (pattern 3, 1 + i%1000): for n <= 99 the whole ramp is < 100 -> answer n-1 (n=16 -> 15).
- duplicate values: NOT a hazard for this operation. The answer is the last qualifying INDEX, which stays unique no matter how many elements share a value ({50,50,500,50,500} -> 3). This distinguishes benchmark 35 from min/max-search benchmarks, where ties make the returned index genuinely ambiguous — no duplicate-semantics decision is needed here.

DEFINED for the oracle but NOT reachable through the stock harness:
- n = 0: the oracle returns 0 (= books.size()); `int i = books.size()-1` narrows SIZE_MAX to -1 (implementation-defined, gcc 13.3 x86-64 gives -1 — measured). The harness cannot reach it: cpu.cc:72 divides by zero (measured SIGFPE, exit 136). Needs custom construction, and would simultaneously enter the unspecified not-found case below.

UNDERSPECIFIED (the only genuine semantic gap):
- no qualifying element (all pages >= 100): the oracle returns books.size() as an out-of-range sentinel (baseline.hpp:22); the prompt never states this. Structurally unreachable because of cpu.cc:72, so it cannot currently produce a false verdict.

Note on the scale axis: none of the above belong to it. small/medium/large is purely the cache-residency ladder 20 KiB / 2.5 MiB / 160 MiB.

benchmarks.budget_adjustment: The 10 s budget is NOT the binding constraint for this benchmark, and I did not adjust LARGE to approach it. First choice LARGE = 2^22 = 4194304, derived from memory feasibility and the cache hierarchy; MEASURED worst-case oracle 0.027194 s, i.e. 368x inside the budget (driver-faithful: 0.000001 s). I then probed UPWARD to check whether a larger LARGE was warranted: 2^23 = 8388608 measured 0.064214 s (comfortably fine), 2^24 = 16777216 was OOM-killed (exit 137, ~670 MB of Books on a contended 7775 MiB WSL2 VM). Adjusted choice: kept 2^22. Reason: at the measured 6.5 ns/element, filling the 10 s budget would need ~1.5e9 Books = ~62 GB of Book storage — memory-infeasible by three orders of magnitude — so the budget can never bind here. 2^23 buys no new regime (both are equally DRAM-bound) while doubling the per-try construction cost, which IS the real harness expense: validate() rebuilds the input 5 times (cpu.cc:67), at ~0.34-0.50 s per try at 2^22. LARGE is therefore memory- and harness-cost-bound, not time-budget-bound; the budget was measured against and satisfied with a 368x margin.

benchmarks.name: 36_search_check_if_array_contains_value
benchmarks.input_form: Two inputs: (1) `std::vector<int> x` of length n, values drawn by fillRand(input, -50, 50) -> integral branch `rand() % (max-min) + min` = rand()%100 - 50, i.e. values in [-50, 49] (max is EXCLUSIVE); (2) scalar `int target` drawn as `(rand() % 200) - 100`, i.e. [-100, 99] (cpu.cc:68), except try i==1 where `target = input[rand() % input.size()]`, a guaranteed hit at a uniformly random index (cpu.cc:66). Only ONE dimension: n = element count. No structure required: unsorted, duplicates allowed, no alignment, no power of two. Result is `bool`, widened to size_t at the call site and compared with exact equality (cpu.cc:74/77/81, utilities.hpp:483-485) — NO epsilon. The target scalar is NOT reachable from the enhanced-spec machinery: ENHANCED_FILL only controls the vector (cpu.cc:63); the target keeps coming from rand().
benchmarks.min_size: Operation: n >= 0 (the empty vector is a fully defined input; contains == false). HARNESS-FORCED floor: n >= 1. The floor is NOT a property of the operation, it is a driver defect: cpu.cc:66 executes `target = input[rand() % input.size()]` on every run (try i==1), which at n==0 is `rand() % 0` -> integer division by zero (SIGFPE) plus an out-of-range read on an empty vector. Empirically confirmed: thesis/results/cache/enhanced/spec_gate_report.jsonl:721/725/733 mark size 0 `baseline_incompatible` for three different patterns, while line 722 marks size 1 `pass`. Additional pattern-level floor: n >= 2 for the k-patterns duplicate_at / sorted_except_one / spike_at (enhanced-fill.hpp header contract: "validated in Python to k in [0, size-1] and size >= 2").
benchmarks.max_size: none forced by the operation or the harness. A soft ceiling follows from the enhanced stage's 60 s per-run timeout (config.yaml:613) combined with fillRand's cost, which dominates the oracle by ~40x: measured 12.5 s of validate() work under mpirun -np 4 at n=16,777,215, so roughly n <= 6e7 (240 MiB/rank) before the timeout becomes a real risk. LARGE at 2^24-1 sits well inside that.
benchmarks.special_conditions: None from the operation. Explicitly NOT required: sortedness (a binary-search candidate is simply wrong here), distinctness, power of two, any matrix/point/geometric form. The only conditions are the harness ones above (n >= 1; n >= 2 for k-patterns). Two domain facts that shape scale points instead: (a) a correct answer of `false` requires inspecting EVERY element, so any candidate that drops a tail or a chunk is only caught when n is NOT divisible by its block/thread/SIMD width -> all three scale points are chosen odd/prime; (b) with the fixed fill range [-50, 49] (only 100 distinct values) a PRESENT target is found after ~100 elements at any large n, so the O(n) cost — and the tail-dropping failure mode — materializes only on ABSENT targets (~50% of the 9 non-forced tries, since target is uniform on [-100,99] and half of that range cannot occur in x).
benchmarks.size_semantics: Element count of the single vector<int> x. TEST_SIZE at cpu.cc:58 is literally `std::vector<int> input(TEST_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:62), so -DENHANCED_TEST_SIZE=N gives exactly N ints = 4N bytes. Not a side length, not a point count, nothing derived (no nnz, no sparsity). Memory per process = 4N bytes; under mpi_ranks=4 every rank holds a full copy (the mpi prompt states "Every rank has a complete copy of x"), so 4 x 4N bytes across the run.
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle `correctContains` = `std::find(x.begin(), x.end(), target) != x.end()` (baseline.hpp:13-15). Worst case O(n) comparisons (target absent, or present only at index n-1); with early exit O(k) where k is the index of the first occurrence. Pure integer `==`, no arithmetic (so no overflow even on INT_MIN/INT_MAX inputs), no allocation, no preconditions. Memory traffic 4n bytes of pure streaming reads -> DRAM-bandwidth-bound once n exceeds the LLC. MEASURED serial throughput on the worst case: 16,777,215 elements in 0.0184 s = 9.1e8 elements/s (~3.6 GB/s).
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
The operation is an unordered membership test — a single linear scan over an unstructured int array. Its only parameter is n, and it has exactly two structural risk axes, neither of which is candidate-derived:

(1) TAIL/CHUNK COVERAGE. Answering `false` is only correct if every element was inspected. The failure mode of any partitioned implementation (thread chunks, SIMD blocks, rank slices) is a dropped remainder. Therefore every scale point is chosen ODD and indivisible by any plausible block width: 1021 is prime; 2^20-1 and 2^24-1 are odd and divisible by no power of two. A power-of-two size would let a 4/8/16-way split come out even and hide exactly the bug the scan is supposed to expose. (Contrast the fft family, where powers of two are mandatory; here they are actively harmful.)

(2) MEMORY-HIERARCHY REGIME. The scan is bandwidth-bound, so the physical scale axis is the cache hierarchy of the evaluation host (measured in-container: i7-12700H, L1d 48 KiB/core, L2 1.25 MiB/core, L3 24 MiB shared):
  - SMALL 1021 (4 KiB) — fits entirely in L1d; the scan is ~64 cache lines. Parallelisation is pure overhead here; this is the regime where boundary/tail handling and "did you even enter the loop" dominate, and where the driver's own default TEST_SIZE (1024, cpu.cc:58) sits — 1021 is the deliberately prime neighbour of it.
  - MEDIUM 1,048,575 (4 MiB) — above a single core's L2 (1.25 MiB), comfortably inside the 24 MiB shared L3. Streaming from L2/L3; chunk partitioning across 4 threads/ranks becomes meaningful and each thread's slice is itself cache-resident.
  - LARGE 16,777,215 (64 MiB) — 2.7x the shared L3, i.e. firmly in the DRAM regime, and 8x the driver's own timed DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE of 1<<21 = 2,097,152 (8 MiB, drivers/problem-sizes.json:326). This is where a per-element synchronisation or an accidental O(n^2) becomes unmissable.

No candidate code was consulted for any of these numbers. The three points come from the cache boundaries of the host, the indivisibility argument, and the budget check below.

benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: no. The prompt (serial/omp/mpi, thesis/prompts/generation-prompts-thesis.json) fully determines the answer for every n >= 0: "Return true if the vector x contains the value `target`. Return false otherwise." There is no unstated precondition, no tie-breaking, no tolerance, and no empty-input ambiguity (the empty vector unambiguously contains nothing). A sortedness or minimum-size sentence must NOT be added — x is explicitly unsorted and a restriction would legitimise binary search. The n==0 problem is a driver defect (cpu.cc:66), not a prompt gap, so it must be fixed in the driver or excluded by the gate, never written into the prompt.
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: no — for the vector. x is a plain std::vector<int> filled at a single canonical call site (cpu.cc:63, ENHANCED_FILL(input, -50, 50)); the generic size + fill-pattern machinery covers it completely and the gate confirms it (all non-zero sizes pass). CAVEAT that belongs in the table: the second, discriminating input — `target` — lies OUTSIDE the spec schema. It is drawn from rand() at cpu.cc:66/68 regardless of the chosen pattern, so the two sharpest cases for this operation, "target present only at index n-1" (the tail-dropping detector) and "target present only at index 0" (early-exit detector), cannot be requested; index n-1 is reached only by luck at try i==1, with probability 1/n. Patterns do give indirect control: extreme_values (INT_MIN/INT_MAX) guarantees "absent" for all 9 non-forced tries, all_zeros/all_same makes presence a 1/200 event, and try i==1 always guarantees one hit. Controlling the target axis directly would require a benchmark-specific construction the current schema cannot express.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
Mathematically DEFINED for this operation (scale axis kept separate):
1. n = 0, empty vector -> false. Defined and unambiguous from the prompt, but NOT executable in the current harness (cpu.cc:66 SIGFPE); gate says baseline_incompatible (spec_gate_report.jsonl:721/725/733). Exclude until the driver is fixed.
2. n = 1 -> single element; target equal or not. Defined AND harness-safe (rand()%1 == 0, input[0] valid); gate line 722 passes. Not usable with k-patterns (need n >= 2).
3. All elements identical (all_zeros / all_same) -> result = (target == that value); also the maximal-duplicate case.
4. Target absent -> the worst case and the only branch that forces a full scan; produced whenever the drawn target falls outside [-50,49] (~50% of the 9 non-forced tries), and guaranteed for every non-forced try under extreme_values.
5. Target present exactly once at index 0 -> immediate early exit; defined, not directly constructible (target axis is outside the spec schema).
6. Target present exactly once at index n-1 -> worst-case found; the single strongest discriminator for chunked/parallel searches that drop a tail. Defined, but only reachable with probability 1/n via try i==1.
7. Target present many times -> defined and NOT ambiguous: `contains` returns bool, so duplicates and ordering are irrelevant. Unlike the index-returning search benchmarks there is no tie-breaking semantics that duplicates could violate — duplicate_at(k) is a weak pattern here.
8. INT_MIN / INT_MAX elements (extreme_values) -> defined; the oracle performs no arithmetic, only ==, so nothing can overflow.
Not degenerate but worth recording: `ascending` at this call site is `-50 + (i % 101)`, a ramp that REPEATS with period 101, so for n > 101 the array is NOT globally sorted — the pattern therefore does not accidentally reward a (wrong) binary-search candidate at medium/large n, but it does at n <= 101.

benchmarks.name: 37_search_find_the_closest_number_to_pi
benchmarks.input_form: One dense 1-D `std::vector<double> x` of length n. Only one dimension: n = number of elements. Values are arbitrary finite doubles; the driver's validation call site draws them uniformly from [100.0, 1000.0] and then forces exactly one uniformly chosen index to 10.0 (cpu.cc:56-58). The timing context uses fillRand over [-10000.0, 10000.0] (cpu.cc:26). Output is a single `size_t` index, compared for EXACT equality (no epsilon).
benchmarks.min_size: 1 (n >= 1). Mathematically: argmin over an empty set is undefined. In code: the oracle reads `x[0]` unconditionally before the loop (baseline.hpp:13), so n == 0 is an out-of-bounds read; and the driver evaluates `rand() % TEST_SIZE` (cpu.cc:58), which at TEST_SIZE == 0 is integer division by zero — MEASURED: the probe binary died with SIGFPE, exit 136. n == 1 is fully defined (oracle returns 0; MEASURED).
benchmarks.max_size: Forced, 16777216 (2^24). Not by the 10 s oracle budget (which is unreachable here) but by the pipeline itself: enhanced_tests run_timeout_seconds = 60 (config.yaml:613) covers the WHOLE 10-try validate(), whose cost is dominated by fillRand's one rand() per element, not by the oracle. MEASURED serial validate() totals: 2^24 -> 23.0 s (fill 21.3 s, oracle+candidate 1.2 s); 2^25 -> 31.2 s; 2^26 -> 123.3 s, i.e. over the 60 s timeout by itself. A second, harder ceiling is memory: the MPI prompt states every rank holds a complete copy of x, so at mpi_ranks = 4 (config.yaml:604) the input alone costs 32*n bytes in a container with 7775 MiB total; 2^28 (2 GiB/copy) was OOM-killed / did not complete in 10 minutes even serially.
benchmarks.special_conditions: No power-of-two, sortedness, sign or magnitude requirement — any finite double vector of length >= 1 is a valid input. The one real precondition is UNIQUENESS OF THE ARGMIN: grading is exact index equality (cpu.cc:69 -> utilities.hpp:483-485, `expected == got`, no epsilon) while neither the prompt nor the oracle documents a tie-break; the oracle silently returns the FIRST minimizing index (strict `<`, baseline.hpp:16). Any input whose argmin set has more than one element is therefore mathematically ambiguous but graded as if it had one answer. Second precondition: all values finite — MEASURED, a NaN at index 0 makes every later `diff < min` false and the oracle returns 0 while the true argmin is elsewhere (silently wrong reference, and reportAndCompareScalar's finiteness guard only inspects the returned size_t, so it cannot catch this).
benchmarks.size_semantics: Element count of a single 1-D double vector. TEST_SIZE is used directly as the vector length (`std::vector<double> input(TEST_SIZE)`, cpu.cc:56) — it is NOT a matrix side length and nothing (no nnz, no point count) is derived from it. Memory footprint is exactly 8*n bytes per copy; the timing context allocates one copy of DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE (cpu.cc:32), validate() allocates a fresh copy per try (10 tries), and the MPI model holds one full copy per rank (prompt: "Every rank has a complete copy of x"), so 4 ranks cost 32*n bytes of input.
benchmarks.complexity: Theta(n) time, O(1) extra space; exactly n-1 comparisons and n sequential 8-byte reads, single pass, no allocation. Streaming argmin -> DRAM-bandwidth bound once n exceeds the last-level cache. MEASURED throughput ~1.6e8-3.0e8 elements/s in the pipeline container.
benchmarks.domain_rationale: min_size = 1 follows from the operation (argmin over an empty set is undefined) and is independently forced by the oracle's unconditional x[0] read and the driver's rand() % TEST_SIZE. The scale ladder is derived purely from the operation's complexity class: the kernel is a single Theta(n) streaming pass with O(1) state, so it has NO algorithmic phase change — the only thing that varies with n is which level of the memory hierarchy feeds the stream, plus (for omp/mpi) the ratio of fixed parallel-launch overhead to the scan. The ladder therefore walks the memory hierarchy in equal geometric steps of 2^7 = 128x: SMALL 2^10 = 8 KiB is L1d-resident (typical L1d 32-48 KiB), where a scan costs 5 us and OpenMP team fork / MPI Bcast+Allreduce latency dominates the actual work — the regime in which a parallel implementation can only lose; MEDIUM 2^17 = 1 MiB sits at the L2 / small-LLC tier, past every private L1 but still cache-served (0.6 ms); LARGE 2^24 = 128 MiB is far beyond any LLC, so the scan runs at DRAM bandwidth (0.107 s), which is the asymptotic regime the operation actually lives in. LARGE is additionally the largest point that the driver's own 10-try validate() can complete inside the pipeline's 60 s per-run timeout with 4 MPI ranks each holding a full copy. No candidate code was inspected or considered.

DEFINED ONLY UNDER A TIE-BREAK CONVENTION, i.e. currently ambiguous: all values equal (all_zeros / all_same) — MEASURED, all_zeros plus the call site's forced 10.0 still leaves 15 of 16 minimizers because |0-PI| < |10-PI|, oracle returns 0; all_same with an overridden range whose midpoint beats 10.0 (range 0..6 -> 3.0) — MEASURED 15 minimizers; extreme_values (+/-DBL_MAX alternating) — MEASURED |lowest()-PI| == |max()-PI| exactly, so WITHOUT the forced 10.0 all n elements tie (with it, 10.0 wins uniquely, so this pattern is safe at the stock call site only by accident); explicit_values with a repeated near-PI entry — MEASURED 4 of 16 minimizers via the real ENHANCED_FILL macro path; two DISTINCT values symmetric about PI (3.0 and 2*PI-3.0) — MEASURED 2 minimizers, which proves a "no duplicate values" restriction would NOT be sufficient. UNDEFINED, must never be generated: n == 0 (argmin over the empty set; oracle reads x[0]; driver SIGFPEs on rand() % 0 — MEASURED exit 136); any NaN in x (oracle skips NaNs and returns 0 if x[0] is NaN — MEASURED, silently wrong reference).
benchmarks.pending_fix: YES — this row is PROVISIONAL pending the argmin tie-break semantics decision. The prompt specifies no tie-break, the oracle silently implements first-minimum (baseline.hpp:16), and grading is exact index equality (utilities.hpp:483-485). Until that is resolved (prompt sentence added, or the comparison/oracle changed, or the spec generator forbidden from emitting tie-inducing fills at this call site), enhanced fill patterns all_zeros(1), explicit_values(10) with a repeated near-PI value, and all_same(2)/alternating(5)/extreme_values(6) under an ENHANCED_FILL_LO/HI range override can produce mathematically ambiguous inputs, and a CORRECT parallel implementation (e.g. an OpenMP reduction or MPI MINLOC that keeps the last rather than the first minimizer) would be graded FAIL for a non-error. benchmarks.name: 38_search_find_the_first_even_number
benchmarks.input_form: One 1-D container: `std::vector<int> x` of length n. Exactly one dimension (n); no shape derivation, no second array, no scalar parameter. Values at the driver's fill site are uniform integers in [1, 99] (`fillRand(x, 1, 100)` -> `rand() % (100-1) + 1`); an enhanced spec may replace the pattern and, via `value_range`, the [lo,hi] bounds, so the value domain of a spec is all of `int` including 0 and negatives. Output: a single `size_t` index, compared with EXACT equality (`reportAndCompareScalar`, no epsilon). The oracle is total: it has no precondition on n or on the values.
benchmarks.min_size: Operation-level: 0 (n = 0 is mathematically defined -> return 0). Currently FORCED to 20 by the driver: `validate()` writes `x[0..19]` unconditionally on try i == 1 while `x` has only TEST_SIZE elements, so every size 0..19 is a heap-buffer-overflow (size 0 a SEGV). Measured with ASan: sizes 0, 1, 2, 7, 19 all abort; 20 and 21 are clean. min_size = 20 until the guard fix lands, 0 afterwards.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — FORCED by the harness, not by the operation: `max_spec_size: 4096` (thesis/config/config.yaml:572), enforced in `validate_spec` (thesis/enhanced_tests/specs.py:293-294, spec rejected with "size N exceeds max_spec_size 4096"). The operation itself has no upper bound and the 10 s runtime budget would only bind around n ~ 4.5e9 (see measurement), so the config cap binds ~10^6 times earlier than the budget.
benchmarks.special_conditions: None from the operation. No power of two, no sortedness, no minimum element count, no structural/matrix validity, no positivity, no uniqueness. The oracle `correctFindFirstEven` is defined on every `std::vector<int>` of every length, including empty. The only real conditions are harness-imposed: (a) n >= 20 today because of the unconditional 20-element write in `validate()` (driver bug, see pending_fix), and (b) n <= 4096 from `max_spec_size`. Note also that the SEPARATE perf path (`reset()`, cpu.cc:33-36) computes `rand() % (3*S/4 - S/4)` and would divide by zero for DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE < 2; the enhanced stage builds with `-DDRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE=(1<<4)`, so this never fires there, but it is a second latent floor in the same file.
benchmarks.size_semantics: Direct element count. TEST_SIZE == the number of `int` elements in the single input vector (`std::vector<int> x(TEST_SIZE);`, cpu.cc:68). Nothing is derived from it — no side length, no nnz, no power-of-two constraint. Memory footprint is exactly 4n bytes; at the cap (4096) that is 16 KiB, i.e. the entire in-domain size range is L1-resident.
benchmarks.complexity: Oracle: Theta(k) where k = index of the first even element, k <= n. Worst case Theta(n) (no even element anywhere -> full scan, returns n); best case Theta(1) (x[0] even); expected O(1/p_even) = O(1) under the driver's own random fill (even density 49/99 -> E[k] ~ 1.02, and the three measured random-fill runs returned k = 1, 2, 0). Auxiliary space O(1). Consequence for sizing: n does NOT control oracle cost under the default fill — only the all-odd / late-first-even inputs make the scale axis visible at all.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
Derived from the operation + the specified domain + the cap, never from candidate code.

min_size: the operation is total (n = 0 returns 0), so there is no mathematical floor; the floor of 20 is purely the driver's unconditional `x[0..19]` write and is documented as such, not smuggled in as an operation property.

max_size / LARGE: the operation is an early-exit linear scan, so the only cost-relevant quantity is the position of the first match. Its in-domain worst case (all elements odd -> full O(n) scan) measures 3.4 us at n = 4096, i.e. ~2.9e6x below the 10 s budget. The budget is therefore non-binding; the binding constraint is `max_spec_size: 4096`. LARGE = 4096 is the largest expressible size and is taken for exactly that reason.

Scale ladder 21 -> 1024 -> 4096. Because the whole domain is L1-resident (<= 16 KiB), the memory hierarchy gives no scale axis here. The axis that the operation and the prompt-specified parallelism DO give is n relative to the decomposition width p (config.yaml:603-604 fixes omp_threads = 4 and mpi_ranks = 4 for the enhanced stage; the mpi prompt states every rank holds a complete copy of x and partitions the index range):
- SMALL = 21: the smallest size the driver can run without corrupting memory (20), plus one so that n is odd. n/p = 5 remainder 1, so both the 4-way and the 8-way index split have a ragged tail. This is the regime where n is comparable to p and the tail chunk is where a first-match reduction goes wrong.
- MEDIUM = 1024: the driver's own authored TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:60) — the size this benchmark was written and calibrated at. It is a power of two and divides evenly by 4, so the decomposition is uniform and the only discriminating variable left is the position of the first match, not the tail. Deliberate contrast to SMALL.
- LARGE = 4096: the harness cap; 4x the authored default; chunk size at p = 4 is 1024, which is the smallest first-match index that leaves rank/thread 0 with no match at all.
The overlap with other 1-D benchmarks at 1024/4096 is not convenience: 1024 is THIS driver's authored constant and 4096 is the global spec cap; both follow from the sources.
benchmarks.prompt_restriction_needed: yes: "If x contains no even number, return x.size()."
benchmarks.custom_input_construction_needed: yes — a "first even element at index k" construction. No pattern in drivers/cpp/enhanced-fill.hpp can place the first even element at an index > 63 when n > 64: explicit_values is capped at 64 values (explicit_values_max_size, config.yaml:586) and fills CYCLICALLY (`x[i] = values[i % count]`, enhanced-fill.hpp:216-218), so its first even repeats at least every 64 elements; all_same makes every element identical; ascending/descending/alternating put an even within the first two elements for any ordinary range; and the three k-patterns cannot force parity at k — duplicate_at copies a random neighbour, sorted_except_one only swaps ramp values, and spike_at writes `numeric_limits<int>::max()/2` = 1073741823, which is ODD. That missing case is precisely the one that separates a correct cross-chunk first-match reduction from one that mishandles the "no match in my chunk" sentinel: at LARGE = 4096 with p = 4 the match must sit at index >= 1024 to leave chunk 0 empty. Everything else (all-odd, all-even, first-at-0, negatives, extremes) is expressible with the existing library.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
Mathematically DEFINED for this operation (scale axis is separate):
- n = 0: defined. No even number exists, oracle returns `x.size()` = 0. Currently SEGV in the driver (measured).
- n = 1: defined. Returns 0 if x[0] even, else 1. Currently heap-buffer-overflow (measured).
- All elements odd (no even at all, any n): defined, oracle returns n. THE central degenerate case: the "not found" answer is n, not -1 and not npos, and the prompt never says so. Expressible today as all_same with `value_range` [1,101] (enhancedMidValue -> 51, odd) — verified: the harness at n = 21/1024/4096 returned 21/1024/4096.
- All elements even, and the all_zeros pattern: defined, returns 0 (0 is even).
- x[0] even: returns 0 (lower boundary of the answer range).
- Only x[n-1] even: returns n-1 (upper interior boundary; forces the full scan). NOT expressible with the current pattern library for n > 64 — see custom_input_construction_needed.
- Negative values (reachable via a negative `value_range`; `fillRand(x,-100,100)` yields [-100, 99]): -4 is even, -3 is odd. The oracle's `x[i] % 2 == 0` is correct for negatives because C++ `%` truncates toward zero; an implementation testing `x[i] % 2 == 1` is wrong on every negative odd value. A genuine value-domain degenerate case, independent of n.
- extreme_values pattern: INT_MIN at index 0 is even -> returns 0. `INT_MIN % 2` is well defined (only `INT_MIN / -1` / `INT_MIN % -1` are UB).
Sizes 0 and 1 are listed here, as degenerate cases, and are NOT the reason for the size floor — the floor is the driver bug.

benchmarks.name: 39_search_xor_contains
benchmarks.input_form: Triple (x, y, val) with x, y integer sequences and val a scalar int; the oracle computes (val in x) XOR (val in y). Mathematically |x| and |y| are independent (the prompt's own example uses |x|=5, |y|=6). The driver restricts to |x| = |y| = n = TEST_SIZE (cpu.cc:69-70); relevant dimensions are therefore the single parameter n, with total input 2n ints = 8n bytes. Values: fillRand(x,-100,100) / fillRand(y,-100,100) at the validate call site, i.e. uniform over the c = 200 integers [-100, 99] (utilities.hpp:144-160: rand() % (max-min) + min). val = rand() % 200 - 100, i.e. uniform over the same 200 values, drawn at cpu.cc:73 INDEPENDENTLY of the fill and NOT steerable by any ENHANCED_* knob. benchmark_shapes.json:350 confirms fill_sites=2, elements_per_site=["n","n"], total "n + n", explicit_values_supported=false.
benchmarks.min_size: 0 mathematically (empty x and empty y: membership is false in both, false XOR false = false; std::find on an empty range is well defined). PRACTICALLY 1 today: the driver crashes at n=0 — cpu.cc:75-76 evaluates rand() % x.size() with x.size()==0. MEASURED with a CORRECT candidate and -DENHANCED_TEST_SIZE=0: "Illegal instruction (core dumped)", exit 132, no output at all. So min_size = 0 (operation) / 1 (driver, until the size-0 guard is added). This is NOT a size floor of the operation — see pending_fix.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — forced by the harness. config.yaml:572 sets stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096 and specs.py:293-294 rejects any spec above it. The operation itself has no upper bound, and neither does the 10 s budget: MEASURED worst-case throughput is 7.5e8 elements/s, so 10 s corresponds to n ~ 3.8e9 per vector (2n = 7.5e9 ints = 30 GB) — about 920,000x the harness cap and unallocatable on this host (7 GB RAM in the container).
benchmarks.special_conditions: No structural precondition at all: no power of two, no sortedness, no minimum element count, no matrix form, no distinctness. Any n >= 0 and any int values are a valid instance. The one non-obvious, genuinely operation-derived condition is STATISTICAL, and it governs whether the benchmark discriminates: with uniform fill over c distinct values, P(val absent from one vector) = (1 - 1/c)^n ~ e^(-n/c), so P(oracle == true) = 2p(1-p) is maximal at n = c*ln2 and collapses to 0 for n >> c. At the driver's call-site range c = 200 the answer saturates at the constant false for n >~ 500. MEASURED over the driver's exact unseeded rand() stream (#true out of the 10 validate iterations): n=1,2,3 -> 0; n=7 -> 1; n=16 -> 1; n=32 -> 2; n=64 -> 4; n=128 -> 6; n=200 -> 5; n=256 -> 5; n=384 -> 1; n=512 -> 2; n=1024 -> 0; n=2048 -> 0; n=4096 -> 0. Consequence, verified end-to-end against the real driver with a deliberately wrong `return false;` candidate: it PASSES at the correctness-stage default (DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE=(1<<8), TEST_SIZE=1024) and at the enhanced default, PASSES at ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE 1, 2, 1024 and 4096, and only FAILS at 7, 16 and 256. The scale points therefore have to be placed against c, not chosen for roundness.
benchmarks.size_semantics: TEST_SIZE = n = the element count of EACH of the two vectors, not a combined total and not a side length. cpu.cc:69-70 allocates x(TEST_SIZE) and y(TEST_SIZE); the total element count is 2n and the memory footprint 8n bytes. benchmark_shapes.json:350 records total_elements = "n + n" with two fill sites. ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE overrides only validate()'s TEST_SIZE (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79 via cpu.cc:61); init()'s vectors stay at DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE, which is (1<<8) in the correctness stage (tools.py:44) and (1<<4) in the enhanced stage (run_enhanced_tests.py:322). DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE=(1<<21) in problem-sizes.json:353-356 is the performance-stage size only and never reaches validate().
benchmarks.complexity: Worst case Theta(|x| + |y|) = Theta(2n) element comparisons, i.e. linear in n; O(1) auxiliary space. baseline.hpp:16-19 is two std::find calls followed by a bitwise XOR of the two bools. std::find EARLY-EXITS, so the realised cost is O(i_x + i_y) where i is the index of the first occurrence (or the full length when val is absent). Best case O(1). This early exit is why the driver-faithful and the worst-case timings differ by an order of magnitude at the same n, and it is the reason a size-based runtime budget is nearly meaningless here.
benchmarks.domain_rationale: The scale axis is placed against the only quantity that changes the operation's behaviour, namely n relative to the fill-range cardinality c = 200 fixed at cpu.cc:71-72, plus the hard harness cap. SMALL = 16: n << c, so P(absent per vector) = (199/200)^16 = 0.923 and the "neither" plus one-sided branches dominate (measured 1/10 true). 16 is also the first scale point strictly above the whole static base set {0,1,2,7} (config.yaml:562), it is exactly one 64-byte cache line of ints per vector, exactly one AVX-512 int lane group / two AVX2 groups, and the smallest n at which a chunked or thread-parallel scan has more than a single chunk. MEDIUM = 128: this is the outcome-balanced regime. The analytic maximum of P(true) sits at n* = c*ln2 = 139; 128 is the nearest power of two, with P(absent) = 0.5264 and P(true) = 0.4986, essentially the theoretical ceiling of 0.5, and it MEASURED the highest outcome diversity of the whole sweep (6/10 true). It is the one scale point at which all four semantic outcomes (in-x-only, in-y-only, both, neither) occur with comparable frequency, so it is the point that actually tests the XOR rather than the scan. LARGE = 4096: the maximum size the enhanced-test spec validator accepts (max_spec_size, config.yaml:572, enforced specs.py:293-294). 2*4096*4 B = 32 KiB, an L1D-sized working set, so it is the largest genuine streaming scan the stage can express. At the call-site range its outcome saturates to the constant false (P(true) = 1.2e-9, measured 0/10), so this point tests the linear scan, the OpenMP decomposition and the MPI rank-0 reduction rather than the outcome logic; to keep it outcome-discriminating a spec must widen the fill range to c ~ 1.44*n, e.g. value_range [-100, 5800) which MEASURES P(absent) = 0.4994 and yields 2/10 true. The ladder is 16 / 128 / 4096, deliberately non-geometric: each point is justified by a distinct property of the operation (sub-c absence regime / n ~ c*ln2 balance point / harness ceiling), not by a ratio. None of it is derived from any observed candidate code.

benchmarks.degenerate_cases: Mathematically DEFINED degenerate inputs for this operation: (1) n = 0, both vectors empty -> false XOR false = false. Defined, but currently a hard driver crash (measured exit 132) — see pending_fix. (2) n = 1 -> defined; all four outcomes reachable in principle, measured 0/10 true in the driver's stream because P(true) = 0.01. (3) |x| != |y|, including exactly one empty -> defined by the operation and shown in the prompt's own example (5 vs 6 elements), but NOT expressible through the driver, which always builds both at TEST_SIZE. (4) all values equal (all_zeros / all_same) -> defined; oracle is false for EVERY val because the two fill sites receive identical content. (5) val absent from both -> defined, result false; this is the runtime worst case (full 2n scan). (6) val present in both -> defined, result false; the driver forces exactly this at i == 1 (cpu.cc:74-77), which is the only planted case it has. (7) val duplicated many times inside one vector -> defined; the operation is membership, not multiplicity, and the prompt example already pins this down (y = [3,4,4,1,1,7], val = 1 appears twice in y and once in x -> both -> false). (8) extreme_values fill (INT_MIN / INT_MAX alternating) -> defined; val is always in [-100, 99] so it is present in neither -> false. NOT degenerate but often confused with it: the "answer saturates to false" behaviour at large n is a SCALE-axis property, not a degenerate input.

benchmarks.name: 40_sort_sort_an_array_of_complex_numbers_by_magnitude
benchmarks.input_form: One 1-D vector `x` of `n` `std::complex<double>`, assembled from TWO independent `double` fill sites `real[]` and `imag[]`, each of length n and each drawn from [-100.0, 100.0] (cpu.cc:59, 68-69, 73-76). Output = the same multiset permuted into non-decreasing |x| (in place). Only ONE dimension is relevant: the element count n. No matrix, no side length, no derived nnz. Shape record: `total_elements = "n + n"`, `fill_sites = 2` (benchmark_shapes.json:360-369).
benchmarks.min_size: 0 (no mathematical floor). Sorting is total on every n >= 0; MEASURED: the oracle runs clean at n=0 (returns size 0) and n=1 (identity). Caveat, not a floor: at n<=1 `validate()` is vacuous (the element-wise loop, cpu.cc:87-92, has 0 or 1 trivially matching entries), and the harness rejects n<2 for the k-patterns duplicate_at/sorted_except_one/spike_at (specs.py:322-326). The static base set already covers 0/1/2/7 (config.yaml:562), so the scale axis below deliberately starts above them.
benchmarks.max_size: 4096 — HARNESS-FORCED, not operation-forced. `stages.enhanced_tests.max_spec_size: 4096` (config.yaml:572) is enforced by spec validation (`size %s exceeds max_spec_size %s`, specs.py:293-294). The operation itself has no upper bound, and the 10 s runtime budget is NOT the binding constraint here: MEASURED serial-oracle medians 4.48 s at n=2^21 and 9.51 s at n=2^22, i.e. the budget would allow ~2.1e6 elements, ~512x the harness cap.
benchmarks.special_conditions:
NO size condition: no power-of-two requirement, no minimum element count, no divisibility requirement from the operation itself. The genuine preconditions are on VALUES, and they come from the graded task, not from the oracle:
(1) DISTINCT MAGNITUDES. `validate()` compares the two sorted vectors ELEMENT-WISE (cpu.cc:87-92, eps 1e-6). Sorting by magnitude does not define a unique output sequence when two elements share a magnitude but differ in value, so the graded answer is only well-defined on tie-free inputs. MEASURED at n=1024: random fill produces 0 exact magnitude ties, but the enhanced patterns ascending/descending/sorted_except_one produce 267 ambiguous adjacent tie pairs and alternating/extreme_values produce 1023 (i.e. one single tie class over the whole array). MEASURED counter-example at n=8 (alternating): two runs of the SAME oracle on two equally legal input orders both satisfy `is_sorted` by magnitude yet fail the driver's element-wise check.
(2) FINITE MAGNITUDE. |Re|, |Im| must stay small enough that std::abs(x) does not overflow. MEASURED: the extreme_values pattern (real=imag=+/-DBL_MAX) yields |x| = inf for every element, the comparator degenerates to "all equivalent", and the driver's element diff is inf > 1e-6.
(3) NO NaN COMPONENT (a NaN makes `abs(a)<abs(b)` an inconsistent comparator -> std::sort UB). Not reachable from any current fill pattern; listed for completeness. spike_at is safe: (DBL_MAX/2)*sqrt(2) = 1.27e308 < DBL_MAX.
The stock range [-100,100] with random fill satisfies (1)-(3).
benchmarks.size_semantics: The size number is the ELEMENT COUNT n of the complex vector — nothing is derived from it. Perf path: `ctx->x.resize(DRIVER_PROBLEM_SIZE)` (cpu.cc:40). Validation path: `TEST_SIZE = ENHANCED_TEST_SIZE_DEFAULT(1024)` (cpu.cc:57), overridden by `-DENHANCED_TEST_SIZE=<n>` (enhanced-fill.hpp:75-79). One spec `size = n` allocates 2n doubles (the two fill sites) + 2n complex (correct + test) = 48 bytes/element in validate().
benchmarks.complexity: Theta(n log n) comparisons (libstdc++ introsort behind `std::sort`, baseline.hpp:12-14), Theta(1) extra space (in place, Theta(log n) recursion). The constant is dominated by the comparator, not by memory: every comparison evaluates `std::abs` on BOTH operands, i.e. 2 * Theta(n log n) `hypot()` calls. MEASURED cost per hypot ~40 ns (derived from 9.5 s / (2 * 2^22 * 22) at n=2^22), which is why this oracle is ~20x slower per element than a plain double sort.
benchmarks.domain_rationale:
All three points are derived from the operation (comparison sort of n complex<double> by magnitude), its Theta(n log n) comparator-bound cost, the cache footprint of 16 bytes/element, the parallelism models named in the prompt, and the harness ceiling — never from candidate code.

SMALL = 64. libstdc++ `std::sort` performs ONLY insertion sort while `last-first <= _S_threshold (16)`; 64 is the first power-of-two size at which introsort actually partitions recursively (log2 64 = 6 levels, 2 partition levels before the base case), so the real algorithm under test is exercised rather than its base case. It is also the smallest size that gives every unit of the stage's fixed 4-way parallel launch (`enhanced_launch: omp_threads 4 / mpi_ranks 4`, config.yaml:602-604) a non-degenerate 16-element sub-problem. Footprint 1 KiB -> fully L1-resident, so the measurement isolates comparator cost. It sits strictly above the static base set 0/1/2/7.

MEDIUM = 1024. ~1.0e4 comparisons (2.0e4 hypot calls): two orders of magnitude more comparator work than SMALL, enough that all three introsort phases matter (quicksort partitions, heapsort fallback at depth 2*log2 n = 20, final insertion pass over <=16 runs). Footprint 16 KiB, still L1-resident, so MEDIUM isolates the ALGORITHMIC step from the memory step. It is additionally the driver's own baked-in `TEST_SIZE` (cpu.cc:57), so the enhanced result at this size is directly comparable with every stock correctness run.

LARGE = 4093. Footprint 65.5 KiB — the first scale point that EXCEEDS a typical 32-48 KiB L1d, so partition passes start streaming from L2 and the memory behaviour of a candidate's partition/merge strategy becomes visible; ~4.9e4 comparisons. 4093 rather than 4096: it is prime, hence divisible by none of the plausible thread/rank counts (2/4/8/16), which forces the remainder path of ANY decomposition — a property of the omp/mpi task statements themselves ("Use OpenMP/MPI to sort in parallel"), not of any observed implementation. It sits at 99.93 % of the harness ceiling max_spec_size = 4096, so it is the largest expressible scale point while still being non-divisible.

Why not larger: `max_spec_size = 4096` (config.yaml:572) hard-rejects bigger specs. Absent that cap, the 10 s budget would put LARGE at 2^21 = 2,097,152 (MEASURED 4.48 s; 2^22 measured 9.51 s = 95 % of budget, rejected; 2^24 measured 82.9 s).

Note on shared sizes: 64/1024/4093 will resemble other 1-D element-count benchmarks. That follows from the operation class (1-D, element-count-parameterised, cache-hierarchy-driven scale points under a 4096 cap), not from convenience; the specific justification for each point above is magnitude-sort-specific (introsort threshold, hypot-bound comparator, 16 B/element footprint).

benchmarks.degenerate_cases:
DEFINED for this operation (mathematically well-posed, and the oracle is in-domain):
- n = 0 — empty sequence sorts to the empty sequence. MEASURED: oracle returns, size 0. Note the driver's grading is then VACUOUS (empty comparison loop), so it is a crash/robustness case, not a correctness case.
- n = 1 — identity. MEASURED: oracle returns the single element unchanged.
- n = 2 — smallest genuine comparison.
- ALL ELEMENTS IDENTICAL (all_zeros, all_same; note enhancedMidValue(-100,100) = 0, so all_same == all_zeros here) — well-posed AND unambiguous under element-wise grading, because every legal permutation is element-wise identical. MEASURED: 0 ambiguous tie pairs at n=64 and n=1024.
- EXACT DUPLICATE ELEMENTS (duplicate_at: both sites duplicate index k, so x[k] == x[k+1] exactly) — benign for the same reason. MEASURED: 0 ambiguous tie pairs.
- ZERO ELEMENT (0+0i) mixed with non-zero — |0| = 0 sorts first; defined.
- ONE HUGE FINITE OUTLIER (spike_at: |x[k]| = (DBL_MAX/2)*sqrt(2) = 1.27e308 < DBL_MAX) — defined and finite. MEASURED: 0 ambiguous tie pairs.
DEFINED AS A MULTISET BUT NOT AS A SEQUENCE (the operation is well-posed, the driver's element-wise grading is NOT):
- EQUAL MAGNITUDES, DIFFERENT VALUES. alternating (only two values, both |.| = 141.421) and, via +/- symmetry of the ramp, ascending / descending / sorted_except_one. MEASURED ambiguous adjacent tie pairs: alternating 63 (n=64) / 1023 (n=1024); ascending/descending/sorted_except_one 16 (n=64) / 267 (n=1024). MEASURED false negative at n=8 alternating: the oracle on x and on reverse(x) both produce `is_sorted`-by-magnitude output, yet the driver's element-wise check returns false.
OUTSIDE THE WELL-POSED DOMAIN:
- MAGNITUDE OVERFLOW. extreme_values (real = imag = +/-DBL_MAX) -> |x| = inf for every element. MEASURED: magnitudes_all_finite = 0; comparator degenerates to "all equivalent"; element diff = inf > 1e-6. std::sort does not misbehave (the ordering is still a valid strict weak ordering), but the graded answer is arbitrary.
- NaN COMPONENTS — would make the comparator inconsistent (std::sort UB). Not producible by any current pattern in this driver; excluded by construction.
